BACKLOG — future improvements to implement when ready
======================================================


[OPEN 2026-08-26 -- opus review of batch-82, MEDIUM] THE 0.85 NWS CEILING IS
  SKIPPED ENTIRELY AT days_out=0
Priority: Medium -- live today for `between` same-day markets, and structural
  for any future same-day fit. Not urgent, but it is a real uncapped weight on
  the live pricing path.
Files: weather_markets.py (_nws_days_out_scale)

Problem:
  _nws_days_out_scale's first guard is
  `if w_nws == 0.0 or days_out <= 0: return weights`. That early return skips
  the DECAY (correct, and batch-82 re-derived why) but it also skips
  `min(w_nws * scale, 0.85)` -- the ceiling that exists "to prevent
  over-concentration when calibrated nws weight is very high".

  Measured 2026-08-26 with weights {ens .05, clim .02, nws .93}:
    d=0 -> nws 0.9300   (verbatim, uncapped)
    d=1 -> nws 0.8500   (capped)
    d=2 -> nws 0.8370
  This is live right now: data/condition_weights.json's `between` entry has
  nws 0.903283623166536, so a same-day `between` market priced through the
  ensemble path gets the full 0.903.

  batch-82 makes it worse in kind, not degree. A SAME-DAY-fitted weight set is
  by construction only ever read at days_out<=0, so it can never flow through
  the capped path in ANY context -- a permanent exemption rather than a
  horizon-specific one. Reachable, not theoretical: 4 of _best_weights' 200
  fixed seed-42 simplex samples have nws > 0.85.

  batch-82 deliberately did not fix it. Applying the cap at d=0 changes live
  same-day `between` pricing (0.903 -> 0.85), and that batch shipped on the
  explicit basis of being a behavioural no-op. Current behaviour is pinned by
  tests/test_weather_markets.py::TestNwsDaysOutScaleAtDayZero::
  test_day_zero_also_skips_the_085_nws_ceiling so it cannot drift unnoticed.

  Whoever picks this up: measure the `between` same-day population before
  changing it, and note that the cap and the decay are separable -- applying
  `min(w_nws, 0.85)` at d=0 without any scale factor is the narrow fix.


[OPEN 2026-08-26 -- opus review of batch-82, MEDIUM] A GRADUATED SAME-DAY FIT
  CAN NEVER UN-GRADUATE, AND IT OUTRANKS THE MULTI-DAY TIER
Priority: Medium -- inert until the first same-day tier clears its floor
  (~60 D+0 rows per condition, roughly 2-3 months at August 2026 accrual).
  Worth deciding BEFORE that happens rather than after.
Files: calibration.py (_preserve_hand_tuned_weights, calibrate_and_save),
  weather_markets.py (_tier_cal)

Problem:
  _preserve_hand_tuned_weights restores any on-disk entry lacking
  `_uncalibrated` whenever the fresh fit declines. batch-82 applies it to the
  three same-day files, each against its own file -- which is what stops a
  graduated same-day fit being thrown away by one thin run.

  The flip side: once a same-day tier clears the brier-improvement gate ONCE,
  no later run can un-graduate it. Only a manual file edit can. That is also
  true of the multi-day files (pre-existing), but it is newly consequential
  because (a) _tier_cal gives the same-day entry PRIORITY over the multi-day
  one at days_out<=0, and (b) the same-day populations are tiny. At the
  _CONDITION_MIN floor of 60 rows the 80/20 split yields ~12 validation rows,
  barely over _MIN_VAL_ROWS=10 -- so one noise-lucky validation window can
  permanently override a well-fitted multi-day tier for every same-day trade.

  Options if this is judged wrong: re-fit-or-expire semantics (drop a
  preserved entry after N runs where it would not re-qualify), a stricter
  floor for the same-day horizon specifically, or excluding the same-day
  files from preservation entirely (accepting that a graduated fit can be
  lost to one thin run).

  Related, same review, LOW and deliberately not fixed: the horizon preference
  is INTRA-TIER, so a multi-day-fitted CITY weight outranks a same-day-fitted
  CONDITION weight at d=0. Inert today -- data/city_weights.json holds zero
  entries -- but it is the same class of ordering question and should be
  settled in the same pass.


[OPEN 2026-08-26 -- surfaced by batch-82 while measuring which blend-weight
  components carry same-day skill] SAME-DAY NWS PROBABILITIES ON 'below'
  MARKETS ARE SEVERELY MISCALIBRATED
Priority: Medium -- it is not currently costing much, but only by accident.
  The live multi-day `below` condition weights happen to give NWS just 0.20,
  which is why same-day `below` prices reasonably today. Nothing designed
  that; a recalibration that raised NWS's `below` weight would expose this
  immediately.
Files: nws.py (nws_prob for temperature markets is derived at ~:359, but
  the NBM-percentile path runs through nws.nws_prob_from_quantiles at ~:434
  fed by mos.py ~:547/652 -- an investigation scoped to nws.py alone would
  miss the quantile path), mos.py, tracker.py (predictions.nws_prob)

Problem:
  Measured 2026-08-26 over settled rows with all three component probs
  populated, scoring each component ALONE as a Brier score:

    condition  horizon   ensemble   climatology   NWS     outcome rate
    below      D+0 (36)   0.3390      0.1975     0.5015      0.583
    below      D+1+ (31)  0.3318      0.3835     0.3022      0.484
    above      D+0 (41)   0.2984      0.2749     0.3117      0.463
    above      D+1+ (58)  0.2886      0.3748     0.3793      0.534

  Same-day NWS on `below` averages a probability of 0.146 against an actual
  outcome rate of 0.583, for a solo Brier of 0.5015 -- worse than a constant
  0.5 (0.25), and worse than a constant base rate (0.243). That is not
  "weak signal", it is a systematic sign-like bias: the component is
  confidently wrong in one direction. The same component at D+1-and-up
  scores 0.3022, so the defect is specific to the same-day horizon.

  It is NOT a clean YES/NO inversion -- 1 - 0.146 = 0.854, which is not the
  0.583 outcome rate either -- so it needs a real investigation of how
  nws_prob is derived for below-threshold markets at days_out=0, not a sign
  flip. Worth checking whether the same-day NWS forecast being fetched is a
  stale previous-cycle value.

  batch-82 deliberately did not fix this: it is a different subsystem (NWS
  probability derivation) from that batch's own surface (blend-weight
  calibration), and the fix needs its own investigation.


[OPEN 2026-08-26 -- noticed by batch-82 while parameterising the calibration
  horizon] THE MULTI-DAY HORIZON PREDICATE IS DEFINED IN TWO PLACES
Priority: Low -- the two definitions are currently identical, so nothing is
  wrong today. This is drift surface, not a live bug.
Files: tracker.py (multiday_predictions view), calibration.py
  (calibrate_condition_weights)

Problem:
  tracker.py's multiday_predictions view carries the comment "All analytics
  queries use this view so the filter is defined once" -- but
  calibration.calibrate_condition_weights does not use it. It selects
  `FROM predictions p` with its own inline
  `(p.days_out IS NULL OR p.days_out >= 1)`, a hand-copy of the view's own
  WHERE clause. calibration._load_rows, by contrast, does use the view.

  batch-82 added TWO same-day sibling predicates (`p.days_out = 0`, once in
  _load_rows and once in calibrate_condition_weights), so the horizon
  boundary is now asserted in FOUR places, not two: the view, the inline
  multi-day copy, and the two same-day literals.

  The fix is narrower than it first looks. Only the MULTI-DAY branch of
  calibrate_condition_weights can point at the view, and doing so is
  provably a behavioural no-op (the view IS `SELECT * FROM predictions`
  plus that exact predicate). The SAME-DAY branch can never use it -- the
  view excludes days_out = 0 by construction -- so at best this gets four
  sites down to three.

  batch-82 did not make the change because it breaks the `_make_db` fixture
  in tests/test_phase2_batch_p.py, which creates `outcomes_valid` but no
  multiday_predictions view, and that file was not in the batch's scoped
  test set. NOTE: an earlier draft of this entry also named
  tests/test_phase3_batch_c.py -- that was wrong, it DOES create the view
  (at :31) and would be unaffected. Any session picking this up must run
  tests/test_phase2_batch_p.py, not just tests/test_calibration.py.


[RESOLVED 2026-08-26 (batch-82)] SAME-DAY TRADES WERE PRICED WITH BLEND
  WEIGHTS FITTED ONLY ON MULTI-DAY ROWS
Files: calibration.py, weather_markets.py, main.py, paths.py, seeds/

Problem:
  calibration._load_rows selected `FROM multiday_predictions p` (the view
  defined as days_out IS NULL OR >= 1) and calibrate_condition_weights
  carried the same predicate inline, so all three blend-weight tables were
  fitted exclusively on multi-day rows -- then applied verbatim to same-day
  trades by weather_markets._blend_weights. Temperature scaling has honoured
  the same/multi-day separation since it shipped (data/temperature_scale.json
  has a dedicated `sameday` key, T=3.829 vs global 4.601, and ml_bias is
  explicit about "no fallback to global/multi-day T"); blend-weight
  calibration never did.

  This mattered more than it used to. The non-`between` METAR same-day lock
  is now closed by design in the unsafe direction by two monotone-safety
  vetoes (3e6af667 LOW, d65decff HIGH), so same-day non-between pricing runs
  through the ensemble path: August 2026 D+0 above/below is 25 ensemble +
  3 hourly_ensemble and ZERO metar_lockout, against 20 of 39 lockout in June.
  (Both counts are above/below-only. June's D+0 NON-BETWEEN count is 47,
  which includes 8 rows with a NULL method -- a different denominator, and
  not the one the 39 belongs to.)

What shipped:
  A horizon dimension on all three calibrators. Each is now fitted twice
  over DISJOINT populations -- multi-day (unchanged) and same-day
  (days_out = 0) -- and the two fits are written to SEPARATE FILES
  (seasonal_weights_sameday.json, city_weights_sameday.json,
  condition_weights_sameday.json, seeded via seeds/ per batch-79's
  mechanism). Separate files rather than a nesting level so that "100%
  separate" (user's words, 2026-08-26) is structural: no same-day
  calibration run can write into a multi-day file at all.

  Read side, weather_markets._blend_weights via the new _tier_cal helper:
  a days_out<=0 row prefers the same-day fit for each tier and falls back
  to that tier's MULTI-DAY fit when the same-day one has not graduated.
  Any other horizon never consults the same-day tables.

The decision, and why it went against the handoff brief's recommendation:
  The brief argued for a wholly separate same-day chain bottoming out at
  the hardcoded schedule, on the grounds that it is "the only option that
  does anything". The measurement falsified that premise. As of 2026-08-26
  NO same-day tier can be fitted:
    - city:      max 11 rows (Minneapolis) vs _CITY_MIN 50
    - condition: above 41, below 36, between 0 vs _CONDITION_MIN 60
    - seasonal:  summer 77 rows -- clears _SEASONAL_MIN 20 AND the 10-val-row
                 floor (train 61 / val 16), but is REJECTED by
                 _BRIER_IMPROVEMENT_GATE. The in-sample search finds
                 clim-heavy weights (0.0017, 0.9239, 0.0744) at train Brier
                 0.20549, which score 0.35478 on the held-out recent rows
                 against 0.29679 for equal weights -- an improvement of
                 -0.05799 against a gate needing STRICTLY MORE than
                 +0.005 (the code rejects on `<=`). Correctly refused.
  A lowered floor would not help: at 41/36 rows the 80/20 split gives val=9
  and val=8, under _MIN_VAL_ROWS=10, and _CONDITION_MIN=60 is the higher
  bar regardless.

  So a separate chain would send EVERY same-day row to the hardcoded
  schedule today, which measures as a regression, not a no-op:

    D+0 condition   today (multi-day cond tier)   hardcoded d=0   delta
    above  n=41            0.25715                  0.25787      +0.0007
    below  n=36            0.21083                  0.35177      +0.1409

  The `below` gap is robust -- t=+3.2396, and a paired bootstrap over the
  per-row squared-error differences gives 95% CI [+0.05791, +0.22251]
  (random.seed(7), B=5000 resamples -- RECORD THESE, the digits are not
  reproducible without them; the normal approximation is [+0.0557,
  +0.2262]). 24 of 36 individual rows favour it, and it is stable across
  older/newer halves (+0.145 / +0.137). The mechanism is the NWS miscalibration filed
  as its own OPEN entry above: the multi-day `below` weights give NWS only
  0.20 and climatology 0.75, starving the two components that are wrong
  same-day, while the hardcoded d=0 schedule hands ensemble 0.611 and NWS
  0.35 -- 96% of its weight to exactly those two.

  The two designs CONVERGE once a same-day tier graduates (~60 D+0 rows per
  condition, roughly 2-3 months at August's accrual); they differ only
  during the wait. User chose per-tier fallback on that basis, with the
  constraint that the calibration DATA stay 100% separate.

Before/after, measured via the production calibrate_and_save against a copy
of the live DB (2026-08-26):
  - All three MULTI-DAY files come back byte-identical to what is live.
  - All three same-day files are written with every entry _uncalibrated;
    no tier graduated.
  So the shipped change is a behavioural no-op on live pricing today. That
  is the finding: the pooling was not costing same-day anything -- it was
  quietly helping -- and this batch is the mechanism that will pick the
  separation up automatically once the data supports it, not a correction.

Other decisions recorded:
  - Horizon boundary is days_out = 0, matching multiday_predictions and
    ml_bias's `sameday` pool. A three-way same/next/multi split was
    rejected on the data: of the rows satisfying the fit's own NOT NULL
    requirements, 89 sit at D+1 and ZERO at D+2-and-up, so a third bucket
    would leave the multi-day fit with an empty population.
  - _nws_days_out_scale's `days_out <= 0` early return STAYS, and is now
    load-bearing for two independent reasons rather than one (same-day
    weights are already at their horizon; borrowed d=1 weights would be
    scaled by 1.0 - (0-1)*0.10 = 1.1, BOOSTING the weakest same-day
    component by 10%). Documented in the docstring and pinned by a test.
  - calibrate_and_save still returns a 3-tuple. cron.py unpacks exactly
    three values at two sites and was not in this batch's owned file set;
    the same-day dicts reach consumers via the mtime sweep and, for the
    CLI, a disk read-back.
  - The row counts in the handoff brief (204 fittable all-horizon, 127 at
    D+1-and-up) were measured WITHOUT _load_rows's own 'between'+shadow
    condition-type exclusion. The real _load_rows population is 166 / 77
    D+0 / 89 D+1-and-up. 348 settled and 77 D+0 were correct.

Tests: TestHorizonSplit, TestSamedayFitIsSeparateFromMultiday,
  TestSamedaySeedFlag, TestCalibrateCLI::test_calibrate_writes_and_
  invalidates_the_sameday_tables (tests/test_calibration.py);
  TestSamedayWeightsAreUsedAtDayZero, TestSamedayUncalibratedFlagIsLoad
  Bearing, TestNwsDaysOutScaleAtDayZero, TestSamedayTablesAreRefreshedFrom
  Disk (tests/test_weather_markets.py); one added to tests/test_paths.py
  (test_sameday_and_multiday_seed_names_are_distinct) and one existing test
  there extended.
  45 tests collected across the batch-82 classes (re-counted at the moment of
  writing this). Ten mutations applied via the Edit tool and each confirmed to
  fail the specific test claiming to catch it; two of them exposed real gaps in the
  new tests (a seed-flag test that only checked one key, and a tier that
  was shadowed and therefore asserted vacuously) which were fixed before
  the mutation was reverted.

Opus review (three independent reviewers: calibration/write side, live
pricing/read side, and a fact-check of every number written here). All
findings addressed; the ones that changed code:

  - HIGH, and a genuine breach of the "100% separate" constraint that this
    batch's own author missed: safe_io.atomic_write_json_with_history prunes
    history with `glob(f"{path.stem}_*.json")`, which ALSO matches the
    backups of a longer-named file sharing that stem plus an underscore.
    Timestamps start with a digit and every sibling suffix starts with a
    letter, so foreign backups sorted last and `existing[0].unlink()` ate
    THIS file's real history first. Writing seasonal_weights.json would have
    drained the multi-day blend-weight backups to zero over ~10 calibration
    runs from the live state (all three were already at the 10 cap).
    PRE-EXISTING, not introduced here -- temperature_scale.json has been
    pruning temperature_scale_pre_emos backups the same way. Fixed at the
    root in safe_io.py by matching the stamp shape exactly
    (_HISTORY_STAMP_RE), with five regression tests in tests/test_safe_io.py
    covering both the batch-82 pair and the pre-existing one.
  - HIGH test gap: cross-horizon content separation was pinned for SEASONAL
    only. Four contamination mutations passed the whole suite -- preserving a
    same-day fit FROM the multi-day file (seasonal, condition) and writing a
    multi-day fit INTO a same-day file (condition, city). Now covered for
    every table. The preservation test needs TWO calibrate_and_save runs:
    _preserve_hand_tuned_weights reads the target file BEFORE the run writes
    it, so on a first run into an empty dir the contamination is invisible --
    the single-run version let the mutation survive a second time.
  - MEDIUM: _nws_days_out_scale's d<=0 guard also skips the 0.85 NWS
    ceiling. Filed as its own OPEN entry above and pinned by a test rather
    than fixed, because fixing it changes live same-day `between` pricing.
  - MEDIUM: a vacuous test of this batch's own writing. The
    "mutation guard" for the d=0 scaling decision imported nothing from
    weather_markets and re-derived the schedule from literals -- green under
    every possible mutation of the module. Rewritten to read the decay off
    the real function.
  - MEDIUM-LOW: the same-day pool excluded metar_lockout rows only by
    accident (all 106 have NULL component probs). Now excluded structurally
    via _SAMEDAY_METAR_EXCLUSION, with a test that seeds locked rows WITH
    all three probs and a positive control proving the same rows arrive when
    the method is anything else.
  - MEDIUM-LOW: cmd_calibrate's new print block indexed disk-sourced dicts
    directly, so a hand-edited *_sameday.json would KeyError and abort the
    command before cache invalidation and before the Platt block.
  - Plus: whole-dict rebind instead of .clear()+.update() in cmd_calibrate
    (Flask threaded=True); all three same-day tables invalidated, not one; a
    WARNING when a malformed non-dict entry is skipped (the isinstance guard
    had converted a loud AttributeError into a silent tier-skip); horizon
    tags on every decline log line; conftest's isolate fixture widened from
    one table to all six; and a test binding calibrate_and_save's write
    literals to the paths.py constants, which nothing had connected.

ROUND-2 opus review, of the round-1 FIXES themselves (the workflow requires
this, and it earned its keep -- two of the round-1 fixes were wrong):

  - The round-1 KeyError fix in cmd_calibrate was justified by a FALSE claim
    ("only the same-day tables come off disk"), and the identical failure was
    still live on the multi-day path three blocks above it.
    _preserve_hand_tuned_weights copies on-disk entries VERBATIM into the
    fresh result, so a hand-edited weights file propagates through
    calibrate_and_save's return value. Reproduced: a
    {"winter": {"ensemble": .5, "climatology": .5}} on disk makes the
    multi-day block raise KeyError: 'nws'. All four print blocks now share a
    gap-tolerant _fmt_weights helper.
  - The same partial-entry shape reaches the LIVE PRICING PATH, which is
    worse: _blend_weights indexes cal["ensemble"] directly, so a present,
    unflagged, partially-written same-day entry raised KeyError at d=0 --
    and did so INSTEAD of the healthy multi-day entry it shadows. _usable_cal
    now requires all three keys and falls through, same as for an absent one.
  - The round-1 mtime-sweep test pinned only the FILENAME literals in each
    refresh tuple, by regex over the function's source. The module-attribute
    name and the loader were unpinned, so pointing the
    city_weights_sameday.json entry at "_CITY_WEIGHTS" would have written the
    SAME-DAY fit into the MULTI-DAY global -- this batch's exact
    contamination -- with a green suite. Replaced by a behavioural test that
    drives the real function, freshening one file at a time with a distinct
    sentinel per loader; mutation-confirmed.
  - The round-1 "all three tables" separation test looped over two. City
    content was asserted NOWHERE in the suite, so writing the multi-day city
    fit into the same-day city file survived everything. Now covered and
    mutation-confirmed.
  - 31 call sites across 8 test files neutralise the three MULTI-DAY globals
    to force hardcoded pricing; none patch the same-day counterparts, which
    load at import from the real data/. conftest now EMPTIES the three
    same-day tables per test rather than snapshotting them -- snapshotting
    fixes leak-out, not leak-in, and leak-in is the half that would perturb
    those 31 tests the day a same-day tier graduates.
  - Smaller: an unthrottled WARNING on a per-market hot path (now log-once
    per distinct problem); two unused `type: ignore` comments; a _seed_db
    comment that was simply wrong about dict.get preserving an explicit None
    (reverted to the plain .get); a backlog citation missing the word
    ENTIRELY; a cmd_calibrate rationale citing a "long-lived process" that
    does not exist (it is one-shot CLI); schema-validator coverage for the
    three new live files; and the mixed-vintage-within-one-tier consequence
    of cron refreshing multi-day immediately while same-day waits for the
    300s sweep.

  Round 2 also CLEARED, with its own verification: the safe_io stamp-regex
  slice (every one of the 41 live .history files is still claimed by exactly
  one owner, so nothing becomes immortal), the SQL NULL semantics of the
  metar_lockout exclusion, the conftest cost (~12 ms across the suite), and
  the _seed_db change being behaviourally inert. It also independently
  confirmed the operator-precedence question the new horizon clause raises --
  tracker._condition_type_not_in_sql parenthesises its fragment, so appending
  the horizon predicate after it is safe.

  One test failure seen during review, investigated and NOT ours:
  test_atomic_write_text_concurrent_writers_never_expose_torn_file fails with
  WinError 5 under load. Confirmed by running the CLEAN HEAD version of that
  file against it -- it fails identically, exercises atomic_write_text (which
  this change does not touch), and safe_io.py's own docstring already
  documents this test as load-flaky on Windows.

The fact-check reviewer confirmed every measured number in this entry
against the live DB and re-ran the production calibrators, and refuted five
prose claims, all corrected above: tests/test_phase3_batch_c.py DOES create
the multiday_predictions view (only test_phase2_batch_p.py lacks it); the
horizon boundary now sits in four places, not three; "every clause is now
false" overstated -- data/ is still gitignored; 10b protects between-NO and
excludes only between-YES; and the bootstrap CI needed its seed and B
recorded to be reproducible.


[OPEN 2026-08-26 -- found by batch-81's second opus review round, which
  noticed the batch had documented this hazard for the rain entry and not
  carried the reasoning across to the temperature one] THE TWO MARKET-IMPLIED
  SIGNALS CANNOT USE THE UNBIASED POPULATION UNTIL IT HAS A DISTINCT-EVENT
  COUNT
Priority: Medium -- nothing is wrong in production and no floor is affected
  today, because batch-81 shipped both entries with attempt_json_key=None
  rather than a count it could not justify. This is the work needed to turn
  that conservative choice back into the ~6-7x accrual gain the rest of the
  signals got.
Files: tracker.py (count_scored_attempt_signal_rows), weather_markets.py
  (the market_implied and market_implied_rain registry entries)

Problem:
  The market-implied distribution is fitted once per EVENT, and
  resolve_market_implied_for_analysis hands the identical fitted value to
  every sibling rung of that event's ladder. `analysis_attempts` keys on
  (ticker, target_date), so one event contributes one row per rung.

  Measured 2026-08-26: 584 scored attempt rows across 514 distinct
  (city, target_date, 6-char market family) groups = 1.14 rows/event, and
  1.51 against the coarser (city, target_date). The worst single group was
  7 rungs (Chicago, 2026-08-01, KXRAIN).

  A COUNT(*) over those rows is therefore not the independent-sample count
  SIGNAL_GRADUATION_FLOOR was derived for -- the floor would clear, and the
  report would print green, on materially fewer real observations than 112.
  That is a smaller copy of the exact affordance batch-81 item 1 removed,
  which is why both entries ship with no attempt_json_key rather than with
  an inflated one. The VALUES are still written to the blob
  (implied_mean/implied_sigma/fit_residual, and implied_mean_rain and
  friends for KXRAIN*M), so no data is being lost meanwhile -- only the
  count is withheld.

What the fix looks like:
  A distinct-event count mode on count_scored_attempt_signal_rows, then
  attempt_json_key restored on both entries. The event key is the hard part
  and should not be guessed: temperature fits are keyed
  (city, date_iso, var) on the produce side, and analysis_attempts stores
  city and target_date but NOT var -- so the var has to come from the
  ticker prefix (KXHIGH vs KXLOW), and rain's event key is
  (city, "RAIN", year, month) instead. Reuse
  market_implied_rain_event_key()/_var_from_ticker_prefix() rather than
  re-deriving either, or the count and the fit will disagree about what an
  event is.

Why not now:
  Getting the event key wrong produces a count that looks right and is
  wrong, which is worse than no count -- and no count is the state batch-81
  deliberately shipped. Wants its own session with the produce-side key
  functions in front of it.


[RESOLVED 2026-08-26 -- option (b), unrolled the loop into direct calls;
  see the RESOLUTION block at the end of this entry. Filed by batch-81,
  which found it while running its scoped suite and confirmed it
  pre-existing against a clean detached worktree at origin/master.]
  tests/test_dead_code_scan.py IS RED ON MASTER -- BATCH-78'S
  TWO PRUNERS ARE WIRED BUT INVISIBLE TO THE SCANNER
Priority: Medium -- nothing is wrong in production (both functions really
  are called every Monday), but a permanently-red test is worse than a
  failing one: the next session to run this file has to re-derive that the
  failure is not theirs, which cost batch-81 a full clean-master run.
Files: cron.py (the Monday sweep's aliased imports ~:1663 and the
  `for _pruner, _days, _what in (...)` indirection loop below them),
  tests/test_dead_code_scan.py (_DEAD_CODE_ALLOWLIST)

Problem:
  test_no_new_dead_code_outside_allowlist fails with:
      tracker.py:prune_ensemble_member_values (TESTED, NO PROD CALL SITE)
      tracker.py:prune_orderbook_depth_snapshots (TESTED, NO PROD CALL SITE)

  Both ARE wired, into cron.py's Monday sweep. The scanner is regex-based
  and looks for `name(` call syntax, and neither name ever appears that way:
  they are imported under aliases (`as _prune_member_values` / `as
  _prune_depth`), then put in a tuple and invoked as `_pruner(days=_days)`. Two
  layers of indirection, each individually reasonable, that together make a
  genuinely-called function read as fully dead.

  Same failure mode weather_markets._count_market_implied_rain already hit
  in 2026-08-02 and solved by matching the factory-call convention exactly
  rather than by an allowlist entry.

What the fix looks like:
  Either (a) an allowlist entry for each with the concrete reason ("invoked
  via the _pruner indirection in cron's Monday sweep"), or (b) restructure
  the loop so the real names appear at a call site. (b) is closer to the
  _count_market_implied_rain precedent and keeps the scanner honest; (a) is
  one line. De-aliasing the imports alone is NOT sufficient -- the call is
  through the loop variable, so the name still never appears with parens.

Why not now:
  Choosing between (a) and (b) is a judgment call about batch-78's own loop
  -- which exists for a stated reason (each pruner wrapped individually so
  one failure cannot suppress the whole sweep for a week) -- and the
  allowlist demands a concrete reason its author is best placed to write.
  batch-81 found it, verified it was not its own, and left it rather than
  quietly widening its scope into another batch's design.

RESOLUTION 2026-08-26: took option (b).

  cron.py's Monday sweep now calls the two pruners directly, each in its
  own try/except, exactly like _prune_scan_runs ten lines below it -- the
  sibling that was never flagged, because a plain aliased call is a shape
  the scanner already resolves. The `for _pruner, _days, _what in (...)`
  loop is gone.

  Option (b) over (a) because an allowlist entry would have exempted two
  genuinely-called functions from dead-code detection permanently: if
  either were later unwired for real, nothing would notice. The repo has
  the same precedent on record -- weather_markets._count_market_implied_
  rain hit this in 2026-08-02 and was fixed by matching the call
  convention rather than by allowlisting.

  The loop existed for a real reason (reviewer B #7: the sweep body is one
  try/except with a `finally` that stamps the 7-day marker, so an unguarded
  exception from any one pruner would skip the VACUUM and suppress the
  whole sweep for another week). Unrolling preserves that per-pruner
  isolation -- but NOTHING WAS TESTING IT, so collapsing the guards back
  would have been a silent regression. Two tests added to
  TestBatch78MondaySweepWindows: one fails the first pruner and asserts the
  second, the third and the VACUUM all still run; the mirror fails the
  SECOND pruner, since guarding only the first would satisfy the other test
  while still letting the sweep abort.

  Mutation-tested three ways: restoring the loop makes the dead-code scan
  fail again (so the unroll is what fixes it, not something incidental);
  removing both guards kills the two new tests; guarding only the first
  kills the mirror.

  Not changed: the scanner itself. Teaching it to follow a name into a
  tuple and out through a loop variable is a much larger change to a guard
  test, with real false-negative risk, to accommodate one indirection that
  had no reason to exist.

[OPEN 2026-08-26 -- found by batch-78 item 2 while sizing a retention
  window; the window decision could not be made honestly without it, but
  cloud_backup.py was outside that batch's file scope] EVERY BYTE KEPT IN
  predictions.db IS PAID 31 TIMES OVER IN THE BACKUP FOLDER
Priority: Medium -- nothing is broken, and local disk is cheap (155 GB free
  on C: as of 2026-08-26). It matters because it silently multiplies the
  cost of every future retention decision by 31, and because the destination
  is a syncing OneDrive folder rather than plain local disk, so the multiple
  is paid against a cloud quota the repo knows nothing about.
Files: cloud_backup.py (backup_data's dated-folder scheme and its 30-day
  prune loop), cron.py (the post-cycle backup_data call)

Problem:
  cloud_backup.backup_data() writes into <sync>/KalshiBot/data/<YYYY-MM-DD>/
  and prunes directories older than 30 days, so the steady state is 31
  dated folders each holding a full, uncompressed copy of every data/ file
  -- predictions.db included. Files are copied via safe_io.backup_sqlite_db
  (a real SQLite backup, correctly WAL-safe) with no compression and no
  de-duplication between days, even though consecutive days differ by well
  under 1% of the file.

  So the sync-folder cost of predictions.db is size x 31, not size x 1. At
  today's 50 MB that is ~1.5 GB. Batch-78 sized ensemble_member_values'
  retention at 365 days, taking the DB to roughly 370 MB steady state and
  the backup folder to roughly 11.5 GB.

  Measured 2026-08-26: CLOUD_BACKUP_PATH is unset, so _find_sync_folder()
  falls through to %ONEDRIVE% (set, and the directory exists), and backups
  are landing in C:/Users/thesa/OneDrive/KalshiBot/data -- 2 folders,
  94.1 MB, on their way to 31. Whether that is free is a function of the
  account's OneDrive tier, which is not knowable from the repo.

Why not now:
  Batch-78 owned tracker.py/cron.py/trade_cycle.py/kalshi_ws.py, not
  cloud_backup.py, and the retention windows were the decision that batch
  was asked to make. Widening it into a backup-format change would have
  bundled two unrelated calls into one diff.

What it would look like (pick one, with the user):
  - Compress each .db on the way out (gzip/zstd). A SQLite file of mostly
    text rows compresses several-fold; nothing else changes.
  - Keep a full copy weekly and a lighter artifact daily, instead of 31
    identical fulls.
  - Exclude the two forward-only observation tables from the backup
    entirely -- they are write-only, not backfillable, and losing them to a
    disk failure costs a panel's history rather than any trading record.
    Cheapest to implement, and the only option that does not touch the
    format, but it is also the only one that loses data on a restore.
  Whichever is chosen, re-derive the x31 figure first: the prune window is a
  literal 30 in backup_data and may have moved.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-25 -- fix applied and the 30 contaminated rows removed;
  found by the independent opus review of the prod-data-guard entry below]
  TEST RUNS WRITE FABRICATED ROWS INTO THE REAL data/predictions.db VIA AN
  atexit FLUSHER THAT FIRES AFTER EVERY TEST-ISOLATION TEARDOWN
Priority: High -- it is writing right now, on every pytest run, into the
  database the bot's own accuracy/calibration work reads. The new
  prod-data-guard (entry below) does NOT catch it, by construction.
Files: tests/conftest.py (pytest_sessionfinish, pytest_unconfigure),
  weather_markets.py:3957/4002 (_member_values_pending / flush_member_values),
  tracker.py (log_ensemble_members_bulk), data/predictions.db.

Problem:
  weather_markets registers THREE atexit flushers (weather_markets.py:1156,
  1271, 4002). conftest's pytest_sessionfinish drains only two of them --
  _forecast_disk_pending and _ensemble_disk_pending. The third,
  _member_values_pending (flushed by flush_member_values, registered at
  weather_markets.py:4002), is not drained.

  Ordering is the whole bug. atexit hooks fire at true interpreter
  shutdown, which is AFTER: (a) monkeypatch has reverted
  isolate_tracker_db's tracker.DB_PATH redirect, and (b) conftest's
  pytest_unconfigure has called prod_data_guard.uninstall(). So the flush
  runs with no isolation and no guard, and
  tracker.log_ensemble_members_bulk() does init_db() + INSERT straight into
  the operator's real data/predictions.db.

  pytest_sessionfinish's own docstring already describes this exact hazard
  for the other two buffers ("the atexit flush fires AFTER this fixture's
  own teardown has already reverted the redirect") -- the fix simply never
  covered the third buffer, which was added later.

Evidence (read-only query against the live DB, mode=ro):
  ensemble_member_values: 37 rows, 7 distinct logged_at batches. Every row
  is test fixture data, not a forecast:

    (1,  'NYC','icon_seamless','2026-08-26','max','2026-08-25_00z',
         'RUN-X', 1, '[70.0]',  '2026-08-25T07:31:46Z')
    (888,'NYC','gem_global','2026-08-28','max','2026-08-25_18z',
         None, 5, '[200.0, 201.0, 202.0, 203.0, 204.0]',
         '2026-08-26T00:03:51Z')

  run_init='RUN-X' is the literal string from
  tests/test_batch64_forward_writers.py::
  test_persist_member_values_records_the_observed_run_init (which calls
  wm._persist_member_values() WITHOUT the `patch.object(wm,
  "_member_values_pending", [])` its neighbouring tests use). The
  [200.0...] array is an out-of-range sentinel from a validation test. The
  [70.0, 71.0, ...] sequences are synthetic.

  Batch sizes are 1-16 rows; a real prewarm scan writes ~300. Autoincrement
  ids reach 888 for 37 surviving rows, so far more has passed through
  historically. Four of the seven batches (16:24, 16:33, 16:49, 17:10 UTC
  2026-08-25) and the 00:03:51 UTC 2026-08-26 batch line up exactly with
  this session's own diagnostic and verification runs -- i.e. the work that
  found this was also feeding it.

Why the new guard does not catch it:
  tests/prod_data_guard.py is installed from pytest_configure and removed
  from pytest_unconfigure. Since the leak happens strictly after
  unconfigure, the guard is already gone. Confirmed empirically: a probe
  plugin reading the buffers at unconfigure time, after a single test,
  showed `_member_values_pending len=2` with the guard already uninstalled.

Fix (not yet applied):
  1. Drain _member_values_pending in pytest_sessionfinish alongside the
     other two -- and derive the list, or assert that every atexit-
     registered flusher in weather_markets has a drained buffer, so the
     NEXT flusher added does not repeat this. That generalisation is the
     actual lesson: this is the second buffer to be missed by a hand-
     maintained list of two.
  2. Stop calling prod_data_guard.uninstall() in pytest_unconfigure.
     Leaving the guard armed until process exit costs nothing and is the
     correct default for an always-on guard. Note flush_member_values
     swallows Exception, so the guard alone would block-but-not-report --
     step 1 is still required.
  3. Register an atexit hook from prod_data_guard.install() that reports any
     violations accumulated after pytest_sessionfinish, so a post-session
     leak is loud rather than dropped.
  4. Delete the 37 contaminated rows from data/predictions.db.

Resolution 2026-08-25:
  1. conftest._ATEXIT_FLUSH_BUFFERS now names all three buffers and
     pytest_sessionfinish drains each. Verified empirically: 634 rows before
     running tests/test_batch64_forward_writers.py (the file whose
     test_persist_member_values_records_the_observed_run_init populates the
     buffer without patching it), 634 after.
  2. conftest no longer defines pytest_unconfigure at all, so the guard stays
     armed through interpreter shutdown; prod_data_guard.install() also
     registers an atexit reporter that prints anything blocked after the
     session ended, since no test can be failed at that point and
     flush_member_values swallows Exception.
  3. tests/test_prod_data_guard.py::TestAtexitFlushersAreAllDrained reads
     weather_markets' source for its atexit.register calls and asserts each
     flusher's buffer is one conftest drains -- so the NEXT flusher added
     cannot repeat this. A hand-maintained list of two had already failed
     once, which is the whole lesson.
  4. 30 synthetic rows deleted (ids listed in the session log); 604
     legitimate rows retained. A consistent snapshot of the DB was taken via
     the sqlite backup API first, since production cron was mid-cycle.

CORRECTION to the count above: this entry originally said 37 rows, derived
  by grouping on logged_at and treating seven small batches as test flushes.
  That heuristic was WRONG and would have destroyed real data.
  tracker.py:10360 inserts with INSERT OR IGNORE against a UNIQUE index on
  (city, model, target_date, var, cycle), so a REAL cron flush only inserts
  combinations not already present -- which can be as few as 3 rows. Seven
  genuine SanFrancisco rows (n_members 30-50, real run_init timestamps) were
  sitting in the same logged_at batches as the test rows.

  The rows were instead separated on CONTENT: run_init='RUN-X', or a member
  array that is an arithmetic run of step 1.0 with integral endpoints
  ([70.0], [70.0, 71.0], [68.0..72.0]), or an out-of-range sentinel
  (+/-200.0F). That gives 30 synthetic (all NYC, n_members 1-5) and 604 real
  (20 cities, n_members 17-50). Verified again inside the delete transaction
  before committing.

  Worth remembering generally: an "obviously test-shaped" small batch is not
  evidence of a test when the writer dedups on insert.

FOLLOW-UP 2026-08-26: draining the buffers was necessary but not
  sufficient, and the guard's own atexit reporter could never have caught
  the gap. atexit is LIFO: weather_markets registers its flushers at IMPORT,
  while prod_data_guard registers its reporter later at pytest_configure, so
  the reporter always runs BEFORE the flushers and cannot observe them. It
  reported nothing across four full-suite runs for that reason, not because
  nothing happened -- a further 13 synthetic rows landed in one flush at
  2026-08-26T00:45:15Z from a transitional state and had to be removed in a
  second pass (605 real rows retained, independently corroborated by the
  batch-75 session's own count).

  pytest_sessionfinish now also calls atexit.unregister() on each flusher
  (conftest._ATEXIT_FLUSHERS), which is ordering-independent and closes the
  residual race where anything repopulates a buffer between the drain and
  true interpreter shutdown. A companion test checks that list against
  weather_markets' real atexit.register calls, same as the buffer list.

  Lesson worth keeping: a last-line-of-defence reporter that registers
  itself LATER than the hazard it watches is inert by construction. Verify
  the ordering, do not assume registration implies observation.

Downstream-consumption check: nothing outside tracker.py's own writer reads
  this table today (grep for ensemble_member_values across the repo returns
  only the CREATE/INDEX/INSERT in tracker.py and two comments in
  weather_markets.py referring to its dedup key). So no analysis has
  consumed the fabricated rows, and the deletion is a clean correction.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-25 -- structural runtime guard + 10 isolation fixtures
  shipped; see resolution below] A PLAIN `pytest` RUN MUTATED THE REAL
  PRODUCTION data/ DIRECTORY -- 567 ATTEMPTS BY DAY, 1,700+ AFTER UTC
  MIDNIGHT, INCLUDING THE LIVE-TRADING KILL SWITCH
Priority: High -- the suite had write access to every piece of live state the
  bot owns. One target is the operator's hard stop on live trading; 20 tests
  DELETED the flag a running cron cycle uses to detect a concurrent run; and
  a whole class of once-per-period gate markers was being stamped, which
  SUPPRESSES the next real production run of whatever each one gates.
Files: tests/prod_data_guard.py (new), tests/test_prod_data_guard.py (new),
  tests/conftest.py (3 phase hooks + 10 new/extended autouse fixtures),
  tests/test_bare_os_replace_guard.py (one allowlist entry).
  NO production module changed.

Problem:
  paths.py deliberately resolves data/ to the MAIN CLONE via
  safe_io.project_root(), so a worktree cron run hits real state rather than
  a stale local copy. The consequence is that EVERY pytest run, from any
  worktree, points at live production state unless the specific path
  constant a test touches happens to be redirected in conftest.py.

  conftest.py had been closing those holes one constant at a time since
  2026-04 -- data/cron.log (467 fabricated lines), data/paper_trades.json
  (batch-62), data/metar_lockout_calibration.json (commit 5d9b6c56),
  data/nearby_station_shadow.json (110 phantom cycles),
  data/signals_cache.json, data/miami_index_state.json,
  data/.halt_transitions.json. Every one was found by accident, after the
  fact. A redirect list can only ever describe leaks somebody already hit.

  Measured with a scratch pytest plugin intercepting open / Path.open /
  sqlite3.connect / os.replace / rename / unlink / remove / touch / mkdir /
  shutil.*, blocking anything under the real data/ (so nothing was damaged
  while measuring). Positive-controlled on all 8 vectors first: each attempt
  both recorded AND prevented, two victim files verified intact afterwards.

  567 real mutation attempts across 25 test files (plus 330 benign
  mkdir(exist_ok=True) re-assertions of already-existing dirs):

    6 production DBs   sqlite3.connect   74 tests each (444 total)
      predictions/execution_log/kalshi/paper_trades/tracker/trades.db, via
      cloud_backup._sqlite_source_is_empty() iterating the whole real
      DATA_DIR -- which then copies every matching file into the operator's
      cloud sync folder under today's date.
    .notify_cooldowns.json   atomic write   28 tests
    feature_importance.jsonl open(a)        25 tests
    .cron_running            Path.unlink    20 tests  <-- DELETE
    .last_calibration_count  write           6 tests
    .watch_state.json        write           4 tests
    cron_web.log             truncate        4 tests
    .cron.lock.mutex         open(a+b)       2 tests
    learned_weights.json     atomic write    1 test   <-- MODEL ARTIFACT
    ensemble_cache/<lat>_<lon>_<date>_min.json         1 test
    .config_hash             write           1 test
    .kill_switch             atomic write    1 test   <-- LIVE TRADING STOP

  THE KILL SWITCH is the worst of these, and the count understates it.
  tests/test_web_auth.py's TestMutationEndpointsRequireAuth POSTs /api/halt
  (lands a real data/.kill_switch) and POSTs /api/resume (does
  `_KS_PATH.unlink(missing_ok=True)`). Depending only on test ORDER, a plain
  `pytest` run could leave live trading HALTED, or silently clear a halt the
  operator set deliberately. The resume/delete side does NOT appear in the
  567 only because /api/resume checks `.exists()` first and the operator was
  not halted at measurement time -- luck, not isolation. KILL_SWITCH_PATH
  was isolated NOWHERE in conftest.py.

  A SECOND, TIME-GATED CLASS was invisible to that sweep entirely.
  cron.py/weather_markets.py's once-per-period maintenance gates read
  utils.utc_today() and compare it to a stored date:

      _today = _utc_today()
      if last == str(_today):
          return          # already ran this period -- skip, no write

  The sweep (12:47 EDT / 16:47 UTC) and the first full verification run
  (~13:00 EDT / 17:00 UTC) both fell on the same UTC day the markers were
  last stamped, so every gate short-circuited on that `return` and never
  reached its write. Re-running the identical suite at 00:13 UTC the next
  day -- zero code changes in between -- produced 79 failures across 1,140
  additional blocked writes: fee_change_check.json (763),
  city_registry_report.json (150), series_drift_check.json (148),
  last_prod_reminder.txt (79).

  These do not corrupt data; they SUPPRESS. A test run stamping
  data/fee_change_check.json with today's date makes the next real cron
  cycle skip the $0-maker-fee guard for the rest of the day. Same shape for
  the series-drift, catalog-drift, city-registry and retirement-probation
  watchers, the ML-retrain / weights-refresh / param-sweep / walk-forward
  gates, and the monthly prod reminder.

  Per-test patching was not enough, and had already failed silently:
  test_state_consistency.py and test_execution_stability.py's TestCronLock
  both patch *main*.LOCK_PATH, but cron.py reads *cron*.LOCK_PATH, so the
  real data/.cron.lock.mutex was still being opened. Likewise this file's
  own notify entry states its tests are "isolated to a tmp_path file via
  monkeypatch -- never touches the real data/.notify_cooldowns.json": true
  of that file, false of the 28 other tests reaching the same writer by a
  different call path.

Resolution:
  1. tests/prod_data_guard.py -- an always-on runtime guard installed from
     conftest's pytest_configure for the whole session. Any write, delete,
     rename, truncate, touch, non-read-only sqlite connect, or NEW-directory
     creation resolving under the real data/ raises ProdDataWriteError at the
     call site AND is recorded. conftest wraps all three test phases
     (setup/call/teardown) with assert_clean(), which fails the test even
     when the raise was swallowed -- necessary because this codebase wraps
     nearly all persistence in `try: ... except Exception: log`.

     This inverts the model: instead of enumerating paths a test must not
     write, nothing may be written, so a state file added to paths.py
     tomorrow is covered with no conftest change.

     Reads are deliberately NOT blocked (some are legitimate -- the five
     git-tracked data/*.json calibration files). Every read is counted and
     printed at session end instead. See follow-up below.

     No opt-out marker, by design: a test needing a real data file must copy
     it into tmp_path first.

     mkdir is checked against EXISTENCE rather than location -- paths.py,
     backtest.py and ab_test.py all mkdir(exist_ok=True) at import, and most
     persistence helpers do `<CONST>.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)` before an
     atomic write. Failing those is 330 false positives protecting nothing,
     since the write that follows is blocked on its own merits.

     Measured overhead ~1.7us per open() call (mode is tested first, a pure
     string check, so a read never reaches the path-normalising code).

  2. Ten autouse fixtures in conftest.py covering every constant found:
     KILL_SWITCH_PATH (six bindings -- paths, cron, main, alerts, trading_
     gates, web_app), WATCH_STATE_PATH, CRON_WEB_LOG_PATH, NOTIFY_COOLDOWN_
     STATE_PATH, LOCK_PATH / RUNNING_FLAG_PATH / LAST_CALIBRATION_COUNT_PATH,
     LEARNED_WEIGHTS_PATH + FORECAST_SNAPSHOTS_DIR, FEATURE_IMPORTANCE_LOG_
     PATH, CONFIG_HASH_PATH, cloud_backup.DATA_DIR, ENSEMBLE_CACHE_DIR, and
     isolate_periodic_gate_sentinels covering all 13 periodic markers.

     The three WEEKLY-cadence sentinels (FEE_SCHEDULE_SCRAPE_PATH,
     CATALOG_DRIFT_PATH, LAST_MONDAY_SWEEP_PATH) had not fired even at
     00:13 UTC, because their period had not elapsed. Isolated anyway: same
     gate shape, same consequence, longer fuse. Waiting for each to surface
     on its own schedule is exactly the habit the guard exists to end.

  3. tests/test_prod_data_guard.py -- 85 tests. Each mutation probe attempts
     a real mutation and asserts both halves of the contract (blocked AND
     nothing changed on disk). The delete probe aims at a deliberately
     NON-EXISTENT path, so it cannot destroy anything even if the guard is
     fully broken, while still detecting a broken guard: unguarded,
     unlink(missing_ok=True) succeeds silently and os.remove raises
     FileNotFoundError -- neither is ProdDataWriteError.

     A TestIsolationFixturesStayWired class asserts every redirected
     (module, attribute) resolves outside the real data/, so deleting a
     fixture names the exact binding that came loose instead of waiting for
     an unrelated test to write through it. Its periodic-gate rows are
     DERIVED from conftest's own _PERIODIC_GATE_SENTINELS table rather than
     re-listed, so a constant added to the fixture cannot end up tested by
     nothing.

Three findings the guard produced that inspection had not:
  - ENSEMBLE_CACHE_DIR was leaking despite conftest already having a fixture

  - tests/test_forecasting.py::TestLearnedWeights::

  - The guard's OWN mutation battery leaked. Dropping "a" from

    ORIGINAL os.remove/shutil.rmtree (the patched ones refuse exactly those
    paths, and the originals work when the guard was never installed at

[RESOLVED 2026-08-25 -- batch-80 item 2. Originally found by batch-68's
  own test run: a real notify.send_system_alert() call raised inside its
  notify thread during tests, and was filed rather than fixed because
  notify.py was batch-69's file.]
  A SYSTEM ALERT LONGER THAN 256 CHARACTERS CRASHES THE DESKTOP-TOAST BACKEND
Priority: Low -- Discord still delivers, and the exception is confined to the
  notify thread, so no caller is affected. But it silently drops the desktop
  half of an alert, and it does so specifically for the LONGEST (i.e. most
  detailed, usually most serious) messages.
Files: notify.py (send_system_alert / the plyer desktop backend) -- no code
  changed by this entry.

Problem:
  notify.py's desktop-notification backend goes through plyer, whose Windows
  implementation packs the message into a NOTIFYICONDATAW struct with a
  hard 256-character field. A longer string raises:

    File "plyer/platforms/win/libs/win_api_defs.py", line 93,
      in get_NOTIFYICONDATAW: notify_data = NOTIFYICONDATAW(*largs)
    ValueError: string too long (333, maximum length 256)

  It surfaced as a PytestUnhandledThreadExceptionWarning, i.e. it escapes the
  notify thread uncaught rather than being truncated or logged.

  At least one shipped caller already exceeds the cap comfortably:
  tracker.audit_settlement's Miami index-mismatch alert body is ~1,499
  characters. That alert has never fired in production (0 disputed rows), so
  the hazard has not been observed live -- but it is armed.

  batch-68 kept its own new hourly-parsing-mismatch alert under the cap
  deliberately (worst-case render measured at 227 characters) rather than add
  a second instance, and left a comment saying why. That is a workaround at
  each call site, not a fix.

Why not fixed now:
  notify.py belongs to batch-69 (INDEX-PANEL-BACKENDS.md, track B), which owns
  notify/cron/alerts. Editing it from batch-68 would collide.

What it would look like:
  Truncate in send_system_alert() before handing the message to the desktop
  backend -- e.g. pass the full text to Discord and a `message[:253] + "..."`
  to plyer -- so the cap is enforced once, centrally, instead of every caller
  having to know a Windows struct limit. Wrapping the plyer call in its own
  try/except so a backend failure can never escape the thread is worth doing
  in the same pass. Then the Miami alert body can go back to being as long as
  it wants.

Resolution (batch-80 item 2):
  notify.py gained DESKTOP_MESSAGE_MAX / DESKTOP_TITLE_MAX and
  _truncate_for_desktop(), applied at BOTH _notif.notify() call sites --
  send_system_alert_detailed's and alert_strong_signal's. Only the desktop
  copy is clipped; Discord, Pushover, ntfy and email are each still handed
  the full original text, which is what keeps this a repair rather than a
  new loss. Every truncation logs a warning naming the field and both
  lengths, so the alert is no longer shortened without a record.

  THREE CORRECTIONS to this entry, all found by re-verifying it against the
  installed plyer (plyer/platforms/win/libs/win_api_defs.py:52-68) and
  against the cited source, rather than trusting the description:

  1. THE TITLE LIMIT IS 64, NOT 256. The entry names only szInfo's 256-char
     message cap. szInfoTitle is a WCHAR*64 and fails identically, four
     times sooner. It is capped too. (szTip, the third string field, is 128
     and takes app_name, hardcoded to the 14-char "Kalshi Weather".)

  2. THE ENTRY'S SECOND SUGGESTED FIX IS NOT IMPLEMENTABLE. It proposed
     "wrapping the plyer call in its own try/except so a backend failure can
     never escape the thread". It cannot: WindowsNotification._notify is
     `thread(target=balloon_tip, kwargs=kwargs).start()`, so plyer spawns
     its OWN thread and returns immediately. The ValueError is raised on
     that thread and no try/except in notify.py is on its stack -- which is
     precisely why it surfaced as a PytestUnhandledThreadExceptionWarning
     rather than as the caught-and-logged failure the existing
     `except Exception` around the call looks like it would produce. Not
     sending an over-long string is the only control available from this
     side, so truncation is the whole fix rather than half of it.

  3. THE MIAMI ALERT BODY IS ~377 CHARACTERS, NOT ~1,499. The Problem
     section above cites 1,499 and that figure is kept there as written, for
     history. Evaluating tracker.audit_settlement's actual f-string with
     realistic values renders ~372-377 depending on ticker length, and an
     AST sweep of the send_system_alert*/alert_strong_signal call sites in
     the top-level modules (12 direct ones; aliased `import ... as _alert`
     forms make an exact repo-wide count awkward, and an earlier draft's
     "31" was not reproducible) puts the longest static body at ~382-388. The defect is unchanged -- 377 still exceeds 256,
     and that alert still loses its desktop half -- but it is ~1.5x over the
     cap, not ~6x.

  Both limits are set one below the array width (255 / 63) so the NUL
  terminator has somewhere to go: measured, ctypes accepts a string of
  exactly the array length but stores it unterminated, and Shell_NotifyIconW
  reads on into the adjacent field.

  Tests: tests/test_notify.py::TestDesktopFieldTruncation, 10 new. The
  load-bearing one builds the REAL ctypes arrays and asserts the constants
  against them from both sides, because the constants are transcribed by
  hand and a wrong transcription would reintroduce the bug while every
  double-based test still passed. Mutation-verified: 255 -> 256 fails two
  tests, `<=` -> `<` fails the at-limit passthrough test, and 63 -> 255
  (i.e. this entry's own wrong assumption about the title) fails THREE --
  an earlier draft said two (opus review L-1).

  NOT fixed here, and deliberately: `successes.append(True)` still runs
  after _notif.notify() returns, even though on Windows that return means
  only "a thread was started". With truncation in place the ValueError can
  no longer be the cause, but a Shell_NotifyIconW failure would still be
  recorded as a delivered desktop channel. That is a separate defect about
  plyer's fire-and-forget contract, not about field widths -- filed as its
  own entry below.

REVIEW FINDINGS ADDRESSED (independent opus review, effort:high):
  - M-1 (the substantive one): THE BUDGET WAS IN THE WRONG UNIT. A WCHAR
    array counts UTF-16 CODE UNITS, not Python characters, so every
    character above U+FFFF costs two -- a string of 129 emoji has len() 129
    but raises ValueError("string too long (258, maximum length 256)").
    Measured on the real ctypes array. So a message clipped to 255 code
    points could still be 510 units and reproduce the ORIGINAL bug, on the
    same uncatchable thread, through a fix that looked correct. Now budgeted
    via _utf16_units(), clipping per-character by width and never splitting
    a surrogate pair. Latent today -- swept every top-level .py and found no
    character above U+FFFF (the two warning signs are U+26A0, BMP) -- but
    notify_templates.json is operator-editable and both templates .format()
    in external `city` and `ticker`, which is the same reasoning that made
    the alert_strong_signal site worth capping at all. Mutation-verified:
    reverting to a code-point budget fails the new astral test with
    "assert 400 <= 255".
  - M-2: corrected above (correction 3). The 1,499 figure came from the
    entry and was propagated into a test comment; both now say ~377.
  - L-1: the title mutation fails three tests, not two. Corrected above.
  - L-7: _truncate_for_desktop was not total for limit <= 1 -- at limit 0 it
    returned `text[:-1] + "…"`, i.e. a LONGER string than it was handed.
    Unreachable with the 255/63 constants, so hygiene only; guarded and
    tested anyway rather than left as a known sharp edge.
  - Reviewer independently confirmed, against the installed plyer rather
    than on trust: the three field widths; that the NUL-reservation
    rationale is real (ctypes accepts exactly 256, raises at 257, and
    szInfo is immediately followed by uVersion); that notify.py's
    `except Exception` genuinely cannot catch the thread's ValueError; that
    no truncation leaks to any other channel; that there is no third
    _notif.notify() call site; and that BOTH call sites are independently
    covered (untruncating either fails tests the other does not mask).

ROUND-2 REVIEW (of the round-1 fixes). No HIGH; the UTF-16 fix held up under a
~9,000-case fuzz sweep against the real ctypes arrays. Three real findings, all
of them defects the UTF-16 fix itself introduced or left:
  - L1: _utf16_units raised UnicodeEncodeError on an UNPAIRED SURROGATE, which
    ctypes itself accepts (both measured) -- a new failure mode the round-1
    len() version did not have, and reachable, since notify_templates.json is
    operator-editable and JSON permits a lone escaped surrogate. Now encodes
    with "surrogatepass".
  - L2: the new `limit <= 1` hygiene guard could itself return an over-budget
    string -- at limit 1 an astral first character is one code point but TWO
    units, so the bare slice was strictly worse than the unguarded path it
    was added to protect. It was the single over-budget case in the whole
    fuzz corpus. Now unit-checked.
  - L3: the isinstance coercion was entirely unpinned (mutating it away left
    all 21 tests green). Given a test rather than deleted -- both call sites
    format templates whose values come from callers, so the branch is live.
  All three are mutation-verified: dropping surrogatepass, restoring the bare
  degenerate slice, and removing the coercion each now fail exactly one test.
  tests/test_notify.py: 23 passed.

      only and an unresolvable prefix fails closed.
  Also fixed from those rounds: _coerce_expiration_value() now guards all four settlement
  branches against NaN/Infinity/bool (float() accepts all three; NaN stores as NULL, making a
  row look unsettled AND disputed while the call reports success); the hourly mismatch path
  alerts instead of only logging, since disputing feeds the hourly rollout gate;
  get_station_bias_by_lead dedups per EVENT rather than per ticker (strikes of one ladder are
  identical observations and shrink se by sqrt(k)); its range guards moved inside the subquery
  so one poisoned row can no longer discard its whole event; _station_bias_stats gained a
  magnitude gate and a zero-variance guard (a constant-error group otherwise read as
  significant at maximum confidence); and the backfill now reports `errored` separately from
  `skipped` plus a count of the var-NULL rows it structurally cannot reach (49 at audit time,
  39 still wrong -- run backfill-ensemble-var first). One docstring figure was corrected:
  'between' is 41 of 209 eligible rows (20%), not 111 of 312 (36%) -- the larger pair was
  measured before the metar_lockout filter the same query applies.

  KXTORNADO MONTHLY TORNADO-COUNT MODEL -- GRADUATION CRITERIA AND THE
