WHAT THE MARKET IS
  KXTORNADO -- "Number of tornadoes in <Month>?", a monthly ladder of ">N"
  brackets. Live-verified 2026-08-25: 83 markets across 7 events
  (26JUN..26DEC), 505,758 cumulative contracts, strike_type "greater" on
  every one. Brackets are 25..275 step 25 on a normal month; the June 2026
  event ran to 425 (17 brackets) because the month ran hot -- the ladder
  length is NOT fixed. Each event opens on the 20th of the PRIOR month and
  closes at midnight ET on the 1st of the FOLLOWING month (~41-42 days).
  Ticker shape "KXTORNADO-26SEP-75"; no day component, so target_date is
  None and the whole path is gated on close_time like the monthly rain/snow
  ladders. Distinct from the legacy annual TORNADO series, which this repo
  has never referenced (re-verified 2026-08-25: KXTORNADO had zero repo or
  backlog mentions before this batch).

  Settlement is SPC's PRELIMINARY storm-report count, from the market's own
  rules text: "If the preliminary number of tornadoes in Aug is above 150,
  then the market resolves to Yes", determined by the "Storm Reports Legend"
  on the "Preliminary Report Summary". Preliminary counts systematically
  OVERCOUNT the final quality-controlled database (duplicate reports for one
  tornado are not yet merged), so the model deliberately models the
  preliminary series itself and never corrects toward final counts.

DATA SOURCE (found by capturing the settlement page's own network traffic)
  https://www.spc.noaa.gov/climo/summary/<YYYY>/ruf/NAT/NAT.json
  "ruf" is SPC's path segment for the PRELIMINARY source; NAT is the
  national aggregate. Its `month` block is exactly the "<year> Monthly
  Statistics" table the settlement page renders -- verified 2026-08-25 by
  reading the rendered table and the JSON side by side for 2026.
  Cross-checked against the only two Kalshi settlements that exist:
    KXTORNADO-26JUN settled with the count in (375, 400]  <-> SPC month 399
    KXTORNADO-26JUL settled with the count in (125, 150]  <-> SPC month 136
  Coverage begins 2004 (1999/2003 404; 2000 is an all-zero placeholder),
  hence a 21-year window (2005-2025) rather than hurricane's 30.

  TRAP, documented in tornado_climatology.py's header and pinned by two
  tests: the JSON's `month` block is CALENDAR-month and its `daily` block is
  SPC CONVECTIVE-day (12Z-12Z). They disagree for 104 of the 259 months in
  2005-2026. March 2023 is the extreme case -- daily["0331"] = 163 (the Mar
  31 outbreak), daily March sums to 253, but month["3"] = 161, because 92 of
  that convective day's reports fell on calendar April 1. `month` is the
  settlement basis; `daily` is used ONLY for a within-month remaining-SHARE
  fraction, so the boundary artifact cancels out of the ratio instead of
  contaminating a subtraction.

THE MODEL
  Climatology + count-to-date bootstrap, the shape
  _analyze_hurricane_count_trade established. For each of the 21 window
  years y:
      total[y] = count_to_date + month_total(y) * remaining_share(y, as_of)
  i.e. this month's real progress plus that year's own remaining portion of
  its own month total. Reduces exactly to plain climatology at as_of=0.

  The remaining term is a rescaled SHARE of that year's month total.
  Getting that share right was the single biggest correctness issue in this
  batch, and the first version was WRONG -- see "WHAT THE REVIEW CHANGED"
  below. Both naive combinations of the two bases carry a one-directional
  UPWARD bias, so the shipped code re-attributes each month's
  (daily - month) discrepancy onto the boundary day it must have come from
  before taking any share, which reconciles to `month` exactly.

  Three phases: a target month still in the FUTURE (the routine case -- each
  event lists 11 days before its month starts) prices pure climatology and
  never touches the current-year feed; an IN-PROGRESS month needs a fresh
  count-to-date and DECLINES outright if the current-year SPC cache is older
  than 36h (a stale count-to-date biases every bracket down at once, so no
  count beats a stale one); a PAST month refuses.

  Already-decided brackets (count_to_date already past the floor) are priced
  0.99 with edge/net_edge/adjusted_edge/kelly/ci_adjusted_kelly all forced
  to zero, so they generate neither an order NOR a shadow prediction row.
  Only a decided-YES is reachable -- a monthly count only rises. Zeroing the
  edge (rather than returning None) satisfies the batch's "price 0/1, don't
  size off them" requirement while keeping trivially-certain rows out of the
  shadow Brier that this entry's own graduation decision reads.

GO/NO-GO RESULT: PASS ON THE LITERAL GATE, NO SKILL DEMONSTRATED
  The batch's gate was "any bracket >10c from a well-calibrated climatology
  early in a month". It passes -- but the numbers are weaker than that
  sentence sounds, and the graduation decision must be made against these,
  not against the headline.

  1. Snapshot, 2026-08-25. The Sep 2026 ladder showed 8 of 11 brackets more
     than 10c from mid (max 26.2c on the -125). Every one of those 8 has
     zero volume, zero open interest and a 40-56c bid/ask spread -- the
     "mid" of a 0.03/0.59 quote is not a price. Confirmed afterwards by
     running the SHIPPED analyze_trade against the live ladder: all 11
     September brackets are rejected by the bot's own universal LIQUIDITY
     gate before the model's number is ever used. The headline gate passed
     on brackets this bot would never trade.

  2. The only live bracket that survives the universal gates today is
     KXTORNADO-26AUG-100 (0.68/0.77, 5,289 contracts): model 0.57 vs market
     0.73, a 15.9c disagreement. That is the one real signal in the family
     right now, and it is late-month.

  3. Decision-time mini-backtest on the only 2 settled events (116
     bracket-observations, market price from 1440-min candlesticks at day
     5/10/15/20/25 of each month, model conditioned on the month-to-date at
     that same date). ALL NUMBERS BELOW ARE FROM THE SHIPPED ESTIMATOR --
     re-derived after the review's bias fix, which improved every one of
     them (the pre-fix figures were +5.5% overall collapsing to +0.5%):
         model Brier 0.0880 | market Brier 0.0982 | skill +10.4%
         excluding JUN-400/425 (the 399-vs-400 coin flip): +6.6%
         JUN only: +34.6%   JUL only: -63.1%
         non-trivial only (market price in 0.05-0.95): +10.3%
         decision day <= 15: +8.9%
     Read this carefully rather than as a win. n=2 EVENTS. The two events
     disagree violently in opposite directions, which is what a 2-sample
     estimate of a noisy quantity looks like; the +10.4% is not a skill
     measurement, it is one good month and one bad month. In July -- the one
     event where the market disagreed with climatology strongly and EARLY --
     the market was right: at day 5 the market priced P(>125) at 0.65 vs the
     model's 0.29, and July finished at 136. The honest summary is unchanged
     from the pre-fix version: NO SKILL IS DEMONSTRATED EITHER WAY at this
     sample size. What the fix did change is that the margin no longer
     vanishes when the single luckiest bracket is removed, so the prior is
     "unknown" rather than "probably zero".

  4. Honest read: the market appears to be pricing information climatology
     cannot see (SPC's Day 1-8 convective outlooks). That is the most likely
     explanation for both the early-month disagreements and July's outcome.
     Blending an outlook-derived expected-count into the remaining-days term
     is the obvious next model step; it was scoped OUT of batch-54
     (AskUserQuestion, 2026-08-25 -- user chose "ship shadow-only as
     specified") because turning outlook risk areas into an expected report
     count is its own modelling project needing its own validation.

  The go/no-go therefore does NOT establish edge. It establishes that the
  market is not simply quoting climatology, which is a necessary but not
  sufficient condition. Shipping now buys the sample clock, not a signal.

THE TIMELINE, STATED PLAINLY
  count_settled_tornado_count_predictions() counts distinct (year, month)
  EVENTS, not the 11-17 brackets each event settles -- all brackets of one
  month settle from the SAME single SPC number, so ticker-counting would
  report 28 independent observations where there are 2 (live-verified
  2026-08-25: 28 settled markets, 2 settled events). At one event per month
  the 20-sample floor is ~20 MONTHS. Exactly 2 events have ever settled, so
  _tornado_count_gates_active() cannot open before roughly mid-2028 even if
  every month settles cleanly from here. This is not a defect to be worked
  around by loosening the counter.

GRADUATION CRITERIA -- all four, not any of them
  1. >= 20 settled (year, month) events with shadow predictions, AND
     TORNADO_TRADING_ENABLED=1. (Mechanical; the gate already enforces it.)
  2. Shadow Brier beats the decision-time market Brier over those events,
     measured the way tracker.brier_skill_score() does it (market_prob AT
     PREDICTION TIME, never the settlement-adjacent last price), computed on
     brackets that actually cleared the universal liquidity/spread/
     extreme_price gates -- see finding 1 above for why an all-brackets
     number would be meaningless here.
  3. The margin survives dropping the single largest-contribution bracket.
     Finding 3 is the reason: one 399-vs-400 coin flip moved the headline
     from +0.5% to +5.5%.
  4. The preliminary-count MATURATION bias has been measured and found
     immaterial, or corrected for. Kalshi closes at midnight ET on the 1st
     and settles ~10h later (expiration_time 14:00Z), so it settles on a
     FRESH preliminary count, while the climatology this model reads is
     built from MATURED ones that kept rising for days-to-weeks afterward.
     The current month's own count-to-date is the freshest number in the
     whole calculation, so the two biases partially cancel -- but neither is
     quantified, because historical SPC snapshots cannot be reconstructed
     from this endpoint. The only evidence today is weakly reassuring: both
     settled events' Kalshi brackets still contain SPC's matured count
     (JUN 399 in (375,400], JUL 136 in (125,150]). Measure it forward by
     recording SPC's count at settlement time and re-reading it 30 days
     later, for each settled event.

KNOWN APPROXIMATIONS (deliberate, documented, not defects to file)
  - as_of_day = today.day - 1 for an in-progress month: the count-to-date is
    treated as complete through yesterday and today onward is bootstrapped
    from history. This double-counts whatever of today SPC has already
    filed; using today.day instead would omit a whole day's activity from
    both terms. The omission is the larger and strictly one-directional
    error (a June day averages ~13 reports), so the smaller, partly
    self-cancelling double-count was preferred.
  - Exposure-cap key is a single national "TORNADO_US" covering every
    bracket of every month, not a per-month key, even though two events are
    open simultaneously for ~11 days of each cycle. Conservative reading for
    an unvalidated family; mirrors hurricane-count's season-agnostic
    per-basin key.
  - A flat unweighted 21-year window, no recency weighting: a trend check
    found none worth correcting (2005-2014 mean annual preliminary count
    1420.4 vs 2016-2025 mean 1427.6).
  - The calendar re-attribution assumes the WHOLE (daily - month)
    discrepancy sits on the month's boundary day. That follows from the
    documented cause -- only the first and last convective days of a month
    can move reports across a month boundary -- and it reconciles exactly on
    every real month checked, but it is an attribution, not an observation:
    SPC publishes no per-calendar-day series to verify it against.
  - monthly_totals()/conditioned_month_totals() DROP a year whose SPC data
    failed to load rather than fabricating a 0 for it -- the opposite of
    hurricane's choice, and deliberate: there a storm-less season is a real
    count of 0, here a missing year is a failed fetch and a fabricated 0
    would be a fake "month with no tornadoes at all" (the smallest month in
    2005-2025 is 1). _analyze_tornado_count_trade therefore declines when
    fewer than 15 years load, matching bootstrap_ci's own CI floor.

WHAT THE FOUR OPUS REVIEWS CHANGED (effort=high, split by subsystem, plus
a fourth round reviewing the fixes themselves)
  1 HIGH plus ~13 MEDIUM and ~28 LOW, all addressed. Five findings changed
  behaviour rather than prose, and none was visible to self-review:

  * THE HIGH -- the estimator was biased. The first version took the
    remaining share straight off the raw convective-day block and argued in
    its own docstring that sharing a basis between numerator and denominator
    made the boundary artifact "cancel". It does not. The residual is
    [s_out*(M - T) + T*s_in] / D with both terms non-negative, i.e.
    one-directional and UPWARD, growing as the month elapses. Re-derived and
    measured independently before accepting: across all 21 window years at
    day 25 the raw form runs +1.4 to +4.2 reports high on average, NEVER ONCE
    negative, with excursions to +29.5 -- a systematic tilt toward YES on a
    ">N" ladder, worst exactly when the remaining term matters most. Fixed by
    re-attributing (daily - month) onto the boundary day; verified exact on
    both spill directions. This is what moved the backtest from +0.5% to
    +6.6% on the robustness cut.

  * A UTC-vs-ET "as of" reference. `_today` used datetime.now(UTC).date(),
    justified as "SPC publishes on a UTC clock" -- which does not address the
    question, since the settlement basis is a US calendar month. For the ~4-5h
    between 00:00Z and local midnight this silently flipped as_of_day to the
    convention the code's own comment rejects, refused to price a still-open
    still-September market on the evening of Sep 30, and flipped a
    not-yet-started month into the in-progress branch early. The identical
    bug had already been opus-review-caught and fixed in
    _analyze_hurricane_next_event_trade; this diverged from that fix.

  * A live HTTP call inside a unit test. The "positive control" line in the
    stale-cache test sat OUTSIDE its own patch block, so it reached
    spc.noaa.gov and asserted against live data that changes daily -- passing
    offline via the stale cache and taking a different path online.

  Also fixed: _safe_parse_close_time never actually normalized to UTC despite
  promising it (an offset-form close_time would have rejected the entire
  family behind a per-market warning); the daily-block validator checked only
  presence, not contents, so a shape change would have produced a degenerate
  distribution with a ZERO-WIDTH CI, which _price_and_size reads as maximum
  confidence; month_to_date validated the year but not the month; a 404 on a
  not-yet-published year counted against a breaker SHARED by all 21 years;
  tornado_climatology._spc_cb was missing from conftest's cross-test breaker
  reset (the live .cb_state.json already held it at 2 of 3 failures); and
  three separate hand-maintained gate lists in tests/ that hardcoded the
  then-5 families -- now all derived from
  tracker._GATE_COUPLED_EXCLUDED_CONDITION_TYPES, which removes that whole
  drift class permanently.

  ROUND 4 -- reviewing the fixes themselves -- found the single most
  important thing in the whole batch, and it is the reason that round exists
  as a standing workflow step:

  * THE ET FIX DID NOT WORK. `_analyze_tornado_count_trade` was corrected to
    resolve "today" in America/New_York, but `tornado_climatology.
    month_to_date()` still resolved its OWN datetime.now(UTC).date() to
    decide "is this the current month". Two clocks, disagreeing for exactly
    the window the fix was written to rescue. Reproduced end to end: at
    22:00 EDT on Sep 30, with the September market still open, the caller
    correctly entered its in-progress branch and month_to_date then refused
    with "2026-09 is not the current month (2026-10)" -- so analyze_trade
    still returned None. Net behaviour change from the round-2 fix on that
    path: ZERO. And the dedicated regression test could not see it, because
    it stubbed month_to_date -- the one function still carrying the bug.
    `today` is now a REQUIRED, KEYWORD-ONLY parameter (a default would just
    re-create the second clock for the next caller), and that test now
    drives the real freshness path off a real cache file instead of a stub.

  * The 4xx breaker carve-out was too wide. Exempting the whole band also
    exempted 403 and 429 -- the two statuses a WAF or rate limiter returns
    during a real outage -- removing the only backpressure on a fan-out
    where one scan prices ~105 brackets and NEITHER cache layer stores a
    failure. A 429 would have been ignored, the burst continued, more 429s:
    self-reinforcing. Narrowed to 404/410 with 429 and 403 tests pinning
    both sides.

  Round 4 also corrected two over-claims of mine and found three more
  fixtures that could not occur in production (an all-malformed daily block
  and an empty one, both of which the validator rejects one layer earlier,
  so the branches they claimed to pin were never reached outside the stub).
  The re-attribution is exact only when at most ONE boundary spills; when
  both do it nets them and under-corrects by min(s_in, s_out) -- bounded at
  <= 12 reports in >= 15 of 252 real month-years, documented rather than
  "fixed", because s_in and s_out are not separately observable from this
  endpoint.

  Two findings across the rounds were right about a defect but wrong about
  its mechanism, and one of my own tests was wrong the same way: the first
  calendar-vs-convective test claimed hurricane's subtraction "would clamp
  the remaining to 0" on the real March 2023 numbers. It does not -- at
  as_of=25 the convective to-date (90) is below the calendar total (161), so
  the clamp never fires. Mutation-testing that specific claim is what
  surfaced it, and the same technique later caught two of my ROUND-3 tests
  passing under their own mutation (a day-1 attribution test whose fixture
  made min(counts) == 1 either way, and a missing 429 test).

Priority: Medium -- nothing is broken today and the tables are tiny for the

Files: tracker.py (ensemble_member_values + orderbook_depth_snapshots

Problem:
  Batch-64 added two tables that only ever grow. purge_old_predictions()
  covers `predictions` and `outcomes` only; a grep for DELETE against either
  new table finds nothing.

  ensemble_member_values: the migration comment shipped with an estimate of
  "~24 rows/day (~9k/year)". That was derived from settled-prediction counts
  and is roughly 50x low. The real driver is batch_prewarm_ensemble's combine
  loop -- cities x target_dates x 2 vars x ~6 fetched models, times 4 cycle
  windows/day. At ~21 cities that is of order 1,200 rows/day, ~440k/year, at
  ~0.3-1 KB of values_json each, i.e. a few hundred MB/year. The comment has
  been corrected in place; the retention gap has not.

  orderbook_depth_snapshots: plain INSERT with no dedup, one row per
  subscribed ticker per DEPTH_SNAPSHOT_INTERVAL_SECS (default 60s). N
  subscribed tickers x 1,440 rows/day, and cron subscribes every scanned
  market.

Why not now:
  The retention WINDOW is a real question, not a mechanical fix, and the
  answer differs per table. A15's rank histogram and A15b's calibration half
  are explicitly long-horizon ("needs months, not days" per
  INDEX-PANEL-BACKENDS.md), so member values should probably be kept far
  longer than depth snapshots, which A4/A17 use for short-horizon replay.
  Picking either window before batches 70/71 exist to say what they actually
  read would be guessing. Batch-64's own scope was the writers, and its
  value decays with delay, so the sweep is deliberately deferred rather than
  bundled.

Plan:

  cloud_backup.backup_data writes into a per-day dated folder and keeps 30

  WINDOWS (AskUserQuestion, deliberately asked per table -- these are not
  the same question):
  - ensemble_member_values: 730 days, matching purge_old_predictions and
    prune_scan_runs, so ONE long-retention constant governs all three.
    Shipped first at 365 (a full seasonal cycle -- summer and winter
    ensemble spread are different populations, and that clears
    INDEX-PANEL-BACKENDS.md's "months, not days" bar with room), then
    raised on the opus reviewer's argument (A#3) after the user asked for
    the trade-off explicitly. Three things decided it:
      * prune_old_analysis_attempts' docstring records this module already
        learning the harder version of the lesson -- an unconditional
        rolling DELETE silently capped an evaluation corpus, and its fix
        note says to "add a much longer second cutoff (730 days would match
        purge_old_predictions' retention) rather than restoring the
        unconditional delete". Same class of corpus, same shape of pruner.
      * Sample count was NOT the reason, and was checked rather than
        assumed: at ~2,400 rows/day even 365 gives ~4,400 samples per
        (city, model, var) cell, so neither window is sample-starved. What
        730 buys is the YEAR-OVER-YEAR axis, which 365 structurally cannot
        -- by July 2027 a 365-day window has dropped July 2026, and model
        version changes (AIFS/GFS upgrades) land on roughly annual cycles.
      * The asymmetry. Too long costs ~640 MB instead of ~320 MB, accruing
        gradually and visibly over two years; too short costs data silently
        and permanently. And nothing is deleted either way until
        2027-08-25, so the two choices were behaviourally identical for a
        full year -- the decision was only ever about which default is
        safer if nobody revisits it.
    Recorded as a reversal of this session's own earlier call, not as the
    original plan. New test pins the pruners' DEFAULT arguments against
    cron's call-site values, since cron passes every window explicitly and
    a drifting default would otherwise be invisible in production.
  - orderbook_depth_snapshots: 30 days (user's pick). A4's ladder walk and
    A17's counterfactual replay are short-horizon by design, and this table
    has no dedup key at all. Still 0 rows, so its volume remains a
    projection: cron subscribes ~590 tickers and stops the WS at the end of
    cmd_cron, giving of order 2,400-10,000 rows/day; a `watch --auto --live`
    session holds the listener up continuously and is unbounded by
    comparison.

  Both migration comments were rewritten in place with the measured numbers
  and the chosen window, replacing the stale estimates.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-26 by batch-78 item 1 -- scan_runs table (schema v77/v78),
  written unconditionally by cron, and get_scan_activity() now splits its old
  "no output" bucket into a real "scanned, nothing survived" and a real "no
  scan". Originally found by the opus review of batch-65 (A12), which caught
  the panel's own docstring claiming a distinction the data cannot make;
  confirmed pre-existing, the funnel only makes it visible.] NOTHING RECORDS
  PER-DAY THAT A SCAN RAN, SO AN OUTAGE AND A FULLY-GATED DAY ARE
  INDISTINGUISHABLE
Priority: Medium -- no trading behaviour is affected, but this is the
  difference between "the cron job is dead" and "the model had nothing to
  say", and the operator-facing panel cannot currently tell them apart.
Files: tracker.py (get_scan_activity, analysis_attempts),
  trade_cycle.py (~566, the `if not analysis` branch; ~612 all_results),
  cron.py (~2389, batch_log_analysis_attempts)

Problem:
  Two tables could answer "did the scanner run on 2026-08-14", and neither
  does:

  - `analysis_attempts` is rebuilt by cron from result.all_results, and
    trade_cycle only appends to all_results AFTER `if not analysis:
    continue`. So a market rejected by any of weather_markets.SCAN_GATES
    never lands there. It records markets that SURVIVED the gates, not
    markets scanned -- 0-45/day on live data against ~590 markets per scan.
  - `predictions` only gets a row for a candidate that reached the
    placement loop.

  A scan where all 590 markets are gated out therefore writes nothing to
  either table and is indistinguishable from the cron job never running.
  That is not a corner case: the 2026-08-25 06:36 scan rejected 549 of 590
  at the gates, and a hot, calm, well-priced day plausibly rejects all of
  them.

  `analysis_attempts` also upserts on (ticker, target_date), so
  re-analysing a market on a later day MOVES its analyzed_at forward rather
  than adding a row -- on live data its per-day count is lower than the
  prediction count on 4 of the last 32 days, twice with zero attempts
  against non-zero predictions. The two counts are not nested and must not
  be drawn as one funnel.

  batch-65's get_scan_activity() was originally written asserting a
  three-way "signals / scanned, no signals / no scan" split. The third
  label was wrong and has been renamed to "no output", with the ambiguity
  documented, rather than shipping an outage indicator that fires on a
  quiet modelling day.
What it would look like:
  A per-cycle scan record cron writes unconditionally -- ticker count
  submitted, count analyzed, started/finished timestamps, and the
  completion flag trade_cycle now computes for the funnel snapshot. That is
  a new table, so it belongs with the migration-owning batches (64/72), not
  with a read-only analytics batch. Once it exists, get_scan_activity()'s
  "no output" state can split back into a real "no scan" and a real
  "scanned, nothing survived", and the panel can stop hedging.

Resolution (2026-08-26, batch-78 item 1):
  Built as described in "What it would look like" above, with one addition
  the plan did not name.

  Schema v77/v78: `scan_runs` (id, started_at, finished_at, markets_fetched,
  markets_scanned, reached_analysis, scan_completed, mode, halted_reason)
  plus idx_scan_runs_started. _SCHEMA_VERSION 76 -> 78; _MIGRATIONS is
  append-only and both entries were appended. The chain was proved to apply
  from an empty DB, to upgrade a DB staged at v76 in place, and to be
  idempotent on re-run -- all three against isolated scratch DBs, never the
  real data/predictions.db (confirmed still v76 with no scan_runs table
  afterwards).

  COUNTS, NOT A FLAG, per this entry's own design note. reached_analysis is
  what separates "ran and gated everything" (0) from "ran and analysed 40
  that all missed the edge threshold" (40); a bare ran/did-not-run row would
  collapse those back together. It is recorded per SCAN rather than per
  market precisely because analysis_attempts upserts on (ticker,
  target_date) and therefore undercounts a re-analysed market -- the same
  property this entry documents above.

  Written from cron.py in a `finally` around run_trade_cycle(), not on the
  success path. Recording only past the `if result is None: return None`
  early exit would have reproduced the exact gap the table closes: a cycle
  that started and died would look identical to one that never launched. On
  the abort and crash paths the counts go in as NULL rather than 0 -- on
  those paths they are genuinely unknown, and 0 asserts "scanned nothing",
  which is the same false certainty pointed the other way.

  trade_cycle.py: `_scan_completed` already existed (it gates the funnel
  snapshot's `complete` field, batch-65 M4) but lived only inside
  run_trade_cycle(). Surfaced as TradeCycleResult.scan_completed so the
  scan_runs row can carry it -- a truncated scan's counts must not be
  recorded as if they covered the whole market universe.

  THE ADDITION THE PLAN DID NOT NAME -- a coverage floor, and it is
  load-bearing. scan_runs is forward-only and starts empty, so every day
  before its first row has no scan record for a reason that says nothing
  about whether a scan ran. Splitting "no output" into "no scan" without a
  floor would have retroactively labelled the entire pre-batch-78 history as
  an outage -- manufacturing a fault record that never happened, which is
  strictly worse than the honest ambiguity it replaced and the same class of
  inversion the A12 docstring already warns about. get_scan_activity() now
  reads MIN(DATE(started_at)) over the WHOLE table (not the window -- a
  window starting after the first row must still treat its own days as
  covered) and exposes it as `scan_coverage_from`. Days at or after it are
  diagnosable; days before it keep the original "no output" label. With the
  table empty, `scan_coverage_from` is None and the function behaves exactly
  as it did before this change.

  get_scan_activity() additions, all additive -- web_app.py passes the dict
  straight through and there is no frontend consumer of these keys yet:
  per-day `scans`, and top-level `scanned_no_survivors_days`,
  `no_scan_days`, `total_scans`, `scan_coverage_from`. `no_output_days`
  keeps its batch-65 meaning (an observed zero of unknown cause) and now
  shrinks toward zero as the window rolls past the coverage floor.

  Retention: prune_scan_runs(days=730), matching purge_old_predictions
  rather than taking a window of its own. One row per cron cycle at ~200 B
  is ~0.3 MB/year, three orders of magnitude below batch-78 item 2's two
  tables, and a long uptime baseline is the entire point of the table.

  Tests: 39 new across both review rounds, none removed (re-counted from
  the staged diff at the moment of writing this sentence, not recalled).
  By class: TestLogScanRun 4 and TestBatch78Pruners 7 and
  TestBatch78ReviewRound2 4 (tests/test_tracker.py); TestScanRunRecord 5,
  TestScanRunRecordHaltedAndTruncated 3 and TestBatch78MondaySweepWindows 2
  (tests/test_cron_integration.py); TestScanCompletedIsExposed 4
  (tests/test_trade_cycle_engine.py); 10 added to TestScanActivity
  (tests/test_scan_funnel.py, 7 -> 17).

  Scoped suite at the end: 1114 passed across test_tracker, test_scan_funnel,
  test_cron_integration, test_cron_group_c, test_cron_lock,
  test_cron_trade_updates, test_cron_watchdog, test_trade_cycle_engine,

  ruff / ruff-format / mypy clean via the real pre-commit hook.

  One existing test was updated rather than deleted:
  test_no_output_is_not_reported_as_an_outage asserted `"no_scan_days" not
  in out`, which was correct when the function could not observe an outage
  at all. Its real claim -- no phantom outage -- is preserved and sharpened:
  it now asserts no_scan_days == 0 and scan_coverage_from is None with the
  table empty, which is a stronger guard than the key's mere absence.

  Mutation-tested via Edit, each claim individually: removing the coverage
  floor (`d >= coverage_from`) fails only
  test_days_before_the_first_scan_row_are_never_called_an_outage; scoping

  test_the_floor_is_read_from_the_whole_table_not_just_the_window; storing

  the suite re-run green afterwards.

  A finding this raised about an ADJACENT existing test, not fixed here:
  tests/test_phase2_batch_h.py::test_monday_check_uses_utc_weekday is

  asserts nothing at all about the UTC-vs-local Monday behaviour it is
  named for. Different subsystem and its own entry's worth of work; filed

OPUS REVIEW (effort:high, two reviewers split by subsystem; every finding
  addressed, none dropped). Reviewer A (tracker.py) died on an API error
  mid-run and was respawned at the user's direction rather than silently
  skipped. Reviewer B (cron.py / trade_cycle.py / tests) returned 13
  findings; the four MEDIUMs materially changed the design.

  B#1 (MEDIUM, the most valuable finding) -- THE FALSE-OUTAGE BUG CAME BACK
    BY ANOTHER ROUTE. The try/finally sat downstream of two early
    `return None` paths: the kill-switch check and the black-swan abort. On
    those days cron RAN, deliberately declined to scan, and wrote no row --
    so get_scan_activity labelled the day "no scan", i.e. an outage, and an
    operator would go hunting a dead scheduler that was working perfectly.
    Strictly worse than the pre-batch-78 "no output", and the same inversion
    scan_coverage_from was built to prevent. FIXED structurally rather than
    patched: a `_record_scan_run()` closure is now the single writer, called
    from all three exit paths, and a halt records counts NULL with
    halted_reason set ('kill_switch' / 'black_swan'). That needed a new
    state, because such a day is neither an outage nor a scan --
    get_scan_activity now discriminates on `markets_scanned IS NOT NULL` and
    reports "cron ran, no scan", with its own `cron_ran_no_scan_days` count.
  B#2 (MEDIUM) -- `watch --auto` scans and places but writes no row, so a
    watch-only day reads as a cron outage. main.py is another batch's file;
    narrowed the claim in code (the state and its docstring now say the
    verdict is about the CRON SCHEDULER specifically) and filed the wiring
    as its own entry above.
  B#3 (MEDIUM) -- the concrete green mutation: nothing anywhere asserted
    `scan_completed is False` from a non-None result, so hard-coding it True
    at the construction site passed the whole suite. That is exactly the
    case the field was added for. FIXED with a test driving the real
    `except TimeoutError` handler (patching concurrent.futures.as_completed,
    which run_trade_cycle imports at call time), plus a cron-side test
    pinning scan_completed=0 WITH non-NULL counts -- the discriminator
    against the abort path, which also records 0 but with NULLs.
    Re-mutated after the fix: now fails 2 tests.
  B#4 (MEDIUM) -- the recorder's failure was logged at debug. A permanently
    broken writer would produce no rows, and no rows is what reads as an
    outage, so the one failure that manufactures a permanent false outage
    history had no trace above debug. Now warning, matching log_scan_run.
  B#5 (LOW) -- `_scan_result is None` conflates a raise, a pre-scan kill
    switch, and a kill switch tripped AFTER the analysis loop finished (that
    third case had real counts, which run_trade_cycle discards on its way
    out). Documented rather than fixed: correcting it means changing
    run_trade_cycle's None-return contract. NULL understates what was known,
    which is the safe direction.
  B#6 (LOW) -- the `finally`'s comment overclaimed. It covers Python
    exceptions only; _install_cron_watchdog's 720s timeout calls os._exit(1),
    which runs no finally blocks, so a HUNG cycle -- the classic "cron is
    dead" symptom -- still leaves no row. Comment narrowed to say so, and to
    record that covering it would need finished_at nullable.
  B#7 (LOW) -- the three new pruners sat inside the shared Monday-sweep try,
    ahead of the VACUUM, whose finally stamps a 7-day marker: one raise would
    skip the VACUUM and suppress the entire sweep for another week. Each new
    pruner now has its own try/except.
  B#8 (LOW) -- the cron tests' SimpleNamespace stand-in could not detect a
    TradeCycleResult field being renamed or removed. Replaced with a real
    keyword-constructed TradeCycleResult via a shared `_fake_cycle_result()`
    builder; dbg/gate_counts stay defaultdicts, with the reason and the
    weakening both stated in the docstring.
  B#9 (LOW) -- `assert seen == [result.scan_completed]` was a one-value
    tautology (both sides True on the only path run). Now exercised on both
    values with a positive control asserting the two runs genuinely differed.
  B#10 (LOW) -- a test docstring pointed at test_scan_funnel.py for
    truncated-scan coverage that does not exist there behaviourally (it calls
    snapshot_scan_funnel directly and AST-checks source). Corrected, and it
    now also records that the mid-scan kill-switch path CANNOT be asserted
    through this field at all, since it returns None.
  B#11 (INFO) -- two contradictory count paragraphs in the isoformat guard's
    docstring, from my own edit. Folded into one sentence.
  B#12 (INFO) -- `reached_analysis` names two different quantities
    (scan_runs' per-scan len(all_results) vs get_scan_activity's per-day
    analysis_attempts COUNT, which upserts). Both sites now say so and say
    not to compare them.
  B#13 (INFO) -- nothing pinned started_at to the scan's START; moving the
    stamp after the call would stay green. Test added asserting
    started_at <= the moment run_trade_cycle was entered <= finished_at.

  Reviewer B also verified and reported clean: `from __future__ import
  annotations` present so the TYPE_CHECKING-only annotation is safe; the
  finally cannot mask or raise; `_scan_result` always bound; WS lifetime
  unaffected; no double-recording; TradeCycleResult's mid-dataclass field
  insertion safe (single all-keyword construction site, no astuple/asdict/
  fields()/pickling anywhere); test DB isolation genuinely autouse and
  covering unittest TestCase; the Monday-sweep test really reaches the Monday
  branch; no new test vacuous under revert; and the modified existing test
  strengthened rather than weakened. It explicitly disclosed that findings

  independently re-confirmed here by actually applying the mutation via Edit

  against the real stamp ordering).

[OPEN 2026-08-25 -- found by batch-65 (A2) while building the calibration
  decomposition panel; measured against the live DB, not inferred.] THE
  WEEKLY BRIER HALT RULE CANNOT SEE A POOLED SCORE THAT IS ALREADY
  SIGNIFICANTLY PAST ITS OWN THRESHOLD
Priority: Medium -- LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED is unset so nothing is halted or
  not-halted today, but the rule exists precisely to be the operator's
  "stop, the model is degrading" signal, and on current data it is silent
  while the pooled score is significantly over the bar it thresholds on.
Files: cron.py (the two-consecutive-weeks Brier alert block, ~2911),
  tracker.py (get_brier_over_time, detect_brier_drift,
  get_calibration_decomposition), utils.py (BRIER_ALERT_THRESHOLD)

Problem:
  The halt rule reads get_brier_over_time(weeks=3) and alerts only when the
  last TWO weekly values both exceed BRIER_ALERT_THRESHOLD (0.22). Three
  separate properties of that query keep it quiet:

  1. It reads the multiday_predictions view, which drops days_out = 0 --
     56% of settled rows as of 2026-08-24. D+0 is invisible to the rule
     entirely, and it is the horizon where the model does worst.
  2. It groups by ISO-ish week. On live data the per-week sample counts run
     2 to 15 rows (measured 2026-08-25: W29 n=7, W30 n=2, W31 n=7, W32
     n=15, W33 n=10). A weekly mean over 2 rows crosses or clears 0.22 for
     reasons unrelated to model quality, in both directions.
  3. It pools every city and every horizon >= 1 into one number.

  Measured on the same filtered population every other Brier-quality query
  uses (outcomes_valid, _excluded_brier_condition_types applied), n = 214:
  pooled Brier 0.259619, standard error 0.015112. The lower end of a
  one-sided 95% interval is 0.2348 -- still above 0.22. The new
  get_calibration_decomposition() reports that pooled cell as "degraded";
  the halt rule has never fired.

  This is a sensitivity question, not a bug in either piece of code: the
  panel and the rule are both correct about their own populations. It is
  filed because the two now visibly disagree on the console, which is worse
  than either being quietly wrong.
What it would look like:
  Decide which population the rule SHOULD threshold on -- most likely the
  same one A14/A2 use (all horizons, condition-filtered) with a sample
  floor and a significance test rather than a bare weekly mean over
  whatever rows happened to settle. Any change here is a change to a
  live-trading safety signal and needs its own batch: it must not be folded
  into a read-only analytics change. batch-65 deliberately did NOT touch
  cron.py or get_brier_over_time.

[OPEN 2026-08-25 -- found by batch-65 (A12) while giving the scanner gates
  a declared order; the gap is pre-existing, the funnel just makes it
  visible.] THE SCANNER FUNNEL STOPS AT analyze_trade -- PLACEMENT-TIME
  REJECTIONS ARE COUNTED NOWHERE
Priority: Low -- no trading behaviour is affected; this is an
  observability gap in the answer to "why did this scan place nothing".
Files: weather_markets.py (SCAN_GATES, _count_gate),
  trade_cycle.py (the `dbg` counters, ~504), order_executor.py
  (MAX_POSITIONS_PER_DATE and the sibling risk limits, ~4234 and ~4673),
  web_app.py (/api/scanner-funnel, /api/scan-stats)

Problem:
  A candidate passes through three stages and only the first is counted in
  one ordered place:

  1. analyze_trade()'s 35 gates -- now declared in order as
     weather_markets.SCAN_GATES and served by /api/scanner-funnel.
  2. trade_cycle's `dbg` edge/threshold counters (no_analysis, mkt_prob,
     divergence, net_edge, prob_edge, placement_gate) -- counted, written
     to signals_cache.json, served by /api/scan-stats as `filters`, but
     with no declared order and no labels.
  3. order_executor's placement-time risk limits -- MAX_POSITIONS_PER_DATE,
     the spend caps, already-open/traded-today dedup. These are logged as
     skip reasons but never counted, so a scan where every survivor was
     stopped by the per-settlement-date cap looks, in every counter the
     dashboard can see, exactly like a scan where nothing survived the
     model.

  batch-65 deliberately covered only stage 1: trade_cycle.py and
  order_executor.py are outside its declared file scope, and stage 3 in
  particular sits in the live-order path.
What it would look like:
  Give stages 2 and 3 the same treatment stage 1 just got -- a declared
  ordered list with human labels, defined beside the checks themselves, and
  a bounded near-miss record for the numeric ones. Stage 3's counters must
  be pure instrumentation with no effect on any gate's own decision, and
  need a test proving a counter failure cannot change whether an order is
  placed.

  prevent.
Files: execution_log.py (record_live_partial_exit, ~1391-1396),
  order_executor.py (_get_live_open_positions, ~2033), main.py
  (cmd_order's exit cascade), order_executor.py (_exit_live_position)

Problem:
  record_live_partial_exit guards its UPDATE with
  `COALESCE(fill_quantity, quantity) >= filled_count`. When the two are
  EQUAL the guard passes and the UPDATE writes
  fill_quantity = current - filled_count = 0, leaving settled_at NULL.
  _get_live_open_positions then reads `fill_quantity or quantity` -- and 0
  is falsy, so it falls back to `quantity`, resurfacing the position at its
  ORIGINAL size with zero real contracts behind it.

  The function's own docstring already worries about exactly this ("a
  negative or exactly-zero fill_quantity is falsy, which
  _get_live_open_positions()'s `fill_quantity or quantity` fallback would
  silently misread") but the guard it chose only excludes the NEGATIVE
  case, not the zero one.

  Reachable with a stale snapshot: caller holds quantity=20, a concurrent
  writer reduces the real row to 3, caller's remaining fill is 3.
  record_live_exit_fill sees 3 < 20 and takes the PARTIAL branch;
  record_live_partial_exit sees 3 >= 3, passes, writes 0. Position
  reappears at 20.

  NOT introduced by batch-60: the same sequence is possible against the
  pre-cascade single-position code and against round-1's cascade. Flagged
  here because batch-60's cascade is a caller and the round-3 review
  surfaced it while reading that path.
What it would look like:
  Change the guard to `>`. An exact-match call is a FULL close and belongs
  in record_live_exit_fill's other branch, so rejecting it here is correct
  -- record_live_exit_fill would then raise its (now accurately worded)
  settled-or-reduced RuntimeError, and main.cmd_order's cascade already
  handles that by re-reading and retrying against the real size, which
  routes it to the full-close branch. Needs its own check of
  order_executor._exit_live_position, the OTHER caller, which does not have
  that retry and would newly see a raise where it previously got a silent
  wrong write; plus a regression test at the execution_log level
  (fill_quantity must never be written 0) and one proving the position does
  not resurface.

  _settle_recovered_exit_order STILL CLOSES ONLY THE OLDEST MATCHING LIVE

Priority: Low today (LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED unset, so no live sell can reach
  this at all), but it is a real-order bookkeeping path and inherits the
  exact severity of the bug batch-60 item 4 just closed on the synchronous

Files: order_executor.py (_settle_recovered_exit_order, ~381-450;
  _recover_pending_orders, its only caller), main.py (cmd_order's
  OrderStatusUnknownError branch, ~6050), execution_log.py
  (record_live_exit_fill, set_exit_row_attribution)

Problem:
  batch-60 item 4 replaced cmd_order's "hand the whole filled count to the
  oldest matching tracked position" logic with a FIFO cascade across every
  match, because record_live_exit_fill clamps the count to that one
  position's quantity -- so selling 10 against positions of 4 and 6 fully
  closed the 4 and left the 6 marked open in execution_log with no
  contracts behind them on the exchange.

  The recovery route still does exactly the old thing. If
  client.place_order raises OrderStatusUnknownError, cmd_order logs the row
  status='unknown' and RE-RAISES (main.py:6063), so the cascade block
  further down never runs at all. _recover_pending_orders later resolves
  that row and calls _settle_recovered_exit_order, which reads the single
  exit_row["closes_position_id"] and passes the whole fill_count to
  record_live_exit_fill against that one position (order_executor.py:414,
  ~435-450) -- same clamp, same phantom-open remainder, just asynchronous.

  Verified 2026-08-25 by reading both functions directly at
  b67fe864+batch-60, not inferred from the round-1 finding's wording.

  Sharpened by batch-60 itself: closes_position_id on that row is the
  PRE-PLACEMENT guess (the oldest match, resolved before the order is sent
  so a crash mid-flight still leaves a reconcilable record). On the
  synchronous route batch-60's new execution_log.set_exit_row_attribution()
  corrects that pointer to the position the last leg actually came from --
  but it is called from inside the cascade, which this route never reaches.
  So recovery reads a pointer that is now known to be provisional, with no
  marker saying so.
What it would look like:
  Give _settle_recovered_exit_order the same oldest-first cascade: re-derive
  the full match list for (ticker, side) via _get_live_open_positions()
  rather than trusting the single stored pointer, consume fill_count across
  it, and reuse set_exit_row_attribution() for the trailing partial exactly
  as cmd_order now does. Needs its own tests (the recovery path has no
  multi-position coverage today) and its own review -- it returns a
  retry-or-not boolean that _recover_pending_orders depends on for whether
  to revert the row to 'unknown', so a partially-completed cascade has a
  retry-semantics question the synchronous path does not have.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-25 (batch-60 item 1) -- originally found by the opus
  review (effort=high) of the KXHIGHNY-26APR17-B70 stale-target_date guard
  immediately above this entry; scoped out at the time per step 27's

  that risks blocking a legitimate long-horizon trade. See resolution
  below.] place_paper_order()'S NEW STALE-TARGET_DATE GUARD
  HAS NO UPPER BOUND
Priority: Low -- no known real trigger today (hypothetical: a mis-parsed
  ticker with a garbage 2-digit year producing a far-future target_date).
Files: paper.py (place_paper_order)

Problem:
  The new STALE_TARGET_DATE_GRACE_DAYS guard (see the entry immediately
  above) only rejects a target_date more than 3 days in the PAST. A
  target_date far in the FUTURE (e.g. from a ticker-parsing bug computing
  the wrong century/year) sails through unchecked -- only one direction of
  the same underlying "is this date sane" question is guarded.
What it would look like:
  Cross-reference each market family's own already-existing MAX_DAYS_OUT-
  style ceiling (weather_markets.py) rather than inventing a new generic
  bound in paper.py, which doesn't know which family a given ticker
  belongs to.

Resolution (2026-08-25, batch-60 item 1):
  This entry's "what it would look like" was right and the batch-60 handoff
  prompt's own framing was wrong: the handoff said to "grep for the real
  max-days-out the scanner already honors (the analysis path has one)".
  There is no one. analyze_trade's days-out gate uses FOUR ceilings --
  MAX_DAYS_OUT=5 (daily temp, and the `else` branch every other family
  falls through to), RAIN_MAX_DAYS_OUT=31, SNOW_MAX_DAYS_OUT=31,
  HURRICANE_MAX_DAYS_OUT=260. Bounding everything by the obvious-looking
  MAX_DAYS_OUT would have rejected a legitimate KXHURCTOT paper trade
  outright: that series' confirmed-live window is ~245 days (open
  2026-04-01, close 2026-12-02). Exactly the failure this entry warned
  about, and exactly the shape of
  [[feedback_validation_bound_sentinel_values]].

  Shipped:
  - weather_markets.max_days_out_for_ticker(ticker) -- the per-family
    lookup, built from the same four constants the gate reads and placed
    beside the family predicates it is built from. Uses the broad
    is_hurricane_ticker() (this file's documented single source of truth)
    rather than the three narrow count/next-event/storm-order carve-outs:
    those are strict substring subsets of it, and the broad form also
    covers the per-city landfall / KXHURCAT tickers a human operator can
    type straight into cmd_order, which share the season-length horizon
    but have no model of their own.
  - paper.validate_target_date_freshness(ticker, target_date) -- one shared
    guard bounding BOTH directions, replacing the inline past-only check in
    place_paper_order. main.cmd_order's live buy calls this same function
    (see the LIVE cmd_order entry below) rather than carrying a second
    hand-written copy.
  - The future bound is family_ceiling + STALE_TARGET_DATE_GRACE_DAYS
    (8/34/263). The grace is deliberate slack, NOT timezone-skew
    compensation -- an earlier draft of the comment claimed the latter with
    the direction backwards, caught by opus review F4 and verified here:
    all 21 cities in weather_markets._CITY_TZ are west of UTC, so
    local_today <= utc_today() always and a date measured against
    utc_today() can only ever read CLOSER than the gate's own figure. A
    trade that cleared the gate could never trip this bound even at zero
    grace. The slack is kept for the paths where the date never went
    through that gate -- cmd_order and the dashboard both accept a raw
    operator-typed ticker, and the guard's own close_time fallback reads a
    UTC instant rather than a city-local date.
  - Fails OPEN to the most permissive ceiling on any lookup failure
    (import error, or a None ticker whose .upper() raises -- opus review
    F8). This is a sanity backstop against a mis-parsed date, not a safety
    gate, so refusing an otherwise-valid trade would be the worse outcome.

  Decision surfaced to the user before implementation (three options:
  per-family with unknown->MAX_DAYS_OUT, per-family with unknown->260, or a
  single universal 260). Chose per-family with unknown->MAX_DAYS_OUT, i.e.
  mirroring analyze_trade's gate exactly.

  Tests: tests/test_batch60_trade_entry_guards.py::TestMaxDaysOutForTicker
  (13 parametrized families + a not-all-equal positive control, since the
  parametrized assertions would pass vacuously if the four constants ever
  held the same value), ::TestValidateTargetDateFreshness (both boundaries
  per family, the 245-day hurricane sentinel, the same date accepted for
  hurricane and refused for temp, None/unparseable no-ops, and both
  fail-open paths), ::TestPlacePaperOrderFutureBound (refusal happens
  before any ledger write; a normal near-future date still books).

  Drift protection, after opus review F16: the first version of the pin
  asserted max_days_out_for_ticker == getattr(utils, <name from a map in
  the test>), which does NOT cover the drift it claimed to -- repointing
  analyze_trade's own `elif _is_monthly_snow:` branch at a different
  constant left all 13 parametrized tests green (confirmed by mutation).
  Replaced with test_gate_branch_wiring_is_exactly_what_the_helper_mirrors,
  which reads the gate's branch->constant wiring out of the source via AST
  and requires the helper to agree family by family, plus a positive
  control proving the reader parses the real source rather than echoing the
  test's own map. That mutation now fails.

  Verification covering all four batch-60 items (counted fresh at the
  moment of writing this sentence): 480 tests pass across the 8 files that

  test_trading_gates, test_p1_remaining, test_paper, test_debug_fixes,

  Answered "the identical guard" -- one shared
  paper.validate_target_date_freshness() (see the entry above), called from
  cmd_order's `if _is_live and action == "buy":` block, not a second
  hand-written copy. A duplicated guard is how batch-57's exclusion-tuple
  drift happened. Re-verified before starting that
  `grep STALE_TARGET_DATE_GRACE_DAYS main.py order_executor.py` still
  returned nothing, i.e. the gap was real at b67fe864.

  Buy only, deliberately: a sell REDUCES exposure, and blocking an exit on
  a stale date would be backwards in exactly the way check_position_limits'
  own buy-only comment already documents for the sibling gate three blocks
  down.

  The order's target_date derivation is now hoisted to a single
  _target_date_ord/_target_date_str_ord pair computed once after the
  analysis block, so the value the guard VALIDATES is provably the value
  the trade is BOOKED with -- two copies could have drifted into checking
  one date and recording another. Three sources in priority order:
  _enriched["_date"], then _analysis["target_date"] (the KXRAIN*M fallback,
  whose _date is None by design), then the date of _market["close_time"].

  That third fallback exists because of opus review F7, which found the
  guard blind on exactly the families the new per-family ceiling was built
  for: both upper sources go dark for monthly rain/snow when analyze_trade
  gates the market OUT -- which is precisely what it does to a far-future
  one -- so `order buy KXRAINNYCM-27JUN-5.0 ...`, ~300 days out and far
  past RAIN_MAX_DAYS_OUT+3, reached the guard as a bare None and would have
  placed a REAL order unchecked. The daily-temp families the tests exercise
  hide this: their _enriched["_date"] survives a gated analysis.

  Two bugs the hoist itself caused or exposed, both fixed here:
  - The hoist initially broke cmd_order's Brier/prediction block, which
    still referenced the removed `_target_date` local. NameError, silently
    swallowed by that block's own `except Exception -> _log.warning`, so
    accuracy tracking for every manual order would have stopped recording
    with nothing but a log line. Found by a mutation run, not by the suite
    -- nothing covered that path. Fixed and now covered by
    test_brier_tracking_receives_the_same_date_the_guard_validated, which
    asserts the real date OBJECT (not the ISO string) reaches both
    log_analysis_attempt and log_prediction.
  - The position-limit check three blocks down re-derived its own date from
    _enriched["_date"] ALONE, without the rain fallback -- so
    check_position_limits received None for monthly-rain orders and its
    city/date, directional, and correlated-group caps were all silently
    skipped. That contradicted both the fallback's own stated purpose ("so
    a manual live order gets the same real exposure-cap/correlation
    grouping key the automated path already has, not a silent None") and
    check_position_limits' docstring, which claims those caps "are no
    longer provably skipped for this ticker family". The original fix wired
    the fallback to the place_paper_order call only and missed the
    exposure-cap consumer it was written for. Now both read the one hoisted
    value.

    BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, not a pure bug fix: a manual buy on a family where
    _enriched["_date"] is None but the analysis/close_time date is real
    (monthly rain, monthly snow) can now be BLOCKED by caps it previously
    sailed past. Dormant today -- cmd_order refuses every KXRAIN*M ticker
    outright while _rain_gates_active() is false, and check_position_limits
    refuses again behind that -- so it starts biting only when
    RAIN_TRADING_ENABLED=1. That is the
    [[feedback_pooled_gate_new_member_blind_spot]] pattern: the day a
    family graduates it would otherwise inherit an all-clear on caps that
    had never once been applied to it.

  Tests: tests/test_batch60_trade_entry_guards.py::
  TestCmdOrderLiveBuyTargetDateGuard (expired and far-future both refused
  before client.place_order, with a sane-date positive control proving the
  harness reaches placement at all, so the two assert_not_called checks are
  measuring the guard rather than a harness that never gets that far; plus
  the close_time backstop and its in-horizon positive control) and
  ::TestCmdOrderPositionLimitTargetDate (a KXRAINNYCM buy whose _date is
  None must still hand the caps a real grouping key; positive control
  asserts _enriched["_date"] is None so the analysis fallback is provably
  the only possible source). Every one mutation-tested by reverting the
  specific line under test.

  `metar._dynamic_lock_in_confidence()` is hard-bounded to [0.72, 0.97]
  (its own docstring states this range explicitly). Run through the real

  writing -- re-check `data/metar_lockout_calibration.json`, cron.py's
  D5 weekly block auto-retrains it) across that ENTIRE input range, the
  calibrated output never exceeds ~0.766 for a YES-lock or ~0.595 for a
  NO-lock -- both permanently below cron.py:1471's `_sig_conf >= 0.80`
  force-close gate. Independently verified by hand-computation (not just
  taking the review's word for it): swept clearance x hour x margin_f=1.0
  through both the raw formula and `apply_metar_calibration`, confirmed
  max(calibrated) = 0.7661 (YES) / 0.5954 (NO) < 0.80 with no exceptions.

  CROSS-REFERENCE 2026-08-26 (batch-82): batch-76 re-derived this same
  compression from scratch on 2026-08-25 without finding this entry, and
  reported 0.54647607 where this entry reports 0.5954. The two figure sets
  look contradictory and are NOT -- they report different quantities at
  different points of the same curve. Written down once here so a third
  session does not repeat the work.
    g = ml_bias.apply_metar_calibration takes P(YES). A lock confidence
  lives in [0.72, 0.97] (metar.py, see the two-sites note below), so g's
  actual input domain is [0.03, 0.28] for a NO-lock and [0.72, 0.97] for a
  YES-lock. Re-verified live against the fitted coefficients on disk
  (a=b=0.2261958294541918, c=0.40007576061723593, n=33):
      g(0.03) = 0.40463162031     g(0.28) = 0.54647607006
      g(0.72) = 0.64878641873     g(0.97) = 0.76608848699
  - This entry's no_ceiling 0.59536837969 = 1 - g(0.03): P(NO) at the MOST
    confident NO-lock. Its yes_ceiling 0.7660884869914 = g(0.97).
  - batch-76's 0.54647607 = g(0.28): P(YES) at the LEAST confident NO-lock.
  They agree exactly -- for a 0.97 NO-lock, g(0.03) = 0.4046 and
  0.4046 + 0.5954 = 1.0.
    ONE THING NEITHER RECORD HAD, and it matters more than the
  reconciliation: THE [0.72, 0.97] BOUND EXISTS IN TWO PLACES, NOT ONE.
  metar.py:104 in _dynamic_lock_in_confidence and metar.py:146 in
  _between_dynamic_lock_in_confidence, both `round(min(0.97, max(0.72,
  conf)), 3)`. Raising "the cap" is therefore TWO edits.
    And the asymmetry that reads as an oversight later, stated precisely
  (a coarser version of this -- "between is not protected by 10b" -- is
  WRONG): _between_dynamic_lock_in_confidence has THREE call sites in
  _metar_lock_in. Two are between-NO and set "monotone_safe": True; the
  third is between-YES and sets it False. weather_markets.py section 10b
  (`# 10b. METAR lock side-agreement override`, with
  `rec_side = _lock_outcome` further down -- find them by those strings,
  the line numbers move every batch) gates on monotone_safe, so it covers
  2 of the 3. It is BETWEEN-YES specifically whose ceiling/floor
  arithmetic 10b does not make safe.

  Separately: `ml_bias.fit_metar_calibration()` is fit on
  `tracker.get_metar_lockout_calibration_data()` rows, which come from
  `weather_markets._metar_lock_in()` -- called with `margin_f=3.0`
  (default) against the daily running-extreme temperature
  (`fetch_metar_daily_extreme`). `settlement_monitor.py`'s T-ticker path
  calls the same underlying `check_metar_lockout()` with
  `margin_f=_SETTLEMENT_MARGIN_F=1.0` against the INSTANTANEOUS reading
  (`obs["current_temp_f"]`). The settlement path's raw confidence scores
  are drawn from a different population (different margin, different
  temperature basis) than the one the model was fit on -- applying the
  entry-path model here is an extrapolation, not a like-for-like
  correction, even though it still moves scores in the right direction.

What it would look like:
  Two independent pieces of follow-up work, only worth doing once the
  settlement monitor is actually scheduled and producing real signals:
  (1) Decide whether/how to rescale cron.py's 0.80 force-close gate for
  the calibrated scale -- note NO-locks cap at ~0.595 (worse than most
  reasonable confidence thresholds) even in the best case, so a single
  shared threshold for both outcomes may not make sense; a real decision
  needs real settlement-lag outcome data, not this synthetic sweep alone.
  (2) Consider fitting a settlement-path-specific calibration model
  (own margin_f/temperature-basis population) rather than reusing the
  entry-path one, once enough settlement-lag rows with real outcomes
  exist to fit one.

Why not now:
  No real settlement-lag data exists yet to inform either fix -- the
  scheduled task has never run. Rescaling cron.py's gate speculatively,
  before any real data shows what the calibrated distribution actually
  looks like in production, risks tuning to the wrong number. Shipping
  the calibration wiring itself (this file's next entry) with the gate
  left as-is is the conservative choice: it fixes the two-calibration-
  regimes disagreement the original entry reported, and the mechanism
  simply stays dormant (as it already has been) until this is revisited.

When to revisit:
  As soon as someone runs `py main.py schedule` to actually register the
  `KalshiWeatherSettlementMonitor` task (or otherwise starts running
  `settlement-monitor` regularly) and settlement-lag signals start
  accumulating with real outcomes -- pull real confidence distributions
  before picking a new threshold, and reconsider whether a
  settlement-path-specific calibration fit is warranted at that point.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-16 -- see resolution below.]
  SETTLEMENT_MONITOR.PY'S FORCE-CLOSE TRIGGER USES THE SAME
  RAW, NOW-KNOWN-OVERCONFIDENT METAR LOCK-IN NUMBER THE ENTRY PATH JUST
  GOT CALIBRATED -- THE TWO SIDES OF THE SAME TRADE NOW DISAGREE
Priority: Medium -- affects paper trades directly (which feed the accuracy
  circuit breaker, which DOES gate live money), not live orders directly.

Problem:
  `metar.py`'s `_dynamic_lock_in_confidence()` -- the same hand-tuned,
  never-outcome-validated formula the entry-path fix below (this file's
  first entry) just measured at 89.6% predicted / 70.4% actual on YES-locks
  and corrected -- has a SECOND live consumer: `settlement_monitor.py:370`
  calls `metar.check_metar_lockout()`, which uses the identical raw
  formula. `cron.py:1471` force-closes matching PAPER positions at
  0.97/0.03 whenever that raw confidence >= 0.80.

  After the entry-path fix ships, `analyze_trade` prices a fresh METAR
  lock at the CALIBRATED probability (e.g. 0.71 instead of 0.90), while
  `cron`'s settlement-lag auto-close treats the SAME underlying signal as
  confident enough to force-close an open position at 0.97/0.03 -- the
  two sides of the same trade are now priced under different calibration
  regimes. Paper P&L from these forced closes feeds the accuracy circuit
  breaker (paper.is_accuracy_halted()), so this isn't cosmetic bookkeeping.

What it would look like:
  Wire `ml_bias.apply_metar_calibration()` (built for the entry-path fix)
  into `settlement_monitor.py`'s force-close confidence check too, using
  the same `data/metar_lockout_calibration.json` model. The `between`
  path in settlement_monitor.py uses its own separate confidence formula
  (not `_dynamic_lock_in_confidence`) and is out of scope here -- only the
  T-ticker (above/below) force-close path at line 370 is affected.

Why not now:
  Genuinely separate module (`settlement_monitor.py`, not
  `weather_markets.py`), separate call chain (`cron.py` ->
  `run_settlement_monitor` -> `check_city_settlement`, not `analyze_trade`),
  separate consumer with its own threshold semantics (a force-CLOSE
  trigger, not an entry price) -- fails the same-payload test the standing
  workflow uses to decide inline-fix vs. follow-up-entry (does this feed
  the SAME output/data-flow the current change is already touching? No --
  it's a different function's own confidence check on a different
  decision). Found via opus review while building the entry-path fix, not
  originally in scope for it.

When to revisit:
  No blocking dependency -- `ml_bias.apply_metar_calibration()` and
  `data/metar_lockout_calibration.json` already exist once the entry-path
  fix ships. Buildable immediately by whoever picks this up.

Resolution (2026-08-16, same session, opus review effort=high on the
  diff before commit):
  Added `settlement_monitor._calibrate_metar_settlement_confidence()`,

  signal()`. Converts the direction-relative `confidence` to P(YES)
  (mirrors weather_markets.py's exact `outcome=="yes" ? confidence :

  confidence on any error or missing model. `between` path untouched, as
  scoped. 8 new tests in `tests/test_settlement_monitor.py`

  Opus review (effort=high) on the diff before commit found the
  orientation/cap logic itself correct (independently re-verified: hand-

[RESOLVED 2026-08-16 -- see resolution below.] METAR SAME-DAY LOCK-IN PREDICTIONS GET ZERO STATISTICAL CALIBRATION CORRECTION -- RAW _dynamic_lock_in_confidence() OUTPUT FEEDS LIVE TRADES UNCORRECTED
Priority: High -- directly affects real-money live trades. `py main.py
  validate`'s same-day calibration curve showed the 7% and 91% buckets
  badly miscalibrated (predicted 90.8% vs actual 72.7% at the high end,
  N=33); root-caused to a specific, quantifiable gap in the live trade-
  analysis path, not a general "same-day needs better calibration" framing.

Problem:
  weather_markets.py's analyze_trade() has an `if not metar_locked: ...
  else: ...` split (~line 11252/12084). The `if` branch (normal ensemble
  path) runs temperature scaling (section 7b), then GBM, then Platt. The
  `else` branch (METAR-locked) never reaches ANY of them --
  `_temp_scaling_applied` is hardcoded False rather than computed (the
  comment there explains this is deliberate: GBM/Platt are trained on
  model-blend outputs and would miscalibrate METAR-derived probabilities if
  applied). So `blended_prob` for a METAR lock is exactly
  `_dynamic_lock_in_confidence()`'s raw output (metar.py, commit `5faa7e4a`
  "L6-D", April 2026) -- a hand-tuned linear formula (0.72 + 0.18*clearance
  factor + 0.07*hour factor) whose only tests check it reproduces its own
  documented example values. It was never validated against real settlement
  outcomes.

  Queried the DB directly (2026-08-16) for `method='metar_lockout'` sameday
  predictions with real outcomes (33 total, condition_type NULL/above/
  below):
    YES-locks (n=27): predicted 89.6% avg, actual hit rate 70.4% -- 19.2pp
      overconfident. 12 of 27 wrong despite claiming 75-97% confidence.
    NO-locks (n=6): predicted ~93% NO-confidence avg, actual NO rate 50.0%
      -- worse, though n=6 is thin.
  Secondary bug found in the same investigation: `train_all_temperature_
  scaling`'s sameday T-fit query pooled in these same metar_lockout rows
  (no method filter) even though that T is NEVER applied to them at
  inference (the else branch never calls apply_temperature_scaling) -- a
  train/serve mismatch dragging the T fit toward data it doesn't actually
  correct.

Resolution (2026-08-16):
  First pass added ml_bias.fit_metar_calibration()/apply_metar_calibration():
  full 2-parameter beta calibration (Kull, Silva Filho & Flach, AISTATS
  2017), g(s)=sigmoid(a*ln(s) - b*ln(1-s) + c), with a fallback to plain
  Platt scaling (the a=b special case) when the full fit degenerated. Wired
  into weather_markets.py's metar_locked branch reusing `_ML_CORRECTION_LIMIT`
  (0.30, the same cap GBM/Platt use) as a safety valve, and a `>=30`-row
  floor framed as Gneiting 2005's 10-per-parameter rule.

  Per explicit user request, TWO independent opus reviews (effort=high) ran
  against that first pass -- one scoped to statistical/mathematical
  correctness, one to live-trading-path integration -- and both
  independently found the design itself was wrong, not just buggy, plus
  several real implementation gaps. All addressed, none deferred:

  REDESIGNED to fit Platt scaling directly instead of "beta calibration
  with a Platt fallback" (both reviews, converging on the same conclusion
  from different angles):
    - ln(s) and ln(1-s) are deterministic functions of each other, and
      METAR lock-in scores cluster in two narrow bands ([0.72,0.97] for
      YES-locks, [0.03,0.28] for NO-locks) -- identifying genuine asymmetry
      needs curvature WITHIN each band, which this scoring distribution
      barely provides regardless of sample size. Empirically: even at
      n=400 with deliberately asymmetric synthetic miscalibration, the full
      fit degenerated to the Platt-equivalent a=b solution in 6 of 8
      random seeds.
    - The full-fit path had no regularization, so a real, plausible
      perfect-separation sample produced unregularized coefficients that
      passed every guard and forced maximum-confidence (0.01/0.99)
      corrections from a nonexistent MLE.
    - The degenerate-fallback logic itself went through two unsafe designs
      first: pinning the offending coefficient at a fixed 1.0 (verified
      unsafe -- acts as an offset term, distorts the other coefficient's
      sign too), then falling back to Platt -- but since the full fit
      degenerates most of the time anyway (see above), Platt WAS
      effectively the primary path, just reached through fragile,
      unregularized, two-optimizer (BFGS+Nelder-Mead) machinery first.
  Fitting Platt directly reuses `_fit_platt`'s existing, already-validated
  bounds (raises if a<=0, |a|>5, or |b|>5) -- closing the separation/blowup
  risk for free -- and is what the real production data (27 YES-locks, 6
  NO-locks) already converged to. Result still stored as (a,a,c) so
  apply_metar_calibration's signature/JSON schema needed no change.

  HIGH fixes beyond the redesign:
    - The magnitude cap was reusing `_ML_CORRECTION_LIMIT` (0.30, sized for
      GBM/Platt's small touch-ups to an already-reasonable probability).
      Verified against the real fitted model that EVERY NO-lock correction
      (delta 0.35-0.38 on the measured 0.03-0.15 raw range) exceeded 0.30
      and was silently skipped, while every YES-lock correction (delta up
      to ~0.20) was applied -- the fix was a no-op on exactly the
      worse-miscalibrated half (measured 93% NO-confidence vs 50% actual)
      while still correcting the other half, a NEW asymmetry that didn't
      exist before. Gave this correction its own `_METAR_CORRECTION_LIMIT`
      (0.60), sized to comfortably cover the full observed range with
      headroom while still catching a genuinely pathological correction.
    - Closed feedback loop: `bias` stayed hardcoded 0.0 in the metar_locked
      branch, so tracker.py's `raw_prob = forecast_prob + bias_correction`
      reconstructed the ALREADY-CALIBRATED value, not the true raw
      `_dynamic_lock_in_confidence()` output. Every future `calibrate` run
      would train partly on already-corrected data, understating the true
      miscalibration and pulling the fit toward identity over successive
      retrains, with no way to recover the true raw series afterward. Fixed
      by setting `bias = pre_correction_prob - blended_prob` for
      metar_locked trades (scoped so the non-metar path's own real bias,
      from get_quintile_bias(), is untouched).
    - `_load_metar_calibration` returned the STALE cached model (not None)
      on a degenerate or out-of-bounds file -- the opposite of
      `_load_platt_models`'s behavior. An operator hand-editing the file to
      neutralize a bad correction would not actually disable it in an
      already-running loop/watch process. Rewired to distinguish 3 cases:
      file genuinely absent (clear cache), transient I/O error on
      exists()/stat() (KEEP cache, retry next call -- a new gap the review
      also caught: the previous version wiped the cache on ANY OSError,
      including a real-but-transient AV-lock/rename-window read failure),
      and file present-but-invalid (clear cache, but record mtime so a
      standing-invalid file isn't re-parsed and re-logged every call).

  MEDIUM fixes:
    - No validation that settled_yes is exactly 0 or 1 -- a corrupted DB
      row could silently distort the fit. Added.
    - No check for non-finite (NaN/inf) fit coefficients before saving.
      Added.
    - The `>=30`-row floor was framed as "Gneiting 2005's 10-per-parameter
      rule" but Gneiting 2005 is a continuous-outcome ensemble-calibration
      heuristic (correctly used elsewhere in this file for EMOS), not a
      classification events-per-variable (EPV) rule -- and even taken at
      face value it should count the MINORITY class, not raw row count
      (real data: 22 y=1, 11 y=0 -- a flat n>=30 floor passes despite the
      minority class sitting at only 11). Replaced with a proper EPV floor
      (Peduzzi et al. 1996: >=10 minority-class events per fitted
      predictor; Platt fits exactly 1 predictor, so min(n_pos,n_neg)>=10).
    - Explicitly documented (not silently left ambiguous) that this
      correction deliberately does NOT check `_city_correction_applied`/
      `_MIN_BIAS_CORRECTION_TRADES` -- that gate uses OVERALL settled-trade
      count as a maturity proxy for GBM/Platt; this correction has its own
      population-specific EPV floor instead, and tying it to an unrelated
      population's sample size would be wrong.
    - `_sigmoid` raised OverflowError for very negative input (plain
      1/(1+exp(-x)) blows up past ~-745) -- apply_metar_calibration is
      reachable from more than just the bounds-checked loader. Rewrote as
      the standard numerically-stable two-branch form.
    - Found (not fixed here -- genuinely separate module/consumer, filed as
      its own entry above, "SETTLEMENT_MONITOR.PY'S FORCE-CLOSE TRIGGER..."):
      settlement_monitor.py's paper-position force-close path uses the
      same raw, now-known-overconfident `_dynamic_lock_in_confidence()`
      output this fix corrects on the entry side only.

  Adjacent fix (unchanged from first pass): sameday T-fit query now
  excludes `method='metar_lockout'` rows -- analyze_trade's METAR-locked
  branch never calls apply_temperature_scaling, so training that fit on a
  population it's never applied to was a train/serve mismatch.

  63 new/updated tests across test_ml_bias.py (Platt-only fit/apply unit
  tests including the exact real-33-row regression, EPV floor with a
  paired positive+negative control, non-binary-label rejection, sigmoid
  overflow, sameday-exclusion, cmd_calibrate wiring) and
  test_weather_markets.py (the H1 magnitude-cap regression using the real
  fitted coefficients, the H2 bias_correction/feedback-loop regression with
  its own positive control, stale-cache-on-rejection, transient-I/O
  resilience, malformed/partial-JSON handling, loader-exception resilience
  inside analyze_trade, plus the original above/below-applies/
  between-excluded/no-file-no-ops/magnitude-cap/caching coverage). 331
  tests collected in the scoped suite. Mutation-tested via Edit (not
  string-replace) on every safety-relevant branch from both review rounds:
  the EPV floor, the magnitude-cap SIZE (not just its existence), the

  Follow-up (2026-08-16, same day): the fit above was still manual-only
  (`py main.py calibrate`), which meant it would go stale indefinitely if
  nobody remembered to run it -- one of the 14 risks raised when reviewing

  unattended weekly block doesn't reintroduce the risk the EMOS gate was
  built to close.
  Extracted the fit+persist+cache-invalidate logic (previously inline in

  D5 block can't drift. Wired into D5's existing `if _should_retrain:`

  retrain failure here can't silently stop the SIBLING retrains (each is
  independently already exception-isolated at the point it's called).
  Incidental fix while extracting: switched from plain `atomic_write_json`

  Settlement_monitor.py's shared-input risk (issue found above, filed

  New tests: `TestFitAndSaveMetarCalibration` (writes file + history
