[RESOLVED 2026-07-31 -- protocol-vs-pattern decision made (build vs. don't),
  see the 2026-07-31 RESOLVED note below for the final call and what shipped]
  NO MARKET-TYPE SEAM -- TEMPERATURE IS THE ARCHITECTURE, NOT A MARKET TYPE
Priority: was Medium-High -- now Low-Medium. hourly-directional (KXTEMPxxxH)
  was the nearest stated expansion and did hit every one of these walls;
  shipping it (2026-07-20, commit 06269b4) closed the concrete complaints
  below via pragmatic single-source-of-truth fixes, not a formal interface.
  What's left (no MarketType protocol) only pays off if rain/snow gets
  picked up next -- see the RESOLVED note below. NOTE: this entry's own
  "check_series_drift() still KXHIGH/KXLOW-only" claim is now STALE -- see
  RE-VERIFIED 2026-07-30 note below; it was fixed as a side effect of Rain
  Step 1/Snow Step 1 shipping, not by this entry's own work.

Problem:
  Market-type knowledge is not behind an interface; it's a set of
  string-match conventions repeated independently across the pipeline,
  and the deepest layer (ground truth/calibration) only has a concept of
  temperature at all. Dispatch: analyze_trade() (weather_markets.py:5145)
  is a ~1,660-line monolith whose market-type "routing" is two
  early-return fast-paths keyed on parsed condition type (precip at
  5340-5347, snow at 5350-5355); everything after line 5357 IS the
  temperature model. There is no third place to plug in an hourly-
  threshold model except a third inline fast-path. Variable derivation by
  ticker substring is duplicated: `var = "min" if "LOW" in series else
  "max"` exists independently at weather_markets.py:5414 and 6248,
  tracker.py:2544-2554 (settlement audit), and paper.py:1148-1154
  (_score_ensemble_members) -- four copies of the same convention, each
  of which a new market type must extend or silently mis-handle
  (paper.py's copy defaults unknown tickers to "max"). Ground truth is a
  temperature column: outcomes stores settled_yes + settled_temp_f
  (tracker.py:122, 310-314). The settlement-audit path explicitly bails
  for anything else -- tracker.py:2554: `return False  # precipitation or
  unknown -- skip`. Everything downstream of settlement -- EMOS training,
  data-driven sigma, dynamic station bias, per-model accuracy, ml_bias
  temperature scaling -- consumes settled_temp_f. A rain market can trade
  today (the precip fast-path exists) but can never learn: no ground
  truth is ever recorded for it, so it's permanently outside the
  calibration loop that is this bot's actual moat. Degraded analysis
  dicts already bite: the precip/snow fast-paths return reduced dicts
  (hardcoded "time_risk": "HIGH" at 4792/4999, no entry_price), which
  already silently disabled the reprice taker-cross for precip markets
  (documented as an "informational finding" in the maker-execution
  entry). check_series_drift() (weather_markets.py:3308) diffs only
  KXHIGH*/KXLOW* (3332-3339) against the hardcoded KNOWN_WEATHER_SERIES
  list -- already flagged in the hourly/rain entries, but note it's the
  same missing seam, not a separate fix.

RESOLVED 2026-07-20 (the concrete complaints above, via pragmatic fixes --
  NOT via the formal MarketType protocol this entry's "What it would look
  like" section describes; that part is still open, see below): shipping
  HOURLY-DIRECTIONAL TEMPERATURE MARKETS Step 2 (commit 06269b4) closed
  every specific verification point in this Problem section:
  - Third dispatch slot: `_analyze_hourly_trade()` (weather_markets.py) is
    now a genuine third branch in analyze_trade(), positioned before the
    precip/snow fast-paths -- "no third place to plug in" is no longer true.
  - Var-convention duplication: a `predictions.var` column (migration v53)
    is now the single source of truth. `paper._score_ensemble_members()`
    and `tracker.audit_settlement()` both prefer the stored value, falling
    back to ticker-substring derivation only for legacy pre-migration rows.
    The two remaining literal `var = "min" if "LOW" in series else "max"`
    copies in weather_markets.py are now purely internal to the daily
    model -- hourly bypasses them entirely.
  - Temperature-only ground truth: `outcomes.settled_value REAL`/
    `settled_var TEXT` (migration v50-v52, shipped in Step 1) are now
    actually populated -- `audit_settlement()` has a dedicated hourly
    branch that writes them before ever reaching the old `return False #
    precipitation or unknown -- skip` line.
  - No calibration-pool separation: `ml_bias.train_all_temperature_
    scaling()` now has a third `'hourly'` pool, explicitly excluded from
    `'sameday'`, with its own no-fallback `apply_temperature_scaling(pool=
    "hourly")` path.
  Of the 5-item MarketType protocol wishlist below, items 1 (series-prefix
  set), 2 (condition parsing), 3 (probability entry point), and 5
  (calibration-pool key) all now exist as concrete, market-type-specific
  implementations (item 4, ground-truth spec, shipped too). But there is
  still NO formal `MarketType` protocol/interface (grepped for `Protocol`/
  `class MarketType` across weather_markets.py and tracker.py -- zero hits)
  -- each of the 5 things is still a separate, hand-wired branch keyed on
  `_is_hourly`/ticker-prefix checks, not slots on a shared interface a third
  market type (rain/snow) could plug into without writing its own parallel
  branches from scratch. Also still true: `check_series_drift()` was NOT
  extended to cover KXTEMPxxxH -- a parallel mechanism
  (`refresh_hourly_target_hours()`) was added alongside it instead, doing
  target-hour recomputation rather than the same live-series-list-diff
  drift check. The precip/snow fast-paths' degraded analysis dicts
  (hardcoded time_risk, no entry_price) were also untouched by this
  commit -- re-verify those are still exactly as described if this entry
  is picked up again, since that part wasn't re-checked this session.

What it would look like:
  A MarketType protocol owning the five things currently keyed on string
  conventions: (1) series-prefix set for discovery/drift, (2) condition
  parsing, (3) probability model entry point (analyze(enriched,
  condition) -> analysis), (4) ground-truth spec -- what observable
  settles it and how to fetch it, (5) calibration-pool key (so hourly
  rows never pollute the daily 'sameday' T-scaling pool -- the exact
  separation the hourly backlog entry already demands). The outcomes
  table needs a generic settled_value REAL + settled_var TEXT shape
  instead of settled_temp_f. The temperature implementation would
  initially just be the existing code behind the interface -- the win is
  that hourly/rain get slots instead of fourth and fifth copies of the
  "LOW" in ticker convention.

Why not now:
  - The ground-truth generalization (settled_value/settled_var) is done --
    see RESOLVED note above. The remaining formal MarketType protocol only
    pays off if RAIN / SNOW / HURRICANE MARKETS (below) is actually picked
    up next -- don't build the abstraction speculatively for a third market
    type that doesn't exist yet; the concrete/pragmatic pattern hourly used
    (a dedicated function + a shared prefix dict + a stored var column) is
    proven now and can be repeated a second time for rain/snow just as
    cheaply as building the interface, unless a third type after that makes
    the interface's payoff clear.

When to revisit:
  - The moment RAIN / SNOW / HURRICANE MARKETS is actually greenlit -- at
    that point, decide whether a third repetition of the concrete pattern
    is still cheaper than building the formal protocol (it likely still is
    for a second repetition; the protocol pays off more clearly on a
    fourth+ market type). Also revisit check_series_drift() then -- it
    still needs the same KXTEMPxxxH-style parallel-mechanism treatment (or
    a real generalization) for whatever new series rain/snow adds.

Problem (as originally scoped, still accurate for the still-open full
Position read-model below):
  A "position" exists in two unrelated persistence models -- paper's JSON
  ledger (data/paper_trades.json, full read-modify-write under
  _DATA_LOCK, paper.py:87/107) and live's execution_log SQLite rows --
  and the live side reaches feature parity by adaptation and replication,
  not sharing. order_executor._get_live_open_positions()
  (order_executor.py:955) reshapes execution_log rows into "whatever keys
  paper's check functions happen to read (verified by reading both
  bodies)". _update_live_peak_profits() (order_executor.py:996)
  *replicates* paper's peak math because paper.update_peak_profits
  ignores its own parameter and re-reads paper's JSON internally --
  i.e., paper's functions are storage-coupled in ways discovered
  per-function. _check_live_model_exits() (order_executor.py:1214) is a
  ~100-line near-clone of _check_early_exits (order_executor.py:1625),
  built as a separate function "to avoid any risk of regressing the
  existing paper-only path". The divergence already produced asymmetry:
  the multiple-positions-per-ticker collapse bug was fixed on the live
  side only, with paper's identical pattern left in production
  (documented in the RESTING EXIT ORDERS resolution above). Beyond the
  structural glue, gate constants are hand-copied as bare literals: the
  24h settlement-convergence gate at four sites (paper.py:1339-1357,

  minimum-hold gate at three (paper.py:2185-2197; order_executor.py:
  1671-1683, 1263-1275) -- none in get_config_fingerprint(). Drift has
  already started at the doc level: _check_early_exits' docstring
  (order_executor.py:1628) says "shifted >15 percentage points" while the
  code gates on `shift > 0.25` (line 1715).

[RESOLVED -- price-convention divergence fixed 2026-08-14, dict-vs-Position
  sourcing fixed 2026-08-22, see both Resolution sections below]
  check_model_exits/_check_live_model_exits/
  _check_early_exits STILL SOURCE POSITIONS AS RAW DICTS, NOT THE NEW
  Position READ-MODEL -- AND THEIR EXIT-PRICE CONVENTIONS HAVE ALREADY
  DIVERGED
Priority: Medium for the price-convention divergence, Low for the dict-vs-
  Position sourcing itself. The dict-sourcing IS cosmetic (see "What it
  would look like" below). But these functions do NOT merely duplicate
  per-trade API-call/analysis STRUCTURE with no price-math risk, as this
  entry originally (and wrongly) claimed: order_executor.
  _check_live_model_exits computes its exit price via _liquidation_price()
  (order_executor.py:1471, bid for YES / 1-ask for NO -- the realizable
  closing price), while order_executor._check_early_exits (paper-only)
  computes its via _midpoint_price() (order_executor.py:1854, the bid/ask
  midpoint) -- verified live by grepping both call sites 2026-08-13, not
  assumed. positions.liquidation_price()'s own docstring explains why this
  matters: pricing at the midpoint instead of the realizable bid/ask
  "overvalu[es] the position by the bid-ask spread ... inflating
  take-profit/exit proceeds." So paper's model-exits book a more optimistic
  P&L than live's would for the identical shift/threshold -- precisely the
  live/paper divergence class this whole backlog entry (see the resolved
  entry above) was filed to eliminate, just found in a different function
  pair than the one that got fixed.

Problem:
  Price-convention divergence (the real issue): paper.check_model_exits
  doesn't compute its own exit price at all (it's a pure recommendation
  generator -- main.py's cmd_brief/watch-mode display decides the actual
  close_paper_early() call and price separately). order_executor.
  _check_early_exits DOES exit paper trades directly and uses
  _midpoint_price(). order_executor._check_live_model_exits exits live
  positions directly and uses _liquidation_price(). Two functions doing the
  conceptually identical job (close a position because the model's
  probability shifted past a threshold) price the close differently.

  Dict-vs-Position sourcing (cosmetic): paper.check_model_exits still calls
  get_open_trades() (raw dicts, full ~20-field trade shape) directly rather
  than PaperPositionStore.get_open(). order_executor._check_live_model_exits
  and order_executor._check_early_exits still call
  _get_live_open_positions()/paper.get_open_trades() directly rather than
  LivePositionStore.get_open(). All three return dicts (not Position) in
  their recommendation payloads, since callers (main.py's exit-signal
  display, cmd_brief) read extra fields (thesis, full market dict, etc.)
  Position deliberately doesn't carry.

What it would look like:
  Price convention: decide which is actually correct (liquidation_price's
  own docstring argues realizable bid/ask, not midpoint, is the right
  convention for a real exit -- the same argument that motivated fixing
  paper's stop-loss/breakeven pricing originally) and make
  _check_early_exits use liquidation_price() too, falling back to
  entry_price like the other exit paths already do when no quote is
  available. Needs its own before/after test proving the P&L booked for a
  model-exit changes (or doesn't, if the spread is usually thin enough not
  to matter -- check real settled-trade data before assuming impact).

  Dict-vs-Position sourcing: not a straightforward swap -- these functions'
  return payloads need the FULL trade/position dict for display, not just
  Position's fields, so routing their position-SOURCING through the stores
  (get_open()) while keeping their OWN return shape as dicts would need
  each function to either look up the original dict by id after getting
  Position objects (like check_paper_position_exits' by_id pattern) or the
  stores would need a "get full record" escape hatch. Worth designing
  properly rather than forcing a fit -- not a mechanical change.

Why not now:
  Price convention: not independently verified yet whether the divergence
  moves real P&L by a meaningful amount (see "What it would look like"
  above) -- needs that check before deciding this is worth a live-order
  code change, not just deferred out of caution. Genuinely NOT scoped out
  because it's low-risk; scoped out because filing it accurately (this
  entry) and fixing it correctly are two different amounts of work, and the
  2026-08-13 session that found it was already mid-review of a different,
  larger change.
  Dict-sourcing: genuinely has no duplication risk (it's structural, not
  mathematical) -- pure internal consistency, not a bug. Pick up
  opportunistically or if these functions are touched for another reason.

When to revisit:
  Price convention: soon -- this is a real, live-order-adjacent pricing
  bug, not cosmetic; the only reason it isn't fixed in this same entry is
  that it was caught by review after the sibling entry's implementation
  was already done and confirmed, not before. Dict-sourcing: no blocking
  dependency.

Resolution (2026-08-14):
  Both remaining execute-a-close sites switched from _midpoint_price() to
  liquidation_price() (positions.py): order_executor._check_early_exits
  (order_executor.py, the automated paper path, cron/watch-driven) and
  main.py's interactive exit-signal menu (~line 6858, the manual y/N close
  reached via check_model_exits' recommendations). Both now price a
  model-exit identically to order_executor._check_live_model_exits
  (unchanged) -- same current_prices dict shape ({ticker: {"bid","ask"}}
  via coalesce_market_price(*YES_BID_KEYS/YES_ASK_KEYS)), and, added during
  review (see Finding 1 below), the same _get_current_book(client, ticker)
  or market WS-then-REST freshness step live already used -- paper's
  pricing now literally mirrors live's, not just conceptually.

  Two scope/design decisions surfaced via AskUserQuestion before
  implementing (terse question, tradeoffs in option descriptions, per this
  project's standing workflow):
    1. Fix both _check_early_exits AND main.py's manual close site
       (chosen) vs. _check_early_exits only. Chosen because leaving the
       manual site on the old midpoint convention would have created a
       NEW divergence (manual paper closes vs. automated paper closes
       pricing the same trigger differently) the moment this entry closed.
    2. Preserve the existing skip-this-cycle-on-bad-quote behavior
       (chosen) vs. this entry's own original "What it would look like"
       text, which prescribed falling back to entry_price "like the other
       exit paths already do." Re-verified against live code
       (order_executor.py, both _check_live_model_exits and
       _check_early_exits) before implementing: that claim was wrong --
       neither existing model-exit site falls back to entry_price on a
       bad quote; both skip the cycle. The entry_price fallback is the
       STOP-LOSS/BREAKEVEN family's convention (order_executor.py's
       _check_live_position_exits, paper.py's stop-loss/breakeven exit
       loop), a different function family with a different contract.
       Implemented as `if exit_price is None or exit_price <= 0: continue`
       -- liquidation_price() returns None on a missing/invalid quote
       (never negative), so this preserves the exact skip semantics both
       existing model-exit sites already had, just checking a different
       function's return contract.

  Real-data impact check (this entry's own stated precondition under "Why
  not now" above): queried predictions.db's price_history table
  (yes_bid_close/yes_ask_close) against all 37 historical paper trades
  settled via the model-exit-family midpoint convention (paper_trades.json,
  outcome="early_exit", exit_reason IS NULL -- this bucket covers both
  _check_early_exits' automated closes and the manual menu's closes, since
  neither tags a reason). Matched each trade's settled_at to the nearest
  price_history candle by ticker; only 12 of 37 matched within 15 minutes
  of the actual exit (price_history's per-ticker coverage is sparse -- the
  other 25 matched a candle 6-48+ hours away and were excluded as
  unreliable, not averaged in). Of the 12 reliable matches: median spread
  ~3c, mean ~4.8c, mean per-trade P&L overstatement (midpoint vs. realizable)
  ~$1.34, max $4.73 on a single trade. Confirms this entry's own suspicion
  under "Why not now": spreads are consistently thin on these weather-market
  tickers, so per-trade dollar impact is modest -- but real, directionally
  consistent with liquidation_price()'s docstring (midpoint always
  overvalues by roughly half the spread), and non-zero, which is enough to
  justify the fix on consistency grounds even before considering compounding
  effects (see Finding 11 below on the paper P&L series becoming
  non-homogeneous across this changeover).

Resolution (2026-08-22, dict-vs-Position sourcing, batch-18):
  All three functions now source positions via the shared Position
  read-model instead of reading raw trade/position-dict fields directly.
  Each Position is built PER-ITEM, as the first statement inside that
  item's own try/except (not batched via a list comprehension ahead of the
  loop -- see the opus review findings below for why the placement inside
  vs. before the try mattered). External contracts are unchanged:
  paper.check_model_exits still returns the full original trade dict in
  each recommendation's "trade" key -- the same loop variable `t` each
  Position was built from, no separate by_id lookup -- since callers
  (main.py's exit-signal display, cmd_brief) read fields (thesis, full
  market dict) Position doesn't carry; order_executor._check_live_
  model_exits/_check_early_exits still return only an int closed-count and
  now close via LivePositionStore.exit()/PaperPositionStore.exit() (the
  same store methods check_paper_position_exits/_check_live_position_exits
  already use) instead of calling _exit_live_position()/close_paper_early()
  inline with a hand-assembled dict.

  Scope decision surfaced via AskUserQuestion before implementing: whether
  to do this Low-priority/cosmetic sourcing change at all this session,
  given it touches order_executor.py's live-order-adjacent exit path for a
  non-bug reason. Chosen to implement, since the design reuses an
  already-shipped, already-tested pattern (check_paper_position_exits'
  own single-fetch/by_id shape) rather than inventing a new one, keeping
  incremental risk low.

  Independent opus review (effort=high) before push found no HIGH/MEDIUM
  findings, 5 LOW + 1 informational specific to this entry (2 more LOW
  findings on the sibling _rating() entry, addressed there), all addressed:
    - LOW, fixed: all three functions originally built their Position via a
      list comprehension BATCHED ahead of the per-item loop
      (`[_trade_to_position(t) for t in open_trades]`) -- a single
      malformed raw record (e.g. missing "id") would raise during that
      batch construction and abort the ENTIRE cycle, dropping every
      position that cycle instead of just the bad one. Fixed by moving the
      adapter call to be the FIRST STATEMENT INSIDE each item's own
      try/except (not merely "per-item," which a first fix attempt got
      subtly wrong for 2 of the 3 functions -- moving the adapter call to
      before the try but still per-item was its own regression, since the
      pre-refactor code deliberately deferred trade["id"]/d["id"] access to
      deep inside the guarded try; building the whole Position earlier,
      even per-item, re-exposed that exact failure point one step too
      early, outside the guard). Caught by writing the malformed-record
      regression tests above and mutation-testing them by hand (Edit-tool
      revert to "before try"): both placements were tried, only "first
      line inside try" passes.
    - LOW, fixed: 3 `except` handlers (paper.py's check_model_exits,
      order_executor.py's _check_live_model_exits and _check_early_exits)
      referenced a Position/lookup variable (`pos.ticker`, `ticker`) that
      would be UNASSIGNED if the adapter call itself raised -- exactly the
      case the finding above is about -- causing an UnboundLocalError
      INSIDE the exception handler that masks the real error. Changed to
      reference the always-present raw dict/loop variable instead
      (`t.get("ticker","?")` / `d.get("ticker","?")`).
    - LOW, resolved by supersession: check_model_exits' original `by_id[
      pos.id]` hard-subscript lookup (a theoretical duplicate-id collapse
      risk, unreachable given the ledger's own duplicate-order guard) is
      gone entirely -- the per-item try/except restructure above means the
      loop variable `t` IS the trade a Position was just built from, no
      separate id lookup needed.
    - LOW, fixed: stale docstrings (order_executor.py's
      _get_live_open_positions, positions.py's Position class) described
      the pre-refactor world; updated. A second independent opus review of
      these fixes then caught that the FIRST docstring update introduced a
      new factual error (claimed _get_current_book() needs the raw dict's
      ticker -- false, it uses the Position's ticker) and left 2 more
      stale "by_id lookup" references (paper.py's check_model_exits
      docstring, and a test docstring) that the by_id-removal above should
      have updated but didn't -- all 3 fixed in the same follow-up pass.
    - LOW, documented as a deliberate no-op (round-2 opus review finding):
      check_model_exits now reaches `side`/`ticker` through _trade_to_
      position's permissive .get()-with-default fields instead of the old
      hard t["side"]/t["ticker"] subscripts -- a trade dict missing "side"
      would previously KeyError (caught, skipped, logged) but now silently
      defaults to "yes" and could produce a model-exit recommendation for
      an assumed-wrong side. Not fixed: this is inherent to using the
      shared _trade_to_position adapter at all (paper.check_paper_
      position_exits already has the identical property, unguarded, in
      production) -- adding extra validation here alone would diverge from
      that established sibling pattern for no real benefit, since
      paper.place_paper_order always writes id/ticker/side and this path
      is genuinely unreachable with real ledger data. The exit-signal
      consumer (main.py's sub=="4" menu) also always requires an explicit
      y/N human confirmation before actually closing anything, bounding
      the blast radius even in the unreachable case.
    - Informational, fixed: the 3 malformed-record regression tests only
      asserted the good record still processed, not that the bad one was
      actually logged (a regression that silently swallowed it with no
      warning would have passed). Added a caplog assertion to all 3.
    - Informational, no action: the live-side malformed-record test has to
      patch _get_live_open_positions to inject a bad dict, since that

      _live_dict_to_position needs -- the isolation fix is genuinely

    - Informational, no action: paper's model-flip exit still records

  SIGNAL GRADUATION IS A CONVENTION, NOT A MECHANISM -- SIGNAL #3 REBUILDS RUN-TREND'S PLUMBING
Priority: Medium -- the log-only->trigger->blend pattern is now this
  project's explicit strategy for all new alpha; its marginal cost is
  currently ~6 touch points per signal.

Problem:
  Run-trend established the graduation *pattern* but implemented it as
  bespoke wiring at every layer, so signals #3-#5 (trade-flow, AFD,
  richer-ML features are all queued in this file) each repeat it.
  Storage: one named migration per scalar (tracker.py:221-223, v40-v42)
  plus dedicated columns per signal -- predictions is now at schema v53
  largely from this accretion (was v42 when this entry was written; the
  hourly-directional work added var TEXT, one more accretion of the exact
  same shape this entry describes). API: a new named parameter on
  log_prediction() (tracker.py:610 run_trend: dict | None) -- the
  signature grows one kwarg per signal, forever. Threading: every
  log_prediction call site updated through order_executor's shared helper
  _prediction_kwargs_from_analysis (order_executor.py:1926) -- CORRECTION
  2026-07-20: main.py's two direct call sites no longer re-import
  get_forecast_run_trend_from_analysis locally; that specific duplication
  was fixed by [RESOLVED 2026-07-17] LOG_PREDICTION KWARGS ASSEMBLY
  TRIPLICATED (below) -- both call sites now route through the same shared
  helper. The core thesis (kwarg-growth-per-signal, no generic mechanism)
  is otherwise unaffected by that fix and still fully holds.
  Enablement: run-trend's trigger (sample floor + correlation check)
  exists only as backlog.txt prose that someone must remember to run by
  hand. Meanwhile the codebase already *has* an in-code activation
  mechanism -- sample-gated auto-activation with one-time notification
  (_regime_blend_active() weather_markets.py:3887 +
  _notify_feature_activation 3852, and siblings: PDO/PNA gate at 3912,
  MIN_BIAS_CORRECTION_TRADES) -- but it's re-derived per feature and was
  not used for run-trend. Blend entry (the eventual step): the core
  blend is a *positional 3-tuple* -- _blend_weights() returns
  (w_ensemble, w_climatology, w_nws) (weather_markets.py:3954-3962). Any
  signal graduating to a real blend weight either changes that arity
  everywhere or joins the growing chain of bespoke post-blend
  adjustments, which is how analyze_trade got to 1,660 lines.

What it would look like:
  (a) log_prediction(..., signals: dict[str, float] | None) persisting to
  a signal_values(prediction_id, name, value) table (or one JSON column,
  matching the blend_sources/run_trend_points precedent) -- new signal =
  new dict key, zero migrations, zero signature/call-site changes; (b) a
  small signal registry (name, extract(analysis) -> value(s),
  sample_floor, correlation_target) driving both a standing
  graduation-report command (runs every pending signal's enablement query
  against settled outcomes -- replaces the per-entry prose triggers) and
  the auto-activation notification machinery that already exists for
  regime/PDO; (c) leave blend *wiring* manual -- the deliberate human
  step is the point of the pattern -- but let graduated signals enter as
  named entries in a weights dict rather than tuple-position N+1.

Why not now:
  - Do (a)+(b) when the *next* log-only signal is built (trade-flow is
    queued post-Belgium) -- that's when the second data point proves/
    disproves the shape, and the cost is near-zero incremental to work
    already planned. Not worth a standalone pass while run-trend's own
    trigger hasn't fired.

When to revisit:
  - When PUBLIC TRADE-FLOW SIGNAL (or any other log-only signal above) is
    next picked up -- build the registry then, not before.

[RESOLVED 2026-07-23 -- as a side effect of GENERALIZED PER-MODEL ACCURACY TRACKING Pass 1, see that entry] THE ANALYSIS-DICT -> TRADE-RECORD BOUNDARY EXPLODES DICTS INTO NAMED SCALARS
Priority: was Medium -- sharpened the GENERALIZED PER-MODEL ACCURACY
  TRACKING entry with the structural root cause; read together.

RESOLVED 2026-07-23: caught while updating that entry's own backlog text
  for its Pass 2 (GEM/UKMO) resolution -- re-reading this entry's "What it
  would look like" against the code found it already fully describes what
  Pass 1 shipped the same day: a single model_forecast_means: dict[str,
  float | None] kwarg replaced the 4 named scalar params end-to-end
  (analyze_trade locals -> result dict -> place_paper_order's signature,
  now one kwarg not four -> trade JSON -> _score_ensemble_members, which
  already iterates the dict generically). Confirmed directly against
  current code, not just inferred from the other entry's text: paper.py's
  place_paper_order takes model_forecast_means as its one kwarg (no
  icon_forecast_mean/gfs_forecast_mean/etc. params survive), and both real
  call sites (main.py, order_executor.py) pass it as a single dict, not
  named scalars. No separate work was needed -- this entry's "when picked
  up, do the dict transport first" instruction was followed without either
  session having explicitly cross-referenced the other by name.

Problem:
  The existing entry frames this as "per-model columns in tracker" -- but
  the tracker column is the *last* link of a six-hop scalar chain, and
  the chain's shape is the real cost. Per-model means travel: analyze_trade
  locals (weather_markets.py:5731-5732) -> return-dict keys (6775-6776)
  -> *named kwargs* at two independent placement call sites
  (main.py:3576-3577, order_executor.py:2663-2664) -> place_paper_order's
  signature (paper.py:853-854) -> trade JSON keys (957-958) ->
  _score_ensemble_members's hardcoded dict (paper.py:1174-1187) ->
  tracker.log_member_score. The comment at paper.py:1180-1186 states the
  consequence: ECMWF "can never earn a data-driven weight... permanently
  stuck at the static seasonal default" -- and the same is true for
  GEM/UKMO/WeatherNext or any future source. place_paper_order's
  signature is itself the pattern at scale: 19 named parameters, each a
  field some analysis produced, meaning *every* new per-trade datum (not
  just model means) pays the same multi-file kwarg-threading toll -- the
  same disease as log_prediction's kwarg growth in the SIGNAL GRADUATION
  entry above, at a different boundary.

What it would look like:
  One model_means: dict[str, float] key on the analysis dict (populated
  by _get_consensus_probs, which is already model-agnostic via
  _model_prob_and_mean -- the generic helper exists at the source end),
  passed through as a single kwarg -> stored as one JSON field on the
  trade record -> iterated by _score_ensemble_members (which already
  loops a dict at paper.py:1191, so the consumer end is *also* ready --
  only the transport is scalar). Keep icon_forecast_mean/gfs_forecast_mean
  as legacy read-fallbacks for settling old trades. This converts "add a
  model source" from a 6-file signature change into a fetch + one dict
  entry, which is precisely what GENERALIZED PER-MODEL ACCURACY TRACKING
  asks for -- that entry should be read together with this one when
  picked up, since the endpoints are already generic and only the
  transport chain needs replacing.

Why not now:
  - Same as GENERALIZED PER-MODEL ACCURACY TRACKING (weeks before learned
    weights activate, needs the which-ECMWF-product decision) -- but when
    picked up, do the dict transport *first*; instrumenting ECMWF through
    the scalar chain and then generalizing would do the plumbing twice.

When to revisit:
  - Same trigger as GENERALIZED PER-MODEL ACCURACY TRACKING -- do the
    dict-transport change as step one of that entry, not a separate pass.

[ONE-SHOT PROCESS LIFECYCLE IS BAKED INTO MODULE STATE -- THE ALWAYS-ON WATCHER INHERITS STALE-STATE HAZARDS]
Priority: Medium -- gated on the same trigger as the VM move; partially
  live *today* via loop/watch, which already call cmd_cron repeatedly
  in-process.

Problem:
  Correctness currently leans on process death as the cache-invalidation
  and config-reload mechanism. Import-time snapshots that feed live
  decisions: _CITY_WEIGHTS/_SEASONAL_WEIGHTS/_CONDITION_WEIGHTS load once
  at module import (weather_markets.py:748-750); _CONDITION_WEIGHTS feeds
  every trade's blend. In an always-on process, a recalibration writing
  new weight files changes nothing until restart. _LEARNED_WEIGHTS
  (2451-2453) is "cached after first load" with a log-*once* TTL warning
  flag -- a once-per-process warning is a once-per-*months* warning on a
  VM. Config frozen at import: utils.py alone has 41 module-level
  os.getenv constants. The operational model "edit .env -> next cron run
  picks it up" silently becomes "edit .env -> nothing happens" on a
  long-lived process. Per-cycle resource lifecycles: the WS client is
  constructed, subscribed, started, and torn down per cron cycle
  (cron.py:1038-1156, stop at 2668-2674) -- every fresh cycle starts with
  an empty book cache, which is exactly what caused the HIGH bug in the
  exit-protection review (REST-fallback shape on "the exact path the
  feature was built for"). An always-on design inverts this: the WS
  becomes the persistent event source and the scan becomes the periodic
  task -- none of the current orchestration is shaped for that
  inversion. Filesystem liveness protocol: cron lock, heartbeat, dead-
  man's-switch reading .cron_last_run mtime, _MONDAY_SWEEP_PATH touch-
  file -- a signaling protocol between *invocations* of a dying process.

What it would look like:
  An explicit cycle-scoped context (fits the headless trade-cycle engine
  entry above): weights/config refreshed at cycle start (or converting
  the import-time trio to the TTL-checked read-through pattern the
  forecast caches already use); log-once flags becoming log-once-per-
  cycle; WS lifted out of the cycle to process scope with reconnect/
  heartbeat ownership; an inventory pass over module globals in
  weather_markets.py/paper.py classifying each as (a) true constant, (b)
  TTL cache -- already safe, (c) load-once snapshot -- the hazard list.
  The existing autouse-fixture machinery (isolate_dynamic_sigma etc.)
  shows the project already knows which globals are dangerous -- that
  list is roughly the (c) list.

Why not now:
  - Same trigger as the VM move. But the inventory pass (c-list) is cheap
    and worth doing *before* the watcher design starts, because it sizes
    the real work; and any *new* module-global cache added between now
    and then should be TTL-checked rather than load-once, so the list
    stops growing.

When to revisit:
  - Same trigger as MOVE OFF LOCAL CRON -- HOST ON A SMALL ALWAYS-ON VM.
    The module-global inventory pass is cheap enough to do sooner, ahead
    of the watcher design itself.

PARTIALLY RESOLVED 2026-07-26 (the module-global inventory pass, plus fixing
  every (c)-list item it found that didn't need the full watcher redesign;
  utils.py's 41 frozen os.getenv constants and the per-cycle WS/filesystem-
  liveness-protocol items below are still open, unchanged):
  Did the inventory pass this entry itself flagged as cheap and worth doing
  now. Classified every module-level global in weather_markets.py/paper.py:
  paper.py had zero load-once snapshots (matches its "always reads fresh
  from JSON/DB" design, already documented in the paper/live-ledger entry
  above). weather_markets.py's (a) constants and (b) TTL caches (including
  _MARKETS_CACHE, verified live via time.monotonic(), and every ForecastCache
  instance) were already safe. Six real (c) load-once hazards confirmed and
  fixed:
  1. _CITY_WEIGHTS/_SEASONAL_WEIGHTS/_CONDITION_WEIGHTS -- correction to this
     entry's own framing: these are NOT unconditionally frozen. cron.py's F3
     auto-calibration and weekly ML-bias-retrain blocks already push fresh
     values into these same dicts in-process (one via .clear()+.update(),
     one via reassignment -- both work, since weather_markets.py's own reads
     always resolve the current module-namespace binding regardless of which
     idiom the writer used). The real gap: that refresh only happens along
     the cron.py call path (cmd_cron/loop). watch mode (main.py's cmd_watch/
     _analyze_once) never runs any cron.py code at all, so on an always-on
     watch process a recalibration written by a separate cron run would
     never be picked up without a restart. Fixed with a new
     _maybe_refresh_calibration_weights() that mtime-checks all 3 JSON files
     and reloads in place (same .clear()+.update() idiom) when changed,
     throttled to once per 300s and called from get_weather_markets() (which
     cron/loop/watch all already call once per scan) -- fixes staleness for
     every caller uniformly without touching cron.py's calibration-triggering
     logic or main.py at all.
  2. _LEARNED_WEIGHTS -- docstring literally said "cached for the session";
     worse, its own 7-day TTL check only ever fired on the very first load,
     so a file that aged past staleness mid-session (without being
     rewritten) stayed served from cache forever, past its own documented
     TTL. Fixed: load_learned_weights() now re-checks the TTL on every call
     (cheap -- one os.path.getmtime() stat) before the mtime-unchanged fast
     path, and reloads whenever the file's mtime changes. save_learned_
     weights() now also records the mtime it just wrote, so the process that
     saves fresh weights doesn't immediately re-read its own write.
  3. _PLATT_MODELS -- docstring literally said "load once per process."
     Fixed: _load_platt_models() now mtime-gates the same way.
  4. _MAE_WEIGHTS_CACHE -- ForecastCache(ttl_secs=float("inf")), a
     deliberate 2026-07-19 design decision (see ForecastCache entry above)
     to preserve the plain dict it replaced. Per-model MAE genuinely drifts
     as new trades settle, so "permanent for the life of the process" meant
     an always-on watch process would trade on day-1 accuracy forever.
     Fixed: reuses _MODEL_CACHE_TTL (4h), the same cadence already used for
     every other model-accuracy cache in this file.
  5/6. _regime_blend_state / _pdopna_blend_state ({"active": None}) --
     "checks once per process, then caches" is an asymmetric hazard: once
     True it's correctly permanent (sample counts only grow), but a still-
     False result was latched forever too, meaning an always-on process
     would silently never notice the graduation moment if the settled-trade
     threshold crossed mid-run -- the same "silently never revisited" bug
     class as the run-trend/GEM-UKMO entries above. Fixed: added a
     "checked_at" timestamp: a False result is now rechecked every
     _REGIME_BLEND_RECHECK_SECS (6h) instead of never; True stays sticky.
     Existing tests reset state via `wm._regime_blend_state["active"] =
     None` (the pre-existing convention) -- kept that working by treating
     active=None as "force a fresh check" regardless of checked_at, not
     requiring every caller to also know about the new field.
  New finding, not in this entry's original text: main.py's cmd_watch --
  THE ONLY LIVE-ORDER PATH per the still-open headless-engine entry above --
  never calls reset_gate_counts() or flush_forecast_disk_cache()/
  flush_ensemble_disk_cache(), even though cron.py's own _cmd_cron_body calls
  all three every cycle. Confirmed via grep: zero references to any of the
  three in main.py before this fix. Consequence for any watch/watch --auto/
  watch --auto --live session: _gate_counts grows for the life of the
  process (low severity -- diagnostic-only, bounded by a small number of
  distinct gate-name keys); _forecast_disk_pending/_ensemble_disk_pending
  accumulate in memory unboundedly, with the disk-cache warm-up they exist
  to persist never actually written except via the atexit handler on a clean
  shutdown -- a crash/kill/OOM would previously have lost the *entire*
  session's warm-cache contribution, not just "until next restart." Fixed:
  cmd_watch's loop now calls flush_forecast_disk_cache() /
  flush_ensemble_disk_cache() / reset_gate_counts() once per iteration
  (flush before reset, so this cycle's own counts are still readable in
  between), bounding the exposure to at most one cycle's worth instead of
  the whole session.
  Explicitly NOT touched (same scope this entry's own text drew): utils.py's
  41 frozen os.getenv constants, the per-cron-cycle WS client lifecycle, and

  Opus review (Agent, effort=high, one isolated worktree pass over the full
  diff) before commit -- found 7 real issues, all fixed:
  1. MEDIUM -- load_learned_weights()'s new mtime-gating broke the
     pre-existing "monkeypatch wm._LEARNED_WEIGHTS directly" test-injection
     convention whenever this function hadn't yet performed a real load in
     the current process: the injected dict would get silently overwritten
     by whatever's actually on disk the instant mtime failed to match.
     Reviewer proved it empirically -- test_forecast_model_weights_uses_
     learned_per_city failed in TRUE isolation on the new code (passed on
     old code), passed only as part of the full class because an earlier
     test happened to populate _LEARNED_WEIGHTS_MTIME first. Fixed: a truthy
     _LEARNED_WEIGHTS with _LEARNED_WEIGHTS_MTIME still None is now honored
     as an external injection and returned immediately, no disk touched --
     re-verified the exact isolated repro now passes.
  2. MEDIUM -- the reload path (both _maybe_refresh_calibration_weights and
     _load_platt_models) unconditionally overwrote a currently-loaded, good
     value the instant a reload attempt came back empty/failed. calibration
     .py's load_*_weights() swallow their own JSON errors internally and
     return {} rather than raising, so a transient/corrupt read (a manual
     edit, a cloud-sync partial write, disk-full truncation) would silently
     wipe live blend-weight or Platt-scaling calibration for the rest of the
     process, with the recorded mtime then blocking any retry. Pre-change,
     a successful import-time load was immune to this -- the always-on
     periodic reload this session added is what introduced the exposure.
     Fixed both: skip the overwrite (and don't record the mtime, so the next
     throttled check retries) whenever a reload comes back empty/fails while
     real data is already loaded; only coerce to {} on a genuine first-ever
     load, matching the pre-existing "no models/weights yet" contract.
  3. LOW -- moving the TTL check ahead of the "not loaded" check meant an
     empty ({}) file older than 7 days now logged the staleness warning,
     contradicting the function's own documented contract ("an empty file is
     silently ignored regardless of age"). Fixed by re-ordering: emptiness is
     checked before staleness again, while still re-checking the TTL on
     every call (not just the first) rather than only at initial load.
  4. LOW -- _CAL_WEIGHTS_MTIMES's import-time seeding stat()'d the 3
     calibration files AFTER already loading their content, a real TOCTOU: a
     write landing in that window would record the new mtime against the OLD
     values, staying stuck until the NEXT write. Fixed by stat-ing before
     loading -- now the recorded mtime can only be as-old-or-older than what
     was actually loaded, which just forces one harmless extra reload
     instead of silently missing one.
  5. LOW -- _maybe_refresh_calibration_weights' .clear()+.update() in-place
     reload is not atomic; web_app.py runs Flask threaded=True and calls
     both get_weather_markets() and analyze_trade() from request threads, so
     a concurrent reader could observe _CITY_WEIGHTS between the clear() and
     the update() and raise KeyError on a plain dict lookup. (This exact
     .clear()+.update() shape already exists in cron.py's F3 auto-calibration
     block too, at a much lower trigger frequency -- this session's new
     periodic reload made an existing narrow race meaningfully more
     frequent, not introduced a wholly new one.) Fixed for this session's new
     code by reassigning each dict wholesale via globals()[key] = fresh (an
     atomic name rebind) instead of mutating in place -- every existing read
     site keeps working since weather_markets.py's own functions always
     resolve the current module-namespace binding on each access.
  6. LOW -- load_learned_weights() stats the file on every call (2 call
     sites, per-market, across up to 8 pool threads); reviewer suggested a
     throttle given data/ is OneDrive-synced in this environment (per the
     open FORECAST_SIGMA.JSON write-contention entry above). Tried a 60s
     monotonic throttle, then REVERTED it after empirically proving it broke
     TestLearnedWeightsTTL.test_fresh_weights_file_is_loaded (the throttle
     window persists across tests in the same process; that test doesn't,
     and per its own "reload on file change" premise correctly shouldn't
     have to, reset it). Left un-throttled, documented in-code as a
     deliberate call: the actual per-call cost is one exists()+one
     getmtime(), which the reviewer's own finding called "cheap on local
     disk" -- not worth a proven test-fragility regression for an
     unconfirmed, speculative perf concern.
  7. LOW -- (a) main.py's original comment claimed "_gate_counts grows for
     the life of the process," which is false (all 31 _count_gate() call
     sites use static string literals, so the dict is key-bounded; only the
     int values grow) -- corrected the comment. (b) cron.py flushes the two
     disk-pending caches near the END of _cmd_cron_body, but this session's
     fix had placed the equivalent calls at the TOP of cmd_watch's loop --
     meaning a cycle's own newly-created entries would only get flushed at
     the START of the NEXT cycle, so a SIGKILL/OOM between cycles would lose
     an extra cycle's worth of warm-up versus cron's own timing. Fixed by
     moving the two flush calls to the bottom of the loop (just before
     time.sleep), matching cron.py's placement; reset_gate_counts() stays at
     the top, which is where cron.py itself resets it.
  Also applied one reviewer-flagged rain-market-test caveat below (not a
  finding in this entry's own diff, but touched by the same review pass):
  _FakeDT.now() was silently ignoring its tz argument and always returning
  UTC -- harmless for this specific fixture (2026-07-02 12:00 UTC is still
  day 2 in Denver too) but would have masked a genuine local-date bug in the
  very datetime.now(_ZoneInfo(tz)).date() call under test. Fixed to honor tz.
  Full regression re-run after all 7 fixes: 551 passed / 4 skipped across
  the same 10 quick-running files, plus test_cron_integration.py/
  test_main_cron_smoke.py (both green, ~7-8 min). ruff + ruff format + mypy
  clean on all 3 changed files.

  assuming; (4) decide a per-cell significance/sample-size floor so a
  city/season/index combo with no real signal stays on
  DEFAULT_AO_SENS/NAO_SENS/ENSO_SENS instead of getting a noisy fitted
  number; (5) wire into AO_SENS/NAO_SENS/ENSO_SENS + new regression-
  locking tests (mirrors tests/test_climate_indices.py's per-season
  hand-computed-value tests); (6) update
  tests/test_city_registry_manifest.py's _KNOWN_GAPS allowlist to drop
  the fixed cities in the same change -- that test's own bidirectional
  staleness check will fail the build otherwise.
  RESOLVED (same session, REVISED same day after an independent opus review
  caught a real methodological gap in the first pass -- see below):
  First pass fetched real NOAA CPC AO/NAO/ONI monthly tables (918/918/917
  months) and joined against each of the 20 cities' already-cached 30yr
  Open-Meteo archive (data/climate_{city}.json, no new fetches needed --
  all 20 already existed locally from the sigma pipeline). Monthly mean
  temp = daily (high+low)/2 averaged per (year, month); anomaly = that
  minus the city's own per-calendar-month climatological normal; linearly
  detrended by year BEFORE regressing against AO/NAO/ENSO (guards against a
  31-year secular-warming trend producing a spurious correlation with an
  index that has its own drift -- checked directly: detrending barely
  moved any slope or p-value, ruling this confound out rather than assuming
  it away). Regressed at LAG 0 (index value for the same month as the temp
  anomaly) per city/season bucket via scipy.stats.linregress, p<0.05 floor,
  fell back to DEFAULT_AO_SENS/NAO_SENS/ENSO_SENS otherwise.
  Independent opus review (before push, per standing workflow) found this
  first pass had a real, live-consequential bug: get_indices() can only
  ever return an ALREADY-PUBLISHED index value -- verified live,
  get_indices(7, 2026) run 2026-07-25 returns JUNE AO/NAO and MAY ONI, not
  July's, because CPC hasn't published the current month's numbers yet by
  the time a near-term market for that month is actually being scanned.
  The first pass's lag-0 fit was testing a relationship the live code can
  never actually exploit. The reviewer independently re-derived the entire
  regression from scratch (own script, live NOAA fetch, own anomaly/
  detrend/bucketing code) both to confirm the first pass's arithmetic (all
  80 cells reproduced exactly -- clean) and to show what refitting at the
  lag get_indices() actually returns does to the results: AO/NAO's lag-1
  autocorrelation is only ~0.3, so most of the fitted AO/NAO signal
  disappeared; ENSO's lag-1 autocorrelation is ~0.97 (El Nino/La Nina
  states persist for months), so ENSO mostly survived. The reviewer also
  flagged that testing 80 cells at a raw p<0.05 threshold, with no
  multiple-comparisons correction, would produce ~4 false positives by
  chance alone, and that the first pass had adopted several cells that
  were only raw-significant.
  Refit at lag 1 (anomaly for month M vs. the PRIOR month's real AO/NAO/
  ONI value) with a Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction at 5% across the 80
  gap-city cells tested (10 cities x 8 cells: AOx3 + NAOx3 + ENSOx2).
  Result: only 4 cells across all 10 researched cities survive both bars --
  all in ENSO's "other" (Jun-Nov) season: Austin (-0.7, n=279, p=0.001),
  OklahomaCity (-0.7, p=0.003), SanAntonio (-0.6, p=0.002), and
  SanFrancisco (+0.6, p<0.001, positive -- the real West Coast ENSO
  teleconnection, opposite sign from the 3 Gulf Coast cities). Every AO and
  NAO cell for all 10 researched cities, and every ENSO-winter cell, stays
  on the flat default -- for 6 of the 10 cities (Washington, Philadelphia,
  Minneapolis, Houston, LasVegas, NewOrleans), NOTHING survived either bar,
  so their table entries are 100% default values. Still worth recording
  explicitly (vs. leaving them out of the dict, which behaves identically)
  because it converts "not yet researched" into "researched, no real
  signal at a usable lag" in the completeness manifest -- a genuine,
  evidenced null result, not an unresearched gap.
  Separately, re-running the identical (lag-1, detrended) methodology
  against the 10 ALREADY-covered cities (informational only, not adopted --
  see the follow-up entry below, whose numbers were also corrected by this
  same review) confirms the disagreement with the hand-set values is, if
  anything, MORE widespread than the first pass's lag-0 sanity check
  suggested: almost none of the hand-set AO/NAO coefficients survive raw
  significance at lag 1 either.
  The 3-Gulf-Coast-city negative ENSO finding (Austin/OklahomaCity/
  SanAntonio) survived the correction and is now, if anything, on firmer
  ground: it's 3 of the only 4 cells that clear the strictest bar applied
  this pass. Per explicit user confirmation (reaffirmed after the
  correction changed which specific cells qualify): adopted as-is, and did
  NOT revise the existing 10 (filed as its own follow-up below).
  Shipped: AO_SENS/NAO_SENS/ENSO_SENS extended to all 20 cities
  (climate_indices.py) -- 6 of the 10 researched cities are all-default,
  4 have exactly one real (ENSO-other) cell. tests/test_climate_indices.py
  updated (_COVERED_CITIES now 20, the "uncovered city" test switched from
  Austin -- now covered -- to a synthetic city name so it keeps testing the
  fallback mechanism itself rather than a real city's now-closed gap; 6 new
  regression-locking tests, including a spring-month case and the
  negative/positive ENSO-other split), tests/test_city_registry_
  manifest.py's _KNOWN_GAPS with the 10 now-stale climate_indices entries
  removed (that test's own bidirectional staleness check would otherwise
  fail the build), tests/test_city_registry_report_logging.py's stale
  "10 cities missing climate_indices" comment corrected. 27 tests pass in
  the scoped climate_indices + city_registry_manifest sweep (plus the 4 in
  test_city_registry_report_logging.py); ruff+mypy clean.

[RESOLVED 2026-07-25] EXISTING 10 climate_indices CITIES' HAND-SET AO/NAO/ENSO VALUES DISAGREE WITH THE REAL 31-YEAR REGRESSION
Priority: Low-Medium -- these values are live in the paper-trading blend

Problem:
  Surfaced as a byproduct of filling the 10-gap-city climate_indices
  follow-up above. Numbers below are from the SAME lag-1 (regress against

  is. At lag 1, almost none of the hand-set 10's AO/NAO coefficients
  survive even raw p<0.05, let alone a multiple-comparisons correction:
  - AO: only Miami-spring (fitted +0.63, p<0.001) is significant, of all
    30 AO cells (10 cities x 3 seasons) across the entire hand-set table.
    Denver's hand-set AO (winter=1.8/spring=1.0/other=0.4) is insignificant
    at all 3 seasons (fitted -0.09 p=0.81, -0.05 p=0.88, +0.13 p=0.72).

    (hand-set winter=1.0/spring=0.8/other=0.3; fitted -0.33 p=0.06, -0.26
    p=0.14, +0.14 p=0.53) -- same physical reason gap-city SanFrancisco
    also came back all-default for AO/NAO: these are Atlantic-sector
    patterns with a weak, statistically-absent Pacific coast signal at a
    1-month lag in the real record.
  - NAO: only Miami-winter (fitted +0.58, p=0.027), Miami-spring (+0.60,

  - ENSO: winter is insignificant everywhere except Seattle (+0.57,
    p=0.003); "other" is significant for Seattle (+0.66), Denver (-0.96),
    Dallas (-0.60), Phoenix (-0.46) -- Denver/Dallas/Phoenix all
    WRONG-SIGNED vs. their positive hand-set ENSO values (0.9/1.0/1.2).
  In short: at the lag the live code actually uses, the hand-set 10's
  AO/NAO table has essentially no statistical support left (1 of 30 AO
  cells, 3 of 30 NAO cells survive raw p<0.05 -- fewer than chance alone
  would produce at that threshold), and ENSO's "other" season has a real,
  currently-mismodeled sign flip for 3 of 10 cities.

What it would look like:
  Re-run the identical regression this session already built (fetch AO/NAO/
  ENSO from CPC, join per-city 30yr Open-Meteo archive, detrend by year,
  regress at lag 1 against the prior month's index value, apply
  Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control across whatever cell count is tested, not
  just a raw p<0.05 floor) against these specific 10 cities and decide
  cell-by-cell whether to replace the hand-set value: agree -> no change;
  fitted disagrees on sign/significance -> revise or fall back to
  DEFAULT_AO_SENS/NAO_SENS/ENSO_SENS. Given how few cells hold up at all,
  the realistic outcome of doing this properly is that most of the
  hand-set 10 collapses toward the flat default too, not a like-for-like
  swap of 30 hand-set numbers for 30 fitted ones. This is a live-blend
  change for cities already trading, not a "gap" fill -- treat it with the
  weight that implies (real tests before/after, likely worth an opus
  review given it touches analyze_trade()'s live threshold-shift path for
  10 established cities simultaneously).

Why not now:
  Explicitly deferred by user decision this session rather than assumed --
  the ask was "do the climate_indices 10-city regression" (the gap-fill),
  not a revision of cities already live in the blend. TRADING_PAUSED holds

When to revisit:

[RESOLVED 2026-07-18] DISPUTED-ROW EXCLUSION PREDICATE HAND-COPIED ~40 TIMES IN tracker.py
Priority: was Medium -- same "one shared rule, many consumers, one gets
  missed" shape this project has hit 7+ times; the existing mutation
  tests protected the 30 *existing* filters but nothing forced a *new*
  query to add one.

Problem (as originally scoped):
  The 2026-07-12 disputed-outcome restoration added the literal predicate
  `AND (o.disputed IS NULL OR o.disputed = 0)` as a hand-copied string to
  every calibration query -- ~40 occurrences by the original estimate.
  The 30-filter mutation test proved existing filters worked, but the
  failure mode that mattered going forward was a NEW function joining
  outcomes on settled_yes and simply not knowing the rule exists -- exactly
  how the original 3-function scope grew to 30 in the first place.

What shipped:
  Took option (a) from this entry's own "what it would look like": a
  `CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS outcomes_valid AS SELECT * FROM outcomes
  WHERE disputed IS NULL OR disputed = 0` in init_db() (right after the
  existing multiday_predictions view precedent), and migrated every
  consumer that should exclude disputed rows to join outcomes_valid
  instead of outcomes -- the view approach over the constant approach
  because it makes the correctness guarantee structural (join the right
  table) rather than "remember to paste the right string," and makes the
  guard test purely mechanical (flag any JOIN/FROM on the raw table
  outside a documented allowlist).

  Live re-count (2026-07-18) found the real number of JOIN/FROM outcomes
  sites was 49, not ~40 -- and a naive single-space regex only found 45 of
  those; 4 more (including get_emos_training_data and
  count_settled_west_coast_multiday) only surfaced after switching to a
  whitespace-tolerant `JOIN\s+outcomes` pattern, since tracker.py's SQL
  formatting inconsistently uses multiple spaces for column alignment
  (`JOIN   outcomes` vs `JOIN outcomes`). Of the 49: 31 already had the
  disputed filter (migrated to the view, predicate line removed -- pure
  refactor, no behavior change); 8 had NO filter and no comment explaining
  why, unlike the 9 legitimately-raw sites (purge_old_predictions:
  deletion by age; sync_outcomes: pre-outcome existence check;
  get_outcome_for_ticker: real position-resolution lookup that needs the
  actual current settlement regardless of dispute status; backfill_emos_
  data: data-repair, not a calibration consumer; get_disputed_count:
  definitionally counts the disputed rows; get_history: intentional raw
  audit listing).

  Those 8 -- count_settled_predictions, count_settled_predictions_rolling,
  count_settled_sameday_predictions, count_emos_ready_predictions,

Problem (as originally scoped, now confirmed already resolved by the
consolidation itself):
  Temperature's consensus bonus raises the ci_adjusted_kelly cap itself
  (KELLY_CAP * KELLY_CAP_CONSENSUS_MULT, 0.33 at defaults) when consensus
  holds, so a strong consensus trade can size up to 0.33. Precip's
  consensus bonus multiplies ci_adjusted_kelly by 1.25 but keeps the cap

  that, precip_consensus trades are capped identically to non-consensus
  ones. Unclear whether this is intentional (precip's higher irreducible
  uncertainty per _CONDITION_CONFIDENCE, 0.85-0.90 vs temperature's 1.00,
  already discounts precip sizing elsewhere) or an oversight from
  temperature's consensus-cap-raise never being ported to precip.

[RESOLVED 2026-07-19] KALSHI CENTS/DOLLARS PRICE NORMALIZATION IMPLEMENTED INDEPENDENTLY 3+ TIMES
Priority: was Medium -- this exact normalization has already produced two

  Shipped utils.coalesce_market_price(market, *keys) -> float (order_

  this entry's own plan almost exactly -- one deviation: placed in

  before deciding) to be a pure TypedDict-only module with zero runtime
  logic today, and utils.py is already the established home for shared

  order_executor._coalesce_cents_or_dollars deleted, all 7 call sites

  and now doubles as regression coverage for the shared function.
  schema_validator.py's third, independently-drifted copy
  (_price_to_decimal) is where this consolidation found a REAL, live bug
  beyond the two the entry cites: unlike the other two copies,
  _price_to_decimal used a uniform `f > 1.0` check for every input type,
  so an integer value of exactly 1 (a genuine 1-cent bid/ask) was
  misclassified as already-decimal and returned as $1.00 instead of $0.01
  -- a 100x error, though low-severity in practice since this function
  only feeds a diagnostic range-check warning, never a live trading
  decision, and 1.0 still happens to pass the [0,1] range check so it
  never even triggered a false alarm. Independently corroborated by a
  pre-existing point-in-time audit doc (docs/grade_audit/outputs/
  schema_validator.py.md, graded 2026-06-29, found by this same session
  rather than trusted blind) that had already flagged the identical `f ==
  1.0` edge case as "theoretical... Kalshi bids are never exactly 1.00 in
  practice" -- the audit correctly identified the mechanism but
  under-stated it as purely theoretical without checking it against the
  other two (correct) copies' int-vs-float branching, which is exactly
  what this consolidation surfaces. Checked that audit doc's other two
  findings (validate_market's DEBUG-not-WARNING logging,
  validate_nws_response's missing ok=False) while in the file -- both
  already fixed in a prior session, stale claims, not re-flagged.
  A real design nuance this call site needed and the other two didn't:
  _price_to_decimal fails SOFT (returns None on unparseable input) since
  schema_validator.py's whole job is to never crash the caller on bad API
  data, while coalesce_market_price is deliberately left unguarded
  (matching order_executor.py's/weather_markets.py's original,
  already-accepted behavior -- both run inside a per-order/per-market
  try/except upstream and are meant to raise on genuinely malformed data
  so it's skipped, not silently treated as $0, which would be MORE
  dangerous for live trading than crashing that one iteration). Rather
  than weaken the shared function for its live-money callers, added a
  local `_safe_price()` wrapper in schema_validator.py (try/except around
  the shared call) that preserves _price_to_decimal's exact fail-soft
  contract. _price_to_decimal deleted; the presence-gate logic ("only
  validate range when both bid and ask are actually present") was
  preserved exactly (same None-check semantics as the original raw_bid/
  raw_ask computation, just restructured as a boolean instead of
  reconstructing the coalesced value twice).
  kalshi_ws.py's ticker-message parser and tracker.py's _candle_dollars
  left untouched, per this entry's own plan -- both are genuinely
  different input shapes (WS ticker messages are always already-dollar-
  format with no cents-int variant ever observed; candlestick sub-fields

  duplication class.
  20 new tests: utils.coalesce_market_price direct coverage (11 tests --

  this entry's own suggestion: split _called_in() into _bare_called_in()/
  _alias_called_in(), and added _resolve_prod_evidence() which, when
  checking whether a candidate function has a real caller in another file,
  first checks whether that other file independently defines its own
  module-level function of the same name (precomputed once via a
  funcs_by_file dict, not re-parsed per candidate). If it does, only an
  explicit alias-import call still counts as evidence -- a bare same-name
  call in that file is its own self-reference, never the candidate's,
  matching how Python name resolution actually works. 4 new synthetic-
  source tests (TestSameNameCollisionResolution) exercise this directly:
  the collision-not-counted case (the actual bug this closes -- confirmed
  by hand that it fails under the old logic if reverted), two no-collision
  baseline cases proving normal alias/bare cross-file calls still count,
  and a mutation-proof case proving an explicit alias import still counts
  even when the other file also defines its own colliding name (rules out
  the fix over-suppressing real evidence). 127 tests pass across
  tests/test_dead_code_scan.py + test_forecasting.py + test_phase4.py, plus
  every test file touching order_executor._current_forecast_cycle
  (test_execution_proof.py, test_p0_10_paper_prelog.py,
  test_prediction_kwargs.py, test_shadow_predictions.py,
  test_trade_improvements.py -- 32 passed). Lint/mypy clean.

  Independently reviewed (Agent, opus) -- clean, no HIGH/MEDIUM issues.
  Verified by hand that the collision logic matches real Python name
  resolution (a bare call in a file that defines its own same-named
  function can only ever resolve to that file's own definition, never
  another file's), that the fix only ever makes the guard MORE aggressive
  (can't introduce a false "live code flagged dead"), and that the
  synthetic tests are genuine regressions rather than passing vacuously.
  Two LOW cosmetic notes, both applied: renamed the now-misleadingly-named
  test_phase4.py class, and removed a harmless-but-confusing no-op
  _strip_def_line call in the collision branch (the only checks that run
  there -- alias-call and string-reference matching -- can't match a `def
  name(` line either way, so stripping it changed nothing).

[RESOLVED 2026-08-07, see final note at the end -- previously PARTIALLY
  RESOLVED 2026-07-25, STALE TITLE CORRECTED 2026-07-30] ForecastCache
  EXISTS, BUT 2 HAND-ROLLED CACHES (climatology.py) REMAIN AN UNDECIDED
  ARCHITECTURAL CALL -- ORIGINALLY "~14 HAND-ROLLED TTL DICTS," NOW STALE
Priority: was Low-Medium -- consistency/tooling debt, not a live bug; each
  hand-rolled cache re-implements expiry slightly differently and each
  needs its own test-isolation hook. Now Low: only 2 caches remain
  undecided, not ~14.

PARTIALLY RESOLVED 2026-07-19: before touching anything, did a full survey
  (via a dedicated Explore pass) of every remaining cache this entry lists,
  since the original text's own line numbers/shapes had drifted and only 2
  of ~14 were actually checked in detail before. Findings that changed the
  scope from what this entry originally implied:
  - `_MAE_WEIGHTS_CACHE` (weather_markets.py) has NO TTL at all -- a
    permanent memoization dict, not a `(value, ts)` cache. Migrating it
    would be a real behavior change (introducing expiry where none existed),
    not a pure refactor.
  - `_DYNAMIC_BIAS_CACHE` (weather_markets.py) stores a 3-tuple
    `(value, count, ts)` -- a different shape needing the count folded into
    the stored value rather than the timestamp slot.
  - nws.py's 5 cache dicts: 2 are permanent (no TTL, same behavior-change
    risk as _MAE_WEIGHTS_CACHE), 1 (`_station_cache`) is disk-persisted
    across process restarts via `.nws_station_cache.json`, and 3
    (`_forecast_cache`, `_obs_cache`, `_precip_cache`) stamp with wall-clock
    `time.time()` instead of monotonic time -- migrating those would be a
    real semantic change, not mechanical, plus `_forecast_cache` alone is
    referenced in 4 test files.
  - climate_indices.py's `_indices_cache` and climatology.py's `_MEM_CACHE`/
    `_sigma_mem_cache`: none store a timestamp in the entry at all --
    freshness is tracked via a sibling module variable or disk-file mtime
    instead. Forcing these into ForecastCache's per-entry model means
    restructuring the freshness mechanism, not swapping a declaration.
  - ml_bias.py's 3 "caches" aren't even TTL'd keyed dicts -- one is a bare
    `tuple | None`, all 3 are load-once memoization backed by pickle/HMAC or
    JSON disk files. Don't belong in this refactor at all.
  User chose (after reviewing this survey) to migrate only the genuinely
  clean, same-shape group now and leave everything above explicitly
  documented as out of scope, rather than force a shape mismatch or an
  accidental behavior change onto code that currently works fine.
  Migrated (8 caches, all plain `(value, ts)` or already-per-entry-TTL
  shapes, all sharing ForecastCache's exact semantics with zero behavior
  change): weather_markets.py's `_NBM_CACHE`, `_ECMWF_CACHE`,
  `_PRECIP_ENSEMBLE_CACHE`, `_HRRR_CACHE`, `_WEATHERAPI_CACHE` (the
  original 5-cache recommendation below), plus `_CONSENSUS_CACHE` (turned
  out to already use the exact `(value, ts, ttl)` per-entry-TTL shape
  `ForecastCache.set_with_ttl()` wants -- an even cleaner fit than the
  original 5), mos.py's `_MOS_CACHE`, and metar.py's `_METAR_CACHE`.
  Real subtlety handled, not glossed over: `_NBM_CACHE`/`_ECMWF_CACHE`/
  `_HRRR_CACHE`/`_WEATHERAPI_CACHE`/`_MOS_CACHE`/`_METAR_CACHE` all
  negative-cache a real `None` result (a known-failed fetch, to avoid
  hammering a dead endpoint within the TTL window) -- plain
  `ForecastCache.get()` can't distinguish "no entry" from "entry present
  with value None," so a naive `.get() is not None` port would have
  silently defeated negative caching (every call to a known-dead endpoint
  would re-fetch instead of respecting the TTL). All 6 read sites use
  `get_with_ts()`'s explicit `hit` boolean instead. `_PRECIP_ENSEMBLE_CACHE`
  and `_CONSENSUS_CACHE` never store bare `None`, so their read sites use
  the simpler `.get()` pattern already established by weather_markets.py's
  pre-existing `_ensemble_cache`/`_forecast_cache`.
  Also found and simplified, while migrating `_NBM_CACHE`: the "don't
  clobber a still-fresh OTHER-var cache entry" check (added 2026-07-17, see
  REAL NBM VIA IEM NBS STATION BULLETINS) previously computed
  `now - raw_ts >= TTL` by hand -- `ForecastCache.get()` already returns
  None for both "no entry" and "expired," exactly the "missing or stale"
  condition that check needed, so it collapses to a plain
  `.get(key) is None`. **Correction (opus review caught this, not
  self-caught):** not quite behavior-identical in one narrow case --
  `.get()` also can't distinguish a fresh negative-cached `None` (a prior
  failed fetch) from "no entry," so this now overwrites a fresh-but-failed
  OTHER-var entry with real data from the current successful fetch, where
  the old raw-timestamp check would have preserved the stale failure.
  Reviewed and accepted as a strict data-quality improvement (the
  replacement is always a genuine max/min derived from the same successful
  response, never a worse or wrong value) rather than reintroducing the
  manual timestamp check just to avoid it -- documented in-code at the call
  site so a future reader tracing this exact discrepancy isn't left
  guessing.
  Updated 4 test files that directly patched these caches as raw dicts or
  hand-seeded raw tuples (test_ecmwf.py, test_nbm.py, test_metar.py,
  test_weather_markets.py) to construct/patch a real `ForecastCache()`
  instance instead -- `.clear()` calls elsewhere (conftest.py's autouse
  METAR-cache fixture, test_mos.py, test_phase2_batch_a.py,
  test_forecasting.py's HRRR test) needed no changes since `.clear()` is
  already a ForecastCache method with identical semantics.
  New regression tests (one per negative-caching cache -- the single most
  important correctness property this migration had to preserve): each
  calls the fetch function twice against a mocked-to-fail backend and
  asserts the SECOND call does not re-invoke the mock, proving a negative-
  cached result is actually respected rather than silently re-fetched every
  call. Mutation-tested directly: temporarily reverted `_NBM_CACHE`'s read
  site to a naive `.get() is not None` check, confirmed the new test failed
  with the exact predicted symptom (a 2nd IEM/Open-Meteo call), then
  restored the real fix -- validates the same pattern used identically
  across all 6 negative-caching sites.
  433 tests pass across every affected file (test_ecmwf.py, test_nbm.py,
  test_weather_markets.py, test_forecasting.py, test_phase4.py,
  test_metar.py, test_mos.py, test_mos_nbs.py, test_phase2_batch_a.py,
  test_forecast_accuracy.py, test_price_and_size.py, test_cron_integration.py,
  test_p1_remaining.py); ruff + ruff format + mypy clean on all 3 changed
  source files (weather_markets.py, mos.py, metar.py).

  FOLLOW-UP, same day -- (1) upgraded from "non-blocking, pre-existing" to
  a real fix after re-checking the actual blast radius rather than taking
  the "pre-existing, low-impact" framing at face value: `get_indices()`'s

  climatological-probability blend `analyze_trade()` uses for live
  trade decisions. Not hypothetical, not pre-existing-and-therefore-fine --
  a real, currently-reachable bug in the live pipeline (this migration
  didn't introduce it, the single-slot key already existed before, but it
  deserved fixing rather than leaving alone once the actual reach was
  traced). Fixed: cache now keyed by `(year, month)` instead of a fixed
  "latest" string -- `year`/`month` computation moved before the cache
  lookup (previously computed only in the fetch-miss branch, after the
  lookup). H-17's "don't cache an all-zero failure" behavior, thread safety

What's still open (confirmed genuinely hard on the second pass's re-check,
not just first-pass caution -- see the survey above for why each one
resisted the corrected, more thorough re-derivation):
  - `_station_cache` (nws.py): persists via a whole-dict dump/load
    (`_save_station_cache`/`_load_station_cache`), a pattern ForecastCache
    has no enumeration API for. Needs either extending the shared
    ForecastCache class with a new capability (touches every already-
    migrated cache, including live-trading-adjacent `_ensemble_cache`) or
    staying a plain dict permanently.
  - climatology.py's `_MEM_CACHE`/`_sigma_mem_cache`: a genuinely different
    architecture -- load-once-per-process, freshness gated by disk-file
    mtime checked only on first load, not an in-memory TTL at all. Forcing
    a ForecastCache TTL onto this would either no-op or introduce new
    re-fetch behavior mid-process that doesn't exist today.
  - ml_bias.py's 3 caches: not TTL'd keyed dicts at all (pickle/HMAC/JSON-
    backed load-once singletons, one isn't even a dict) -- excluded from

    the run-trend pattern) -- not needed by anything migrated across either
    pass (none of the 15 needed a shorter miss-TTL than their hit-TTL

    any of this).

    conftest fixtures -- still just 1 real fixture (METAR's) plus a handful

  (per standing practice) and re-verified both remaining pieces directly

  -- both held up exactly: _station_cache (nws.py) is still a permanent,
  disk-round-tripped map with no TTL semantics; climatology.py's
  _MEM_CACHE/_sigma_mem_cache are still load-once-per-process singletons
  gated by disk-file mtime, not an in-memory TTL. Presented 3 options via
