[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- see resolution below.] execution_log.py and tracker.py never explicitly close SQLite connections
Priority: LOW (audit id AUD-0048, status CONFIRMED, confidence HIGH, evidence E1)
Files: execution_log.py, tracker.py

Problem:
  _conn() in both files returns a raw sqlite3.connect(...) object used via `with _conn() as con:`. sqlite3.Connection's context-manager protocol only commits/rolls back the transaction on exit -- it does not close the connection. Neither file ever calls con.close().
  Root cause: The `with _conn() as con:` idiom is commonly (and incorrectly) assumed to close the connection the way file-object context managers do; sqlite3.Connection's __exit__ only manages the transaction.
  Evidence: Independently re-ran the grep: execution_log.py has exactly 21 `with _conn() as con:` blocks and 0 `con.close()` calls; tracker.py has exactly 105 and 0 respectively -- both counts match the finding's own citation exactly. Confirmed execution_log.py:108-113 `_conn()` returns a raw `sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH, timeout=30)` with no pooling wrapper.
  Financial risk: None observed.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- see resolution below.] trade_cycle.py's prewarm ThreadPoolExecutor tasks are not cancelled on timeout and outlive the phase that spawned them
Priority: LOW (audit id AUD-0050, status CONFIRMED, confidence HIGH, evidence E1)
Files: trade_cycle.py, cron.py

Problem:
  _run_batch_prewarm_for_pairs submits up to 8 per-city-date prewarm tasks and waits on as_completed(warm_futures, timeout=200); on TimeoutError it only logs and falls through, and the finally: warm_pool.shutdown(wait=False) does not pass cancel_futures=True (default False) and cannot stop already-running worker threads regardless. Already-submitted _warm_one_tracked calls keep running on background threads while run_trade_cycle proceeds into the next (analysis) phase.
  Root cause: shutdown(wait=False) only stops new task submission; it neither cancels queued futures nor interrupts running ones, so the 'prewarm phase' the rest of the code treats as finished is not actually over.
  Evidence: Read trade_cycle.py:1136-1173 and cron.py:2375-2377 directly: as_completed(..., timeout=200) at line 1157, TimeoutError handling at 1164-1170 (log + fall through, no cancellation), shutdown(wait=False) at 1172, and cron.py's watchdog os._exit(1) hard-kill (no cleanup) at 2375-2377.
  Financial risk: Low — the touched caches are internally locked, so this is a performance/hang-risk finding rather than a P&L-affecting one.
  Recommendation: Pass cancel_futures=True to shutdown() (Python 3.9+) to at least drop queued-but-not-started tasks, and consider whether already-running prewarm threads need an explicit cooperative-cancellation flag if their side effects (cache writes) should not race with the next phase's reads.
  Full record: audit/AUDIT_REPORT.json (id AUD-0050), audit/AUDIT_REPORT.md.

Resolution (2026-08-24, re-verified during batch-48's backlog review, fix landed via AUD-0050, commit 0d601705):
  trade_cycle.py:1309-1314 now has an explicit "# AUD-0050:" comment and
  `warm_pool.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)`. The soft "consider
  a cooperative-cancel flag for already-running threads" half was never a
  hard requirement -- ThreadPoolExecutor has no way to interrupt an
  already-running worker thread regardless.

  The 2 remaining findings were about the shared safe_io.CrossProcessLock
  primitive itself (safe_io.py), not specific to this entry, but fixed
  here since this is where the primitive was first exercised end-to-end:
  (a) LOW -- CrossProcessLock.acquire()'s docstring promised "never raises"
  but a BaseException (e.g. KeyboardInterrupt) landing inside the retry

  propagate with the file handle left open (relying on CPython's

  for an OS-level byte-range lock). Fixed by wrapping the retry loop in
  try/except BaseException: close the handle, then re-raise. New test

  masked the exact gap this fix closes). Mutation-tested: reverting the
  try/except makes the direct `fh.closed` check fail. (b) LOW/vacuous
  test -- the original TestCrossProcessLock::
  test_two_threads_racing_have_exactly_one_winner asserted
  results.count(True) == 2, which is true both under a correctly-serialized

  test_two_threads_racing_both_eventually_acquire_but_never_overlap and
  rewrote to record each hold's [enter, exit) interval and assert they
  never overlap. Mutation-tested by gutting acquire() to `return True`
  unconditionally: the new version correctly fails (intervals overlap); the
  old version would have passed. Also fixed as pure cleanup, no separate
  test needed: a stale doc cross-reference in safe_io.py (10s -> 30s, see
  AUD-0030's own note), a hardcoded 5s test-only timeout in
  settlement_monitor.py hoisted to a module constant

[PARTIALLY RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-61 item 1; headline /api/trades double-read fixed earlier by 0d601705 (batch-12), multi-read-per-request waste fixed now; single-read-per-request routes deliberately left uncached, see Resolution] web_app.py's /api/trades route loads the entire paper ledger twice in one request, with no caching across the ~7 routes (plus the /api/stream SSE loop) that each independently call get_open_trades()/get_all_trades()

Resolution, part 1 (2026-08-22, batch-12, commit 0d601705):
  The headline symptom -- api_trades() calling get_open_trades() AND
  get_all_trades() for the same request -- was fixed there: the route now
  makes one get_all_trades() call and derives open trades with a local
  `not t.get("settled")` filter (see the `# AUD-0053:` comment in
  web_app.py's api_trades). That half needs no further work.

Resolution, part 2 (2026-08-24, batch-61 item 1) -- REMAINING SCOPE NARROWED:
  Added paper.load_ledger_snapshot() (one _DATA_LOCK-held _load() returning
  the whole ledger dict) and, in web_app.py, a REQUEST-SCOPED cache of that
  snapshot keyed on the live request object: _req_ledger() / _req_balance() /
  _req_open_trades() / _invalidate_req_ledger(). Converted the three call
  sites that read the ledger more than once per request. Their ledger-
  accessor reads go 3 -> 1, 2 -> 1 and 2 -> 1 respectively.
  Side benefit: balance and open_count in a given response now come from the
  SAME file read, so a settle landing mid-request can no longer pair a
  post-settle balance with a pre-settle position count.

  MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED (opus review): the win is real but much narrower
  than "/api/status now does one read". Instrumenting paper._load() over one
  real /api/status request gives 16 calls before and 14 after -- 12.5%, not
  3->1. The other 12 come from paper-internal helpers the same route calls
  (fear_greed_index, get_daily_pnl, get_peak_balance,
  drawdown_scaling_factor, get_max_drawdown_pct, get_portfolio_expected_value,
  and simulate_portfolio's own get_balance), each of which calls _load()
  inside paper.py where a web_app-level cache cannot reach. The SSE loop,
  whose ONLY ledger reads are the two this change converts, really is halved:
  6 _load() calls per 3 ticks before, 3 after. The first draft of this
  resolution and the code comments claimed the 3->1 figure for the whole
  route; both have been corrected.

  Why NOT a module-level memo on _load() (the obvious reading of this
  entry's "no shared/memoized read path"): paper_trades.json is written by
  other processes (cron, watch) and stores its own SHA-256 content checksum.
  A process-lifetime cache would serve trades that no longer match the file
  and could mask a real corruption -- strictly worse than the redundant I/O
  it saves. An mtime-keyed cache was also rejected as carrying real
  invalidation risk for a LOW-priority perf entry.

  DESIGN CORRECTION vs. the batch-61 handoff: the handoff asserted a flask.g
  cache is "safe by construction because a request is short-lived". That is
  FALSE for this app. /api/stream wraps an INFINITE generator in
  stream_with_context, which keeps the request context -- and therefore
  flask.g -- alive for the entire life of the SSE connection. Verified with
  an isolated Flask probe: a naive g-cache re-served the very first snapshot
  on every tick. The SSE loop therefore calls _invalidate_req_ledger()
  explicitly at the top of each tick; this is mandatory, not an
  optimization, and any future long-lived streaming route needs the same.
  _invalidate_req_ledger() is also called right after the two ledger-WRITING
  routes (/api/paper-order, /api/close-position) so nothing added below them
  later can read back a pre-write snapshot.

  Aliasing contract: cached trade rows are SHARED within a request and must
  be treated as read-only. /api/trades deliberately keeps its own uncached
  paper.get_all_trades() call because it writes current_yes_bid/
  current_yes_ask into the rows it returns -- and, per part 1 above, it
  already reads the ledger only once, so it had nothing to gain. The three
  converted sites' consumers (monte_carlo.simulate_portfolio,
  weather_markets.detect_hedge_opportunity, paper.corr_kelly_scale) were
  AST-scanned and confirmed non-mutating.

  _req_balance()/_req_open_trades() use `["balance"]`/`["trades"]`
  subscripts, not .get() with a default, so a malformed ledger fails exactly
  as loudly as the uncached paper path did (a 0.0 default would have
  rendered "$0.00" on the dashboard where the operator previously got a
  500). The per-row test is `not t["settled"]`, byte-for-byte
  paper.get_open_trades()'s own filter: an intermediate draft used
  .get("settled") and opus review caught that it silently turned a 500 into
  a 200 counting the row as an open position, AND would have made /health
  (still calling paper.get_open_trades() directly) report a different open
  count than /api/status for the same file.

REVIEW FINDINGS ADDRESSED (independent opus review of this diff):
  - flask.g is APP-context scoped, not request-scoped. RequestContext.push()
    reuses an existing app context, so two requests handled inside an outer
    `with app.app_context():` would have SHARED one snapshot -- silently
    becoming the process-lifetime cache this design rejects. Reproduced by
    the reviewer. Nothing pushes an app context in this repo today, but the
    cache now keys on the live request object (held by reference, compared
    with `is` -- deliberately not id(), whose uniqueness only holds among
    live objects) so it is per-request however contexts nest. Regression
    test added.
  - _invalidate_req_ledger() was called on the success path only in both
    ledger-writing routes, so a write that raised PART WAY through would
    have left a pre-write snapshot behind -- not the guarantee the comment
    claimed. Both are now try/finally, each with its own test that drives
    the real route with the write raising (both assert the route reached the
    write via a 500 positive control, so `spy.called` cannot pass vacuously).
  - The comment on /api/close-position claimed the route reads open trades
    through the cache; it reads them via the uncached paper.get_open_trades().
    Corrected.
  - paper.load_ledger_snapshot() had ZERO executed coverage -- every
    web_app test patches it out, so its `with _DATA_LOCK: return _load()`
    body was never run. 4 real tests added to tests/test_paper.py (whole-dict
    shape, agreement with the individual accessors on the same file, lock
    actually held during the read, and corruption propagating rather than
    being swallowed). Mutation-tested: dropping `with _DATA_LOCK:` fails the
    lock test.
  - The unreachable `except ImportError` flask fallbacks were removed
    (web_app.py's module-level `from flask import request` already makes
    flask a hard requirement, so the branch and its comment were both false).
  - Test hygiene: the class fixture is now a factory rather than a
    shallow-copied class attribute (it was handing every test the same
    trades list and row dicts -- the weakest possible place to detect the
    aliasing violation these tests exist to catch); the SSE test uses
    itertools.islice rather than zip(), which pulled an unasserted 4th tick
    that exhausted side_effect and logged a spurious warning every run; and
    the filter test now actually compares against paper.get_open_trades()
    instead of only asserting settled rows are excluded, paired with a
    positive control on a row missing `settled`.
  - Added a test pinning that /api/trades deliberately does NOT use the
    shared snapshot (it mutates the rows it returns).
  - Item 2 (auth removal) drew NO findings at any severity: the reviewer
    independently re-derived it and probed a live app with a password set,
    confirming every path -- including both de-decorated routes, static
    files, 404s and /api/stream -- still 401s without valid credentials, and
    that the CSRF gate still rejects a correctly-authenticated POST missing
    X-Requested-With.

WHY THIS STAYS PARTIALLY RESOLVED (what is deliberately still open):
  Routes that read the ledger exactly ONCE per request -- /health,
  /api/live_signals, /history, /api/trades, and the three load_paper_trades()
  sites (~L1811/2024/2359) -- still each do their own full read. A
  request-scoped cache cannot help them BY CONSTRUCTION: there is no second
  read in the same request to share with. Eliminating that residual would
  require a cross-request cache (mtime-keyed or otherwise), which is exactly
  the invalidation risk rejected above. If this entry is revisited, the open
  question is specifically "is an mtime-keyed cross-request cache worth the
  corruption-masking risk for a LOW-priority perf item?", not "add
  memoization" generally.

  Tests: 7 new in tests/test_web_app.py (TestRequestScopedLedgerCache) --
  one-read-per-request, per-request isolation, invalidation, the real
  /api/stream route driven for 3 ticks, no-request-context fallback, the
  settled filter, and an /api/status route-level positive control asserting
  the actual returned numbers (not just the read count). tests/test_web_app.py
  87 passed (was 80). Mutation-tested via Edit: removing the SSE invalidate
  froze all three ticks at the first balance (1 test failed); removing the
  cache entirely (3 failed); swapping flask.g for a process-lifetime module
  cache (4 failed, including the per-request-isolation test).
  Scoped suites all green: test_web_app / test_web_auth / test_web_analytics
  / test_paper / test_paper_metrics / test_paper_cross_process_lock (301
  passed) and test_batch24_alerting / test_live_execution / test_prelog /

  Root cause: The module's own docstring states this is intentional ("Logs warnings on violations rather than crashing"), so functionally this is logging-only by design rather than a broken gate that regressed.   Evidence: Independently read schema_validator.py in full (196 lines) confirming all three functions return bool per docstring.   Financial risk: Low/indirect — downstream consumers generally already use .get() with defaults and None-checks, so this is a missed defense-in-depth layer rather than an active bug path.
  Recommendation: Either wire the boolean into the callers (skip processing malformed records) if that protection is actually wanted, or change the return type/docstring to make clear these are logging-only, to prevent a future caller (or the nws.py circuit-breaker comment's own apparent original intent) from...
  Full record: audit/AUDIT_REPORT.json (id AUD-0060), audit/AUDIT_REPORT.md.

Applied at weather_markets.get_weather_forecast's per-model _fetch_one closure (validate_forecast's check moved inside the existing try, raising into the same except that already calls _forecast_cb.record_failure() -- matches the is_all_null dead-model pattern immediately above it) and nws.get_nws_daily_forecast (a malformed response now calls _nws_cb.record_failure() and returns {} instead of _nws_cb.record_success() unconditionally -- this also makes the function's own pre-existing comment, "validate BEFORE recording success so a malformed response doesn't credit the circuit breaker," actually true; previously it stated an intent that wasn't wired in).
  kalshi_client.py's TWO call sites (get_markets' list-build, get_market() singular) were NOT touched -- CORRECTION: a get_markets() list-filter fix was implemented mid-session, then the ENTIRE file was reverted via `git checkout -- kalshi_client.py` (confirmed zero diff, `git log -1 -- kalshi_client.py` still shows batch-09's commit) after discovering kalshi_client.py is owned by batches 02/05/09 (batch-09 already committed, touching this exact file), genuinely out of batch-13's scope despite AUD-0060's own Files line listing it. This item is therefore only PARTIALLY resolved by this session -- both kalshi_client.py call sites remain exactly as documented in the Problem section above, deferred to whichever batch legitimately next touches that file. (Note: get_market() singular would likely stay deliberately warn-only even then, matching this same class's own _validate() helper's existing stance and the 15+ call sites across the codebase that depend on it always returning a dict -- but that's a decision for whoever picks this up, not pre-made here.)
  Testing: weather_markets.py: new test_malformed_response_recorded_as_failure_not_used (mutation-tested). nws.py: new test_malformed_response_records_failure_not_success + a positive-control well-formed-response test (both mutation-tested).

Resolution (2026-08-24, batch-62 item 5) -- the two kalshi_client.py sites this
entry was left partially-resolved for are now decided, differently from each
other as the 2026-08-22 note predicted:

  get_market() (singular): kept DELIBERATELY warn-only, now with a docstring
  saying why. Returning None/{} on validation failure would be a breaking
  contract change for 15+ call sites that all assume a dict, and would convert
  a data-quality problem into an AttributeError far from here. Matches the
  class's own _validate() stance for the response envelope.

  get_markets() (list build): filters -- but only on STRUCTURAL failure, via a
  new local _is_structurally_usable() rather than validate_market's aggregate
  bool. This corrects the batch's first draft, which gated on that bool
  directly. Opus review showed validate_market mixes "this dict is unusable"
  with "this book looks economically odd," and the second half rejects REAL
  market states -- verified directly: a locked book (yes_bid == yes_ask == 52c)
  and a settled-YES market (100/100) both trip its inverted-spread check.
  get_markets feeds settlement sync (refresh_hurricane_count_to_date,
  settlement_monitor) and compute_hourly_temperature_proxy's ladder, where a
  dropped entry is a silently WRONG number rather than a missing one -- a
  dropped rung shifts the computed proxy temperature instead of failing. So
  only entries no consumer could read at all are dropped: not a dict, no
  ticker, or no name under either the legacy or current alias for one of
  bid/ask/volume. Price-range and spread violations still get
  validate_market's WARNING and still flow through; the caller's gates decide.

  Plus a fail-open guard: if EVERY entry on a non-empty page is unusable, the
  page is passed through with an ERROR rather than returning []. The likely
  cause of that state is an API-wide field rename, not N simultaneously-corrupt
  markets -- and [] would be indistinguishable from "this series has no open
  markets", which weather_markets._fetch_series would then cache as healthy for
  its full 60s TTL (it only sets `degraded` on an exception).

  Each dropped ticker is logged at ERROR, not just validate_market's WARNING,
  so a silently-lost settlement is traceable.

  Testing: test_kalshi_client.py -- 4 new tests (structural drop with the
  ticker in the log; locked/settled/no-quote markets KEPT, with a positive
  control that validate_market really did object to them; the all-unusable
  fail-open page; get_market still warn-only). Mutation-tested: gating on
  validate_market's bool instead of the structural check fails the
  "real market states are kept" test.

[PARTIALLY RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-62 item 6; scope narrowed, fix deliberately deferred to graduation. See resolution below.] Far-tail rain climatology blend's additive dry-tilt shift is floor-clipped at 0.0, under-applying the correction for near-zero precipitation distributions
Priority: INFO (audit id AUD-0066, status CONFIRMED, confidence HIGH, evidence E1)
Files: acis_precip.py, weather_markets.py

Problem:
  acis_precip.py:499's `shifted = [max(0.0, s + damped_shift_in) for s in remaining_sums]` applies a floor-at-0.0 additive shift to a distribution that is mostly exact zeros (dry days). A negative (dry-tilt) shift gets asymmetrically clipped toward zero more than a positive shift would be. Confirmed shadow-only/log-only: the far-case tilted values feed only forecast_blend_signal['rain_forecast_blend_prob'] (a metadata/logging dict), while blended_prob (the value that actually drives recommended_side/sizing) comes from a separate, earlier remaining_sums_tilted computation.
  Root cause: An additive shift model applied to a zero-heavy, non-negative distribution mechanically produces an asymmetric floor effect for negative shifts.
  Evidence: acis_precip.py:499 read directly and confirmed verbatim. weather_markets.py:8858-8873's in-code comment matches this characterization near-verbatim ('mostly exact zeros... dry SEAS5 tilt gets clipped... Not fixed here... shadow-only'). Traced weather_markets.py:8912-9052 line by line: combined_totals only feeds forecast_blend_signal (a dict merged into a 'signals' metadata key at L9051-9052);...
  Financial risk: None currently -- confirmed not to feed the live-trading-affecting blended_prob/recommended_side/sizing path.
  Recommendation: Consider a multiplicative or rank-preserving tilt instead of a floor-clipped additive one if/when this signal is graduated out of shadow-only status.
  Full record: audit/AUDIT_REPORT.json (id AUD-0066), audit/AUDIT_REPORT.md.

Resolution (2026-08-24, batch-62 item 6) -- NARROWED, NOT FIXED. Deliberate,
with the measurement that decided it:

  The defect is real and reproduced: the `max(0.0, s + damped_shift_in)` floor
  under-applies a dry tilt on a zero-heavy distribution. On [0.0]*19 + [4.0]
  the realised mean shift is 1/20th of the requested one.

  A redistribute-the-clipped-remainder fix WAS implemented, tested (hand-
  computed multi-pass cases, degenerate inputs, mutation-tested) and then
  REVERTED after opus review measured its effect on the quantity the caller
  actually consumes. _analyze_monthly_rain_trade reads an EXCEEDANCE
  PROBABILITY -- the fraction of members above a strike -- not a mean.
  Redistribution preserves the mean shift exactly, but only by moving the
  surviving wet-tail members far past the +/-25%-of-mean per-member clamp the
  function documents. Measured:
    [0.0]*19 + [4.0], dry tilt:  clamp 0.0500, actual max per-member move
      1.0000 (20x);  P(> 3.0 in) 0.050 -> 0.000  (floor-clip leaves it 0.050)
    sparse snow-like 20y series: clamp 0.2025, actual 0.8375 (4.1x);
      P(> 0.1 in) 0.300 -> 0.200  (floor-clip leaves it 0.300)
  acis_snow re-exports the same function, so the snow ladder inherits it, and
  snow distributions are more zero-heavy still.

  Trading a documented per-member bound and the tail shape for a mean the
  consumer never reads is the wrong trade. The correct fix remains the
  multiplicative / rank-preserving tilt this entry already recommends, which
  moves central tendency without flattening the tail -- and it belongs WITH
  graduating rain_forecast_blend, not before it. That registry entry is still
  ungraduated and shadow-only, so nothing here reaches a live order today.

  RESIDUAL (what keeps this entry open): implement the multiplicative tilt as
  part of graduating rain_forecast_blend / RAIN_TRADING_ENABLED, and re-verify
  the exceedance probabilities at that point.

  What DID ship: apply_seasonal_tilt's docstring now states the limitation, the
  measurement, and why the obvious fix was rejected, instead of leaving a
  future reader to rediscover it; weather_markets.py's own "accepted,
  documented limitation" comment at the tail-tilt call site is annotated with
  the same. New tests (test_acis_precip.py
  TestDryTiltFloorClippingIsAcceptedNotFixed) PIN the current under-application
  and the intact far tail, so a future graduation change has to update them
  deliberately rather than silently altering the shadow signal.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-62 item 3; see resolution below.] ForecastCache disk snapshot is last-writer-wins across independent processes
Priority: INFO (audit id AUD-0074, status CONFIRMED, confidence HIGH, evidence E1)
Files: forecast_cache.py

Problem:
  ForecastCache/PersistentForecastCache's store is strictly in-process (self._store: dict), so separate cron/watch/web_app processes each hold an independent copy; dump_to_disk/load_from_disk round-trip through a single shared JSON file with no cross-process merge — the last process to dump_to_disk() wins and silently discards any newly-learned entries a losing process added.
  Root cause: dump_to_disk builds its serialized payload purely from the calling instance's own in-memory self._store and does a full atomic_write_json overwrite; load_from_disk likewise fully replaces in-memory entries from whatever the file currently contains — no read-merge-write.
  Evidence: Read forecast_cache.py:185-227 directly, confirming the full-overwrite/full-replace shape with no merge step.
  Financial risk: None — the caches affected are documented as permanent/idempotent derived facts (e.g. station lookups) that get re-derived next time needed, not trading state.
  Recommendation: No action needed given the low-impact caches involved; if this pattern is reused for higher-value state in the future, a read-merge-write should be considered.
  Full record: audit/AUDIT_REPORT.json (id AUD-0074), audit/AUDIT_REPORT.md.

Resolution (2026-08-24, batch-62 item 3):
  Confirmed as filed. dump_to_disk built its payload purely from the calling
  instance's own _store and did a full atomic_write_json overwrite, so
  whichever of cron/watch/web_app dumped last silently discarded every key the
  others had learned.

  Fixed as read-MERGE-write. Conflict rule, stated explicitly: on-disk entries
  are loaded first and this instance's applied last, so LOCAL WINS on a key
  collision and disk-only keys are carried through. Newest-fetch-wins is NOT
  available without a schema change -- the on-disk format is {key: value} with
  no per-entry timestamp, and the in-memory timestamp is time.monotonic(),
  which is not comparable across processes. Local-wins is strictly better than
  the old behaviour regardless: it never loses a key, and on a collision keeps
  exactly the value the old code kept. For the one real consumer (nws.py's
  station-ID cache, whose entries are immutable station->coord facts) the
  collision case is a no-op.

  Opus review caught three things, all fixed:
  - A corrupt/unparseable snapshot originally RAISED, which would have made
    every subsequent dump raise forever -- and nws._save_station_cache swallows
    that at DEBUG, so nothing would ever be persisted again, invisibly. The
    pre-merge overwrite was at least self-healing. Now logs at ERROR and
    overwrites, keeping the self-heal while making the loss traceable.
  - load_from_disk raised on a key str_to_key could not parse, discarding the
    WHOLE snapshot -- and since dump now carries disk keys through verbatim,
    that bad key would be written straight back, so the load stayed broken
    permanently. Now skips the key with an ERROR and keeps the rest.
  - The class docstring claimed load_from_disk "fully replaces" the store. It
    does not and never did -- it merges, disk-wins. Corrected.

  Four residual limitations are now documented on dump_to_disk rather than left
  implicit: not cross-process atomic (window narrowed from "always" to the
  read-to-rename gap); the file can exceed max_size; DELETION CANNOT BE
  EXPRESSED (clear()/prune_expired()/eviction no longer reach disk); and on
  Windows the new read holds the file open, so a concurrent os.replace can hit
  WinError 5 (bounded by _replace_with_retry's 1s deadline).

  Priority was INFO and the change was kept to that weight -- no schema change,
  no timestamps added.

  Testing: test_forecast_cache.py -- new tests for the cross-process scenario
  (mutation-tested: reverting to the overwrite loses STATION_A), the local-wins
  rule, a first-ever-dump positive control, both self-heal paths, the
  skipped-bad-key path, the documented deletion limitation, and a
  lock-held-across-the-read probe.

  automated permission classifier has previously blocked deleting

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-62 item 4; see resolution below.] ml_bias.py's HMAC sidecar write bypasses the codebase's atomic-write convention (but fails safe on a torn write anyway)
Priority: INFO (audit id AUD-0078, status CONFIRMED, confidence HIGH, evidence E1)
Files: ml_bias.py

Problem:
  _write_hmac() writes the HMAC sidecar via a plain Path.write_text() call rather than safe_io.atomic_write_text/atomic_write_json. A process kill mid-write here could leave a truncated/corrupt .hmac file.
  Root cause: This write path was not included in the atomic-write migration passes or their bypass-guard tests, likely because it writes via Path.write_text directly rather than a bare os.replace() (the specific pattern those guard tests check for).
  Evidence: Direct read of ml_bias.py:72-75 (_write_hmac) confirms no safe_io import/usage. Direct read of ml_bias.py:78-155 (_load_models) confirms every rejection path returns {} rather than loading unverified data.
  Financial risk: None identified.
  Security risk: None -- the HMAC check also incidentally covers the reliability case.
  Recommendation: Low priority: route _write_hmac (and the adjacent .pkl write) through safe_io.atomic_write_text/atomic_write_bytes for consistency.
  Full record: audit/AUDIT_REPORT.json (id AUD-0078), audit/AUDIT_REPORT.md.

Resolution (2026-08-24, batch-62 item 4):
  The _write_hmac half was already fixed (b755498e, atomic_write_text). This
  closes the other half: ml_bias.py's model .pkl write was still a bare
  _MODEL_PATH.write_bytes(), because safe_io had no binary primitive.

  Added safe_io.atomic_write_bytes, mirroring atomic_write_text's signature and
  reusing the SAME _atomic_write_payload core rather than introducing a third
  write convention -- that core was generalised from `payload: str` to
  `str | bytes`, with the binary branch feeding both of its open() calls (the
  primary temp write and the emergency copy). ml_bias's call site now uses it.

  emergency_copy=False at that call site, contrary to the first draft
  (opus-review-caught): on AtomicWriteError the raise happens BEFORE
  _write_hmac runs, so the emergency copy would be a lone .pkl with no matching
  sidecar; an operator restoring it gets an HMAC mismatch, which _load_models
  turns into a cached empty model set -- bias correction silently off, strictly
  worse than the intact previous pair the atomic write just preserved. There is
  no command in the repo to recompute the sidecar, the models are reproducible
  via `train-bias`, and cron.check_emergency_copies() would have paged an
  operator every cycle about an artifact they must not use.

  Explicitly NOT closed: the .pkl + .hmac PAIR is still non-atomic. A kill
  between the two replaces still leaves a new .pkl beside an old .hmac, which
  _load_models rejects. That window is unchanged in size by this fix -- what
  the fix removed is the different case where a torn .pkl write destroyed an
  otherwise-good pair in place. Real pair-atomicity needs the digest inside the
  pickle or a stage-both-rename-both sequence; out of scope, and now stated in
  _write_hmac's docstring rather than implied away.

  Adjacent safe_io fixes from the same review: atomic_write_text now rejects a
  bytes payload and atomic_write_bytes rejects a non-bytes one (the shared core
  picks its mode from the runtime type, so atomic_write_text(b"...") would
  otherwise have silently started writing raw binary, and a memoryview would
  have failed only after ~3s of retries); tmp_path_str is bound before the
  retry loop (its except branch could hit UnboundLocalError); and
  check_emergency_copies' system-temp scan was keyed to data/*.json, silently
  excluding every non-JSON payload the module can write -- including
  atomic_write_text's HURDAT2 .txt cache -- in exactly the disk-full scenario
  that fallback exists for.

  Guard test: YES, added -- tests/test_bare_write_bytes_guard.py, an AST scan
  forbidding bare Path.write_bytes() in production code (zero call sites remain
  after this change). It uses os.walk with in-place pruning rather than rglob:
  the sibling test_bare_os_replace_guard.py's rglob shape takes ~8 minutes when
  run from the main clone, whose .claude/worktrees/ holds every checkout
  (measured; filed separately). Its scope limitation -- it does not catch
  open(path, "wb") -- is stated in the module docstring; broadening it would
  need an allowlist for paper.py's fdopen and web_app.py's subprocess log
  handle.

  Testing: test_safe_io.py -- new atomic_write_bytes tests (non-UTF-8 round
  trip, full overwrite, retry/raise with a real caller_name log assertion,
  binary emergency copy, previous-file-intact-on-failure), all mutation-tested.
  test_ml_bias.py TestModelWriteRoutesThroughAtomicWriteBytes drives the REAL
  train_bias_model and asserts the call, its path, its payload and
  emergency_copy=False. The earlier version of that coverage was vacuous -- it
  never invoked ml_bias at all, so reverting the call site left it green --
  caught by opus review and replaced. Mutation-tested: restoring the bare
  write_bytes fails both it and the guard.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-62 item 1; see resolution below.] tests/conftest.py's mock_balance_1000 fixture does not actually isolate paper.DATA_PATH -- tests using it read/write the REAL production data/paper_trades.json
Priority: HIGH -- real production trading-data corruption risk, though not itself a live-money safety gate

Problem:
  mock_balance_1000 (tests/conftest.py) does:
    monkeypatch.setattr("paper.DATA_PATH", tmp_path / "paper_trades.json")
    import importlib
    import paper
    importlib.reload(paper)
    yield paper
  importlib.reload(paper) re-executes paper.py's module-level code AFTER the
  monkeypatch has already been applied, which re-runs
  `DATA_PATH = _project_root() / "data" / "paper_trades.json"` and silently
  overwrites the patched value back to the real path -- the reload undoes
  the very patch that was just applied one line above it.
  Root cause: patch-then-reload ordering. A monkeypatch applied to a module
  attribute does not survive that module being reloaded, since reload
  re-executes every top-level assignment in the module body.
  Evidence: confirmed empirically this session by writing a throwaway test
  using the mock_balance_1000 fixture and printing paper.DATA_PATH inside
  it -- it resolved to `C:\Users\thesa\claude kalshi\data\paper_trades.json`
  (this machine's real main-clone production file, confirmed via git status/
  mtime to be the actual live paper-trading ledger, not a test fixture),
  which at the time of this check already contained 200+ real trades
  including one for the exact test ticker this session had picked,
  causing a spurious "duplicate order" test failure that only made sense
  once the real cause was found.
  Financial risk: None directly (paper-only data, no real money), but a
  real data-integrity risk: any test using this fixture that calls
  place_paper_order, settle_trade, or similar write paths could corrupt
  genuine trading history with fabricated test trades, and any test that
  reads open-trade state (get_open_trades, get_balance, exposure
  calculations) gets real production numbers instead of the deterministic
  $1000-start fixture state its own name promises, making test assertions
  against "expected" values potentially flaky depending on live account
  state at the moment the test happens to run.
  Recommendation: Either (a) drop the importlib.reload(paper) call entirely
  -- reload appears to exist only to reset paper.py's module-level
  singleton state between tests, but the DATA_PATH patch alone plus
  per-test isolation of any other module-level caches (audit which, if
  any, actually need resetting) may be sufficient, or (b) re-apply the
  monkeypatch.setattr AFTER the reload (patch, reload, patch again) so the
  final state actually reflects the intended isolation. Whichever fix is
  chosen, audit every one of the ~90+ tests currently using this fixture
  (grep `mock_balance_1000` across tests/) for accidental assumptions
  about starting from a genuinely empty/deterministic $1000 ledger --
  some may have been silently passing only because they happened not to
  collide with whatever real trades existed in production data/
  paper_trades.json at the time they were written or last run, and could
  start failing (correctly) once real isolation is restored.
  This session's own new tests (tests/test_batch01_live_position_visibility.py)
  avoid this fixture entirely, patching paper.DATA_PATH directly with no
  reload.

Resolution (2026-08-24, batch-62 item 1):
  Root cause confirmed by reproduction: under the fixture, paper.DATA_PATH
  resolved to the REAL data/paper_trades.json (248 trades, balance $948.93).
  monkeypatch.setattr sets the attribute; importlib.reload(paper) then
  re-executes paper.py's module body, recomputing DATA_PATH (and
  _LOSS_OVERRIDE_PATH/_ACCURACY_HALT_OVERRIDE_PATH) from
  safe_io.project_root(), discarding both this fixture's patch AND the autouse
  isolate_paper_data patch. The reload was present in the fixture's first
  commit (a7981fee) with no stated reason and nothing needs it, so it was
  removed rather than re-applied after.

  SCOPE CORRECTION vs. this entry and vs. the batch-62 handoff: real usage is 8
  tests across 2 files (test_paper.py 6, test_drawdown_tiers.py 2) -- not
  "~90+ tests", and not the 3 files the handoff claimed.
  test_batch01_live_position_visibility.py only MENTIONS the fixture in prose;
  its module docstring documents this very bug as the reason it rolls its own
  isolation. That docstring is now corrected to say the bug is fixed.

  What shipped:
  - conftest.py: mock_balance_1000 drops the reload, depends explicitly on
    isolate_paper_data, seeds a real $1000 ledger via paper._save (so the
    documented balance no longer depends on $STARTING_BALANCE), and fails
    closed with an explicit RuntimeError -- not an assert, which -O removes.
  - New conftest helper _point_paper_at + repatch_paper_paths fixture: ONE
    definition of "isolated" (all three path constants), reused by the autouse
    fixture and by every test that must reload paper.
  - test_paper.py: removed 4 monkeypatch.setattr(paper, "DATA_PATH",
    mock_balance_1000.DATA_PATH) lines that LOOKED like isolation but
    re-asserted the post-reload production path, plus a dead _reload() helper.
  - New tests/test_conftest_paper_isolation.py: the isolation assertion PAIRED
    with a positive control -- writes a real trade through the fixture, asserts
    it landed in the temp ledger, asserts the ticker is absent from the real
    data/paper_trades.json. Compares on content, not bytes+mtime: the live bot
    writes that file on its own schedule and a cron cycle landing mid-test
    would otherwise report a fake isolation breach.

  BLAST RADIUS -- the same bug existed outside this entry's cited sites, found
  by sweeping every importlib.reload in tests/ and classifying each by
  patch-vs-reload ORDER. All fixed here:
  - test_p1_remaining.py TestGetAccuracyHaltReason: patch-then-reload in
    setup_method AND in 3 tests. Probe-confirmed to resolve to the production
    path. Reloads removed.
  - test_state_consistency.py (4 sites): one runs main.cmd_cron inside
    `except BaseException: pass`, so a production write would have been
    swallowed. Reordered to reload-then-repatch.
  - test_trade_improvements.py (2 sites): Kelly sizing had been running
    against the REAL balance and peak.
  - test_drawdown_tiers.py test_tier_constants_are_absolute: its reload IS
    load-bearing, so isolation is re-applied after it; the test now also
    restores the ORIGINAL DRAWDOWN_HALT_PCT and reloads again, with a
    self-check outside the finally. Without that it left
    paper.MAX_DRAWDOWN_FRACTION frozen at 0.30 for the rest of the session
    (mutation-verified: a follow-on test read 0.3 instead of 0.2).
  - test_starting_balance.py: reloads were never undone, leaving
    paper.STARTING_BALANCE at 2000.0 and utils.STARTING_BALANCE at 750.0 for
    the whole session -- demonstrated to break
    test_paper.py::TestKellyCompounding::test_initial_balance_is_1000 in file
    order. Fixed with an autouse restore fixture that resets os.environ
    EXPLICITLY (pytest gives no ordering guarantee between an autouse fixture
    and one the test requests, and relying on monkeypatch having run first was

[RESOLVED 2026-08-25 -- batch-58 item 4] _exit_live_position's docstring claims a reduced gate; the code runs the FULL LiveTradingGate, silently disabling every protective exit once the daily-loss halt trips
Priority: MEDIUM -- narrow trigger (daily-loss halt must already be active) but the consequence is exactly backwards for a protective mechanism

Problem:

  which side to change.
  Financial risk: the daily-loss halt is precisely the condition under which
  open positions are most likely underwater and most need their protective
  stop-loss/breakeven/model-exit to keep firing. From the moment it trips,

RESOLVED 2026-08-25 (batch-58 item 4):
  DECISION (user, via AskUserQuestion -- this was surfaced explicitly, not defaulted): make the
  CODE match the docstring. A kill switch exists to stop opening new risk, not to trap existing
  risk, and this entry's own priority note says the consequence is "exactly backwards for a
  protective mechanism." This is a real live-trading behaviour change.

  New `trading_gates.pre_live_exit_check()` runs only the never-skippable half of the gate:
  TRADING_PAUSED, kill switch, prod-ness (from the client's own base_url), and
  LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED. It deliberately does NOT run is_paused_drawdown, is_streak_paused,
  is_daily_loss_halted, is_accuracy_halted or graduation_check -- every one of those exists to
  SIZE OR STOP NEW exposure, and an exit removes exposure. The four kept checks are the ones whose
  reasoning does not depend on how much risk is already open: two operator "touch nothing"
  instructions and two real-money interlocks (a reduced gate that skipped the latter would let a
  misconfigured demo/shadow run fire real SELLs).

  Implemented by extracting `LiveTradingGate._check_never_skippable()` so the full gate and the
  reduced gate share ONE definition rather than two that can drift -- this repo's recurring
  forgot-one-copy-of-a-shared-check bug class. Verified behaviour-identical for the full gate: the
  only deleted lines in trading_gates.py are the `def check` line and its docstring, both re-added.

  SCOPE, and a sibling bug this entry did not name: _replace_live_order and _amend_live_order
  carried the IDENTICAL false "kill-switch/trading-paused only" docstring while also running the
  full gate. Their docstrings were corrected to match their code, and their gate was deliberately
  left UNCHANGED -- a reprice modifies a resting ENTRY order that can still fill and create new
  exposure, so the "an exit reduces risk" argument does not carry over. Only
  _exit_live_position uses the reduced gate; a test pins that 6/1 split so a future path cannot
  quietly adopt it without the same explicit decision.

  OPERATOR ALERT added for a gate-blocked exit (the entry notes the failure previously surfaced
  only as a _log.warning). Scoped, per opus review L6, to the two operator ACTIONS -- kill switch
  and TRADING_PAUSED. It deliberately does NOT alert for LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED-unset or a non-prod
  client: both are legitimate steady states (a disarmed operator holding positions is how this bot
  sits today) and send_system_alert's cooldown is 6h, so alerting on them would re-nag forever for
  a state the operator chose.

  COORDINATION with backlog L30045 (batch 63, the dashboard/CLI half): 63 had not landed at
  implementation time, so this did not inherit its decision. This change deliberately leaves
  L30045's question open -- the kill switch and TRADING_PAUSED still block an exit, and the answer
  to "how does an operator close a position anyway" must be an explicit operator action, not this
  gate deciding on their behalf. Opus review L5 also corrected the runbook: main.cmd_order's
  manual sell runs the FULL gate and is blocked by the same condition, so "close it manually" is
  not an alternative to clearing the block -- Kalshi's own web UI is the only path that bypasses
  it. L4 corrected a stale call-site citation in _exit_live_position's docstring (cmd_order's gate
  call is at main.py:5599, inside its own `if _is_live:` branch, not main.py:4522).
  Files: trading_gates.py, order_executor.py, main.py, LIVE_TRADING_RUNBOOK.md,

[RESOLVED 2026-08-25 -- batch-58 item 5] 'unknown'-status live orders have no age cap or operator alert -- an unresolvable row is re-checked forever at 3 authenticated GETs per recovery pass with no visible escalation
Priority: LOW -- narrow trigger (Kalshi order history aging out past what _get_orders_by_status can still find, or a malformed client_order_id), and the runbook now tells operators to check manually if a row persists
Files: execution_log.py, order_executor.py, LIVE_TRADING_RUNBOOK.md

Problem:
  execution_log.get_unknown_live_orders() is unbounded with no age cutoff,
  and every _recover_pending_orders() call (cron startup, each
  run_trade_cycle, cmd_watch's own standalone call) re-checks every
  'unknown' row via 3 authenticated GETs (_find_order_by_client_id). A row
  that can never be resolved -- e.g. it eventually ages out of what Kalshi's
  own order-history pagination can still return, or (defensively handled,
  but still a dead end) has no stored client_order_id at all -- gets
  re-checked forever with no operator-visible alarm, while the same
  ticker+side stays dedup-blocked for 7 days (was_ordered_recently) the
  whole time.
  Financial risk: Low directly (a stuck 'unknown' row blocks a RETRY, it
  doesn't itself misrepresent a position as open/closed), but it's an
  indefinitely-growing blind spot an operator has no automated signal for.
  LIVE_TRADING_RUNBOOK.md's new Alert-thresholds row ("status == 'unknown'
  order row / persists past a few cycles / manually check") is a stopgap,
  not a fix -- it depends on an operator actually running the daily-checks
  script and noticing.
  Recommendation: Add an age cutoff (e.g. after N days, log at ERROR/emit a
  distinct alert rather than silently retrying forever) and/or a dedicated
  "unknown rows older than N" check surfaced in the daily-monitoring script
  itself, not just documented in the runbook prose.

ADDENDUM 2026-08-19 (batch-02, AUD-0007, design note not a bug): the
  reconciliation lookups inside place_order()'s exception handler run in the
  same synchronous call as the POST failure -- a POST that timed out
  client-side after the exchange actually accepted it may genuinely not be
  visible yet in GET /portfolio/orders by the time the immediate re-check
  runs, independent of the pagination fix above. This is a pre-existing
  race inherent to any synchronous same-request reconciliation design, not
  something this batch introduced or could fully close without a retry-
  with-backoff redesign (a bigger scope decision than this batch's fix).
  Practical mitigation already in place: this exact race is why 'unknown'
  triggers periodic re-checks via _recover_pending_orders rather than a
  single point-in-time verdict -- a same-millisecond false negative on the
  FIRST check gets a second (and third, ...) chance on every subsequent
  recovery pass, which the old 'failed'-on-first-try behavior never gave it.


RESOLVED 2026-08-25 (batch-58 item 5):
  DECISION (user, via AskUserQuestion): alert past an age threshold, then park at a terminal
  status so the row stops being re-polled -- rather than alerting but polling forever, or reusing
  'failed'.

  Added: `_UNRESOLVED_AGE_MINUTES` (order_executor, default 1440 = 24h, overridable via
  UNRESOLVED_ORDER_AGE_MINUTES, floored at 1, non-numeric falls back rather than raising at import;
  documented in .env.example), `_park_stale_unknown_order`, `execution_log.park_unresolved_order`
  (atomic, `WHERE status='unknown'`, mirroring claim_unknown_order/claim_sent_order),
  `get_unresolved_live_orders`, and the terminal status 'unresolved'.

  WHY 'unresolved' AND NOT 'failed' -- the entry left the terminal state open, and this is the
  reasoning: 'failed' means the bot POSITIVELY CONFIRMED the order never landed, and every dedup
  and spend guard in execution_log excludes it. 'unresolved' means the bot never found out. It
  appears on none of those NOT-IN lists, so a parked row keeps blocking a re-placement and keeps
  counting toward daily live spend and open positions, exactly as it did while 'unknown'. Reusing
  'failed' would have unblocked dedup and let the bot re-place an order that may be resting live.
  All five status predicates plus the exposure/settlement/tax-export consumers were checked
  individually; the dashboard renders any non-'filled' status at warn level, so it displays
  sensibly with no frontend change.

  Two things the escalation deliberately does NOT do, both found by opus review, both real:
    H1 (HIGH, self-inflicted): an unresolvable EXIT row (closes_position_id set) is now ALERTED
      BUT NEVER PARKED. Parking it abandons settlement of the POSITION it closed, and that
      position stays live=1/status='filled'/settled_at=NULL/closes_position_id=NULL -- exactly the
      shape get_filled_unsettled_live_orders() treats as open. The exit scanner would then keep
      placing fresh REAL SELL orders for contracts the account no longer holds, every cycle,
      forever. The retry loop those branches were written for (batch-02's own round-2 fix) IS the
      protection, so it must survive the age cap. Re-polling costs nothing extra now that item 6
      hoisted the lookup. The exit alert names the orphaned position row, not just the exit row.
    L2: a row is only parked when this pass's reconciliation lookup ACTUALLY EXECUTED.
      _find_orders_by_client_ids reports uncertainty at PASS level, so one persistently-failing
      status bucket would otherwise abandon every live unknown row at the 24h mark because our own
      API access was broken -- the worst possible reason to stop tracking a possibly-real order.
      Such a row keeps retrying and gets its own distinct alert ("Kalshi lookup failing"), since a
      >24h broken lookup is itself an incident.
    M1: the alert uses a PER-ROW cooldown_key. send_system_alert's cooldown is 6h and
      disk-persisted, keyed on that string, so the original shared key meant that when an outage
      stranded four rows in one pass, exactly ONE alert was delivered and the other three were
      handled silently -- each of which may be a real resting order.
    M2: the alert text was factually wrong for exit rows (it claimed the row counts toward open
      positions and daily spend; both queries filter closes_position_id IS NULL, so it counts
      toward neither). Now branched.

  Also fixed (opus review L1): the recovery loop re-derived the stored client_order_id inline
  instead of using the shared helper, so a row with a non-string id was excluded from the lookup
  set and then "confirmed" not-found without ever being looked up, and a row with malformed
  response JSON raised past the age cap entirely -- the one permanently-stuck shape this item was
  supposed to cover. LIVE_TRADING_RUNBOOK.md documents 'unresolved', the exit carve-out, the
  lookup-failing case, and how an operator clears a parked row.
  Files: execution_log.py, order_executor.py, .env.example, LIVE_TRADING_RUNBOOK.md,
  tests/test_live_execution.py.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-25 -- batch-58 item 6] _recover_pending_orders' unknown-row loop re-walks the account's full order history once PER unknown row instead of once per recovery pass
Priority: LOW -- latency/round-trip-count issue, not a correctness bug; bounded (not unbounded) after round-2's own pagination page-cap fix
Files: order_executor.py, kalshi_client.py

Problem:
  Each 'unknown' row in a recovery pass calls
  client._find_order_by_client_id(client_order_id), which internally does
  its own fresh 3-status paginated fetch (resting/executed/canceled) via
  kalshi_client._get_orders_by_status. With N unknown rows in the same
  pass, that's 3N full paginated traversals of the same underlying order
  history, even though every row in the pass is being reconciled against
  the exact same account state.
  Financial risk: None directly -- this is a round-trip/latency multiplier,
  not a misclassification risk. Now bounded (50 pages/status, limit=1000
  each) rather than unbounded, per round-2's own _get_orders_by_status fix
  in the same review round, which substantially reduces the practical
  severity of this finding.
  Recommendation: Fetch each status list (resting/executed/canceled) ONCE
  at the top of the unknown-rows loop in _recover_pending_orders, then
  match each row's client_order_id against the in-memory lists instead of
  calling _find_order_by_client_id per row. Needs care: _find_order_by_
  client_id's per-pass "uncertain" tracking (did THIS specific lookup fail)
  would need to become a pass-level concept shared across all rows in the
  same recovery call, not re-derived per row -- worth its own careful
  design pass and test coverage rather than folding into an already-large
  review-response round.


RESOLVED 2026-08-25 (batch-58 item 6):
  Added `KalshiClient._find_orders_by_client_ids(set_of_ids)` -- ONE walk of each of the three
  status buckets per recovery pass, matched against every unknown row in memory -- and hoisted the
  call out of _recover_pending_orders' per-row loop. N unknown rows now cost 3 fetches per pass
  instead of 3N. Done together with item 5 as the batch file directed; item 5's escalation also
  bounds the worst case that made this expensive.

  This entry's own deferral note said the per-row "uncertain" tracking would have to become a
  pass-level concept and that this needed its own design pass. It does, and it did:
  reconciliation_uncertain is now True for every id in the set if ANY of the three walks failed.
  That is at least as conservative as the per-id form (a failed walk could be hiding any id's real
  match) and being conservative is the safe direction -- uncertain=True is what stops a caller
  confirming an order "never landed" and unblocking a retry. The consequence for item 5's age cap
  is handled explicitly there (a pass-level uncertain no longer permits a terminal park).

  `_find_order_by_client_id` is deliberately NOT reimplemented on top of the batched form: its own
  hot caller is place_order's exception handler on a live-order error path, and routing it through
  the batch version would turn one paginated fetch into three, every time. The shared judgement
  the two DO need to agree on -- whether a CANCELED order with a given fill count nonetheless
  landed -- was extracted to `_canceled_order_landed` so it cannot drift.

  Opus review confirmed semantic equivalence (bucket precedence preserved; get_open_orders /
  _get_orders_by_status return materialised lists, not generators, so the per-walk try genuinely
  covers the whole paginated fetch; hoisting is safe because _matches is keyed by client_order_id
  and one row's resolution cannot invalidate another's match, with claim_unknown_order still
  guarding cross-process races). One real fix from it (L3): `cid in client_order_ids` raises
  TypeError on an unhashable client_order_id from a reshaped payload, from OUTSIDE the per-walk
  try -- which would abort the whole batched lookup and poison every row in the pass. The single-id
  form used `==` and never raised. Guarded with isinstance.
  Files: kalshi_client.py, order_executor.py, tests/test_kalshi_client.py,
  tests/test_live_execution.py.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-22 -- see resolution below.] order_executor._poll_pending_orders' natural-settlement P&L formula applies the taker fee only on WINNING outcomes, so a taker-entered position that LOSES at settlement is recorded fee-free, understating that loss
Priority: LOW -- same-direction consequence as AUD-0003 (the daily-loss circuit breaker under-tripping), but on the losing side, and against a formula convention that predates and is broader than this fix
Files: order_executor.py, execution_log.py, backtest.py

Problem:
  AUD-0003's batch-03 fix correctly makes _poll_pending_orders' WINNING-outcome
  branches (`qty * (1 - price) * (1 - _fee)`) select the real KALSHI_FEE_RATE
  for a taker-entered position instead of always the $0 maker rate. The
  LOSING-outcome branches (`-qty * price`) apply no fee at all, in either
  case -- this was harmless while _fee was always 0.0 (maker), but now that
  a taker entry can select a genuinely nonzero _fee, the losing branches
  silently continue to charge nothing.
  Root cause: This win-only-fee convention is not new to this fix -- it
  matches the codebase's existing documented pattern elsewhere (see
  backtest.py's own fee-on-winnings-only comment and
  order_executor._exit_live_position's identical convention/comment,
  neither touched by batch-03), on the assumption that Kalshi's real fee is
  charged against winnings specifically, not as a flat per-trade cost. That
  assumption was never verified against a live/demo trade (AUD-0003's own
  audit record explicitly lists this exact limitation: "Did not execute a
  live or demo trade to observe an actual taker fee being charged").
  Financial risk: Understates realized losses for any taker-entered position
  that loses at natural market settlement, feeding execution_log.add_live_loss()
  -> get_today_live_loss() -> the daily-loss circuit breaker the same way
  AUD-0003's overstatement direction did -- a real loss recorded as slightly
  smaller than it was makes the breaker marginally less likely to trip when
  it legitimately should. Currently non-operative (LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED
  unset).
  Recommendation: Before changing the formula, verify Kalshi's real fee
  schedule against an actual live or demo taker trade (both a winning and a
  losing outcome) to confirm whether the fee is genuinely winnings-only or
  applies to every taker fill regardless of outcome -- this is an empirical
  question the codebase has never verified, not an implementation choice.
  If it turns out to apply to losses too, extend batch-03's per-order
  maker/taker fee selection (order.get("order_type") == "limit") to the
  losing branches as well, and audit backtest.py/_exit_live_position for the
  same gap, since they share the identical win-only convention.

Resolution: batch-22 (`7dbd7ee3`) replaced the win-only `(1 - _fee)` flat-rate
  approximation in _poll_pending_orders' settlement branch with an
  unconditional fee subtraction -- `_fee_dollars` (maker via
  utils.kalshi_maker_fee, taker via utils.kalshi_taker_fee, selected by
  order_type) is now computed once per fill and subtracted from gross_pnl
  regardless of win/loss outcome (order_executor.py, `_poll_pending_orders`,
  the `_fee_dollars = kalshi_maker_fee(...) if ... else kalshi_taker_fee(...)`
  / `pnl = round(gross_pnl - _fee_dollars, 4)` block -- verified present in
  current code this session; the empirical fee-schedule question this entry
  raised was separately resolved by adopting Kalshi's documented curved
  per-contract formula instead of guessing). The identical entry-side gap
  for early-exited (not naturally-settled) positions remains open as its own
  follow-up entry (see "record_live_exit_fill never charges the ENTRY-side
  taker fee ... early exit" below) -- do not conflate the two; this
  resolution covers the natural-settlement path only.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-19/20 -- see resolution below.] ENSEMBLE MODEL QUALITY
  DEGRADED FROM ~100% TO 30% DIRECTIONAL ACCURACY OVER 3 MONTHS -- NO
  MECHANISM EXISTED TO AUTOMATICALLY EXCLUDE AN ACUTELY-DEGRADED MEMBER
Priority: Medium-High -- affects the paper-trading track record the
  eventual live-trading graduation decision is based on, not live capital
  directly (LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED unset throughout).

Problem:
  cron.py's cmd_cron flagged "ensemble pin expiring but directional_
  accuracy=0.30 < 0.70 -- not auto-renewing; check model quality" (2026-08-
  19 scan). Investigation (querying paper.get_all_trades()/tracker's
  multiday_predictions directly) confirmed a real, gradual decay: chunked
  chronological win rate on the ensemble method's multi-day trades went
  100% (May 19-28) -> 60% -> 50% -> 60% -> 40% -> 30% (Aug 7-14) -> 50%
  (partial, Aug 15-19). Root-caused via tracker.get_member_accuracy(days_
  back=60): gfs_seamless MAE=5.37F, the worst of every tracked model (an
  externally-reported GFS warm-bias issue, dated ~2026-08-06, lines up with
  the sharpest accuracy drop). ecmwf_aifs025_ensemble's own MAE (2.64F) was
  actually good despite a separate, externally-documented "overdispersion"
  (spread-calibration, not mean-bias) issue -- confirmed NOT the culprit by
  MAE, ruling out an initial hypothesis that both flagged members needed
  down-weighting.
  The existing weight_from_mae()/get_ensemble_temps()/batch_prewarm_
  ensemble() blend already soft-down-weights a bad member via inverse-MAE,
  but both blend loops compute `repeats = max(1, round(w * 2))` -- the
  max(1, ...) floor means even a weight driven toward 0 still includes at
  least one copy of that model's members. No mechanism existed to actually
  exclude an acutely-degraded member, only to lightly discount it.
  Also found and fixed in passing: cron.py's "[EMOS] ... READY" message
  hardcoded a 40-row floor (_EMOS_TRAIN_GATE, the Gneiting-2005 statistical
  minimum for the ens_var fit) even though the user's own recorded decision
  (this file, EMOS entry, UPDATE 2026-08-18) raised the real go-live bar to
  ~80 rows -- the banner was printing "READY" prematurely between 40 and 79
  rows.

Resolution (2026-08-19/20):
  Added a generic, per-ensemble-member EWMA drift guard (weather_markets.py,
  new section preceding _model_bias -- scan_member_quarantine()/
  load_member_quarantine_state()/get_quarantined_members()), enforced at
  the model-selection layer (get_ensemble_temps()'s ensemble_models_with_
  ecmwf list, batch_prewarm_ensemble()'s blend_models list) rather than by
  trying to zero a weight, since the max(1,...) floor makes that structurally
  impossible. Design, adversarially reviewed twice (5 parallel Explore
  passes, 2 internal rounds each, at the user's explicit request) before
  implementation:
    - Non-overlapping recent(14d)/baseline(60d-excluding-the-most-recent-14d)
      windows (tracker.get_member_accuracy() gained an end_days_back param)
      -- an overlapping design was found to mute real, ongoing drift toward
      z=0, since the recent window's own bad data also drags the baseline
      it's compared against; confirmed on live data (GFS's z came out
      negative under the original overlapping design).
    - EWMA-smoothed z-score (lambda=0.2) of recent-vs-baseline MAE,
      normalized by baseline's own std (tracker.get_member_accuracy() also
      gained a std key) -- reacts to sustained drift, not a single noisy
      scan. Seeded at 0.0 for a model with no prior state (not the first raw
      z), so an extreme first reading can't single-handedly trip quarantine.
    - Asymmetric hysteresis: trip at ewma_z>=2.0, release only at ewma_z<=0.5
      -- standard circuit-breaker practice to prevent flapping right at a
      boundary.
    - Explicit, hardcoded 3-name candidate set (icon_seamless, gfs_seamless,
      ecmwf_aifs025_ensemble) -- review found tracker.get_member_accuracy()
      returns every tracked model including ecmwf_ifs025 (a DIFFERENT
      blend's model) and gem_global/ukmo_global_ensemble_20km (tracking-
      only); iterating its raw keys would have let an irrelevant model
      corrupt the active-member floor count.
    - 2-of-3 minimum-active floor with worst-first quarantine ordering,
      capped by available room; anything blocked by the floor is logged, not
      silently dropped. Known, stated limitation: this only protects against
      one simultaneously-bad member out of 3 -- a second one gets only the
      pre-existing soft down-weight.
    - get_ensemble_temps()'s cache key now includes the current quarantined-
      set (review found the original design would silently keep serving an
      already-cached blend for up to 6h after a quarantine/release change).
    - batch_prewarm_ensemble()'s Tier-1 fetch loop was fixed to iterate the
      full 3-model set (not blend_models) so a quarantined model keeps being
      fetched/tracked and can recover -- catching this during implementation
      (not the design review) since the original blend_models/fetch_models
      split would have silently stopped tracking a quarantined model,
      making quarantine effectively permanent.
    - New tests/conftest.py autouse fixture (isolate_member_quarantine)
      isolates the new data/member_quarantine.json path for every test --
      review found existing tests (e.g. test_bias_subtracted_from_raw_
      members_before_blend) assert gfs_seamless specifically appears in the
      blend and would have gone non-deterministically flaky against a real
      on-disk quarantine file otherwise.
  Daily scan wired into cmd_cron (cron.py, alongside the existing
  auto_retire_strategies() call), gated by a LAST_QUARANTINE_SCAN_PATH
  marker file (same once-per-day idiom as the existing Monday sweep) so
  back-to-back cron cycles don't re-scan. Runs only inside _cmd_cron_body,
  i.e. only after _acquire_cron_lock() succeeds -- a double-run under a
  broken lock is the same already-tracked cron-lock TOCTOU risk (see the
  live-trading-risk-gate audit's cron-lock finding, a disjoint subsystem
  from this change) every other line in that function has, not a new one;
  bounded impact (lost update to member_quarantine.json, self-heals next
  scan).
  cron.py's EMOS banner fix: added _EMOS_GOLIVE_BAR=80 alongside the
  existing _EMOS_TRAIN_GATE=40, repointed the ens_var_n-gated branches (and
  fixed a third branch's DISPLAY string that also referenced the stale 40,
  caught by review) to the real bar; left _EMOS_TRAIN_GATE and main.py's
  actual emos-train --activate gate (a genuinely different, correctly-40
  concern) untouched. EMOS activation itself remains explicitly out of
  scope -- current count (51) is still short of the 80-row bar.
  Tests: tests/test_tracker.py (TestGetMemberAccuracyStdAndEndDaysBack, 6
  tests -- std/end_days_back correctness, non-overlapping-window positive
  control), tests/test_weather_markets.py (TestMemberQuarantineScan, 11
  tests -- warm-up floors, cold-start seeding, sustained-drift-not-single-
  scan, asymmetric hysteresis, floor+tiebreak, stray-tracked-model
  isolation, persistence; TestMemberQuarantineBlendHooks, 3 tests -- real
  behavioral get_ensemble_temps/batch_prewarm_ensemble exclusion+cache-key+
  continued-tracking checks, mirroring the existing gem/ukmo tracking-only
  test's mocked-HTTP style), tests/test_main_cron_smoke.py (EMOS banner
  parametrize table extended to the 40/79/80 boundary plus a dedicated
  branch-2-display test; TestCmdCronQuarantineScanWiring, 5 tests -- marker-
  file gating, WARNING-level logging, failure isolation). Full scoped
  regression sweep (tests/test_weather_markets.py + tests/test_tracker.py +
  tests/test_main_cron_smoke.py, 732 passed/4 skipped/1 failed) found one
  unrelated pre-existing failure (test_log_prediction_falls_back_to_
  recomputed_days_out_when_absent, a UTC-vs-local-today date-boundary flake
  in code this change never touches) -- not fixed here, different
  subsystem. ruff/ruff-format/mypy all pass via the real pre-commit hook.
  Not yet done at the time of this entry: independent opus review (effort=
  high), optional member-quarantine/unquarantine CLI commands (mirroring
  cmd_retire_strategies/cmd_unretire_strategy), commit/push.

UPDATE 2026-08-20 (independent opus review, effort=high, run per this
  project's standard workflow before commit): found 4 HIGH + 7 MEDIUM + 8
  LOW/INFO. All addressed (per this project's "every finding, not just
  HIGH/MEDIUM" rule) -- no finding dropped as informational-therefore-
  ignorable.
  HIGH-1/HIGH-2 (real regressions, independent of whether quarantine ever
  fires): get_ensemble_temps()'s new 5-element cache_key (city, date, hour,
  var, quarantine-tuple) never matched batch_prewarm_ensemble()'s still-
  4-element blended-entry write -- the entire prewarm blend cache became
  permanently dead (every get_ensemble_temps call fell through to 3
  uncached per-city network fetches, bypassing the whole rate-budget
  tiering the prewarm exists for), AND a nested tuple as a cache-key element
  doesn't survive the disk cache's JSON round-trip (tuple -> list on reload,
  which is unhashable -- the first such poisoned key raised inside
  _load_ensemble_disk_cache()'s load loop and silently truncated every
  entry after it, on every future process start). Fixed by (a) a single
  shared _quarantine_cache_tag() helper (a flat joined STRING, not a
  tuple/list -- JSON-round-trip-safe) used identically by both
  get_ensemble_temps()'s cache_key and batch_prewarm_ensemble()'s blended-
  entry key, and (b) an existing test (tests/test_forecasting.py::
  test_cache_hit_returns_ensemble_without_fetch, NOT in the original scoped
  sweep -- a real gap in what got regression-tested) plus 3 more test
  read-sites in test_weather_markets.py updated to the new key shape, one
  of which (my own new test) also had a leak-sentinel bound loose enough to
  pass even with gem/ukmo's absurd tracking-only values leaking through --
  tightened to a real bound.
  HIGH-3/HIGH-4 (the statistic as designed would never have caught the
  actual failure): the original design normalized by baseline.std (the raw
  per-observation std) instead of the standard error of the MAE difference
  (~std/sqrt(n)) -- desensitizing the trip threshold by roughly sqrt(n),
  requiring a near-total model failure to ever trip. Worse: re-querying the
  real DB found gfs_seamless's OWN recent-vs-baseline z came out NEGATIVE
  (its worst stretch had aged out of the 14-day recent window while still
  dragging the 15-60-day baseline) -- the self-relative/own-history framing
  itself doesn't detect "this model is currently the worst of the three,"
  only "this model got worse than its own past," which isn't what happened
  here. Also: gfs/icon's real baseline windows are themselves too data-thin
  (n=17, below the 20 floor) for the mechanism to ever fire at all right
  now. Redesigned to PEER-RELATIVE comparison: z = (own recent MAE - mean
  of non-quarantined peers' recent MAE) / (own std / sqrt(own n)) --
  statistically correct normalization, directly targets "worse than peers
  right now" (the actual observed failure), and removes the fragile long-
  history baseline dependency entirely (tracker.get_member_accuracy()'s
  end_days_back param, added for the old design, was removed as unused --
  its 4 dedicated tests removed with it, the 2 std-specific tests kept).
  Peer set explicitly excludes any peer already quarantined going into the
  scan (using pre-scan state to avoid circularity) so an already-known-bad
  peer can't inflate what counts as "normal" and mask a second bad member --
  new dedicated regression test proves this (test_peer_mean_excludes_
  already_quarantined_peer).
  MEDIUM-5: member_quarantine.json was missing from main.py's
  _PERMANENT_DATA_FILES -- cleanup_data_dir() (runs on every CLI invocation)
  would silently delete it after 2 days of cron downtime, releasing a
  confirmed-bad quarantine with no log line. Added.
  MEDIUM-6: LAST_QUARANTINE_SCAN_PATH was missing from tests/conftest.py's
  isolate_cron_generated_files fixture (the global one covering every other
  real file _cmd_cron_body writes) -- any of the 67 other cmd_cron(
  invocations across 10 test files would stamp the REAL production marker,
  suppressing the next actual daily scan for 24h. Added.
  MEDIUM-7/MEDIUM-8: two new tests' docstrings/assertions didn't actually
  test what they claimed (cold-start test never asserted "does not trip";
  hysteresis dead-zone test's numbers landed above the trip line, not in
  the dead zone -- so it couldn't have distinguished asymmetric from
  symmetric hysteresis). Both rewritten with correct math and now assert
  the claimed property directly; also split the cold-start test into two
  (ordinary-bad-reading-doesn't-trip vs extreme-reading-legitimately-can),
  since both are true and conflating them is what produced the original
  mismatch.
  MEDIUM-9: the module docstring's "the only way to actually stop trading
  on it" overclaimed scope -- analyze_trade's model_consensus check (and
  hence order_executor's Kelly-halving) still independently compares
  icon/gfs regardless of quarantine. Docstring corrected to state the real
  scope (excludes from the ensemble BLEND only); actually fixing
  model_consensus is filed as its own new entry below rather than expanding
  this change into order_executor.py (a different consumer, needing its own
  signature change -- see workflow rule on same-payload vs. genuinely
  separate consumers).
  MEDIUM-10: get_quarantined_members() only intersected/floored at WRITE
  time (inside scan_member_quarantine()) -- a hand-edited or future-bug-
  corrupted state file could report all 3 candidates quarantined with
  nothing stopping it at READ time, emptying the blend entirely. Added the
  same floor enforcement (intersect with the real candidate set, clamp to
  the worst N-MIN_ACTIVE by ewma_z) at the read accessor itself.
  MEDIUM-11: release logic only lived inside the data-sufficient branch, so
  a quarantined model whose data went thin could never be evaluated for
  release again -- frozen indefinitely with no visibility. Fixed by
  stamping last_scan_at even on the skip path (so "never scanned" is
  distinguishable from "scanned, still insufficient data") and logging a
  WARNING each such scan a quarantined model can't be judged, rather than
  silently doing nothing. New regression test:
  test_quarantined_model_stays_quarantined_when_data_goes_thin. (Separately,
  this scenario is now much less likely to actually occur in practice under
  the peer-relative redesign, since it no longer depends on the fragile
  60-day baseline window that produced the real n=17 shortfall found during
  review -- only the 14-day recent window, continuously fed by
  batch_prewarm_ensemble's unconditional Tier-1 fetch of all 3 real models.)
  LOW/INFO (all addressed): logging.error -> _log.error for consistency
  with the rest of the section; `candidate_models or default` -> `is None`
  check (an explicitly-passed empty tuple was silently falling back to the
  default); added mtime-memoization to load_member_quarantine_state() (was
  re-parsing the file on every get_ensemble_temps() call, i.e. per market
  per scan); corrected a stale "~40 rows" comment left over in cron.py's
  EMOS block from before the 80-row fix; removed unnecessary raising=False
  from 5 new test monkeypatches on an attribute that definitely exists;
  converted a test class's implicit xunit setup_method into an explicit
  autouse fixture so its ordering relative to conftest's isolation fixture
  is unambiguous rather than merely empirically-correct; added a missing
  assertion to test_scan_failure_does_not_crash_cron (that the marker file
  is NOT stamped on failure, so a transient error retries next cycle
  instead of suppressing the real scan for a full day).
  Verified correct by the reviewer and left unchanged: the fetch-loop/
  blend-list split in batch_prewarm_ensemble (the near-miss bug from this
  entry's own implementation phase, re-checked and confirmed actually
  fixed); recovery/tracking-continuity for a quarantined model; the EMOS

  before the market fetch (same-cycle effect).
