[RESOLVED 2026-08-22 -- see resolution below.] execution_log.py's phantom-position sentinel-flag file (the unsettled-exit alert AUD-0026's fix relies on) bypasses safe_io entirely -- no atomic write, no lock -- and fails OPEN (returns []) on a corrupted/truncated file, silently dropping the operator's only recurring warning
Priority: LOW-MEDIUM
Files: execution_log.py (~1024-1036 record_live_early_exit_with_retry's read-modify-write, ~1046-1070 get_unsettled_exit_flags, ~433-441 _set_degraded_flag for contrast -- that one fails CLOSED correctly)

Problem:
  The sentinel file (tracking AUD-0026-style unmatched-sell rows still
  needing manual settlement) is read, appended to in Python, and written
  back via a plain write_text() -- no safe_io.atomic_write_json, no lock.
  Two processes (cron and watch --auto --live run deliberately unserialized
  per AUD-0013's own design) can lose one record to a lost update; a
  crash or AV lock mid-write truncates the WHOLE accumulated list, not just
  the newest entry. get_unsettled_exit_flags() swallows JSONDecodeError and
  returns [] on read failure -- the operator's one recurring warning about
  a still-open phantom live position silently disappears rather than
  erring loudly, the opposite of _set_degraded_flag's correct fail-closed
  behavior a few hundred lines away in the same file.
  Recommendation: Route through safe_io.atomic_write_json plus the module's
  existing _append_lock; have get_unsettled_exit_flags() log at ERROR
  (not silently return []) on a decode failure.
Resolution (2026-08-22):
  Routed through safe_io.CrossProcessLock (guards the whole read-modify-
  write as one critical section, same class settlement_monitor.
  run_settlement_monitor already uses -- not the module's own in-process-
  only _append_lock, since the real risk here is cross-PROCESS, per AUD-0013)
  and safe_io.atomic_write_json for the actual write. Kept the sentinel
  file's existing on-disk shape (a bare JSON list) rather than wrapping it
  in a dict to satisfy atomic_write_json's dict-typed signature -- changing
  the file format is out of this batch's scope (safe_io.py belongs to a
  different batch per INDEX.md) and would have broken every existing reader;
  used a local `# type: ignore[arg-type]` instead (json.dumps handles a list
  identically to a dict at runtime). get_unsettled_exit_flags() now logs at
  ERROR (not silently) on a JSONDecodeError/OSError before returning the
  same safe [].
  Tests: tests/test_execution_log.py TestRecordLiveEarlyExitWithRetry gained
  2 tests (atomic_write_json actually called via a spy; a corrupt prior file
  doesn't block a new record) and a new TestGetUnsettledExitFlagsCorruption
  class (3 tests, incl. caplog-verified ERROR logging on a corrupt file).

[RESOLVED 2026-08-22 -- fixed together with the win-only-fee entry above (both live in the same formula) -- see that entry's Resolution note for the full writeup.] record_live_exit_fill's realized-P&amp;L fee model uses a flat percentage of gross profit; Kalshi's actual taker fee formula (already correctly documented in this codebase's own utils.py) is a curved per-contract function of price, producing errors up to ~27% on individual exits in BOTH directions
Priority: MEDIUM-HIGH -- this is the realized ledger that feeds add_live_loss -> get_today_live_loss (the one live-aware daily-loss brake that exists) and the tax export, not an EV estimate; errors don't cancel because protective exits cluster where price has moved, not at 50 cents
Files: execution_log.py (~1163-1169), utils.py (~77-83, documents the real formula verbatim: fee = round_up(0.07 * C * P * (1-P)) per contract, rounded UP to the cent -- "7% is the coefficient in that formula, not a flat 7% of winnings")

Problem:
  Current formula: gross_pnl = qty*(exit-entry); pnl = round(gross_pnl *
  (1-KALSHI_FEE_RATE), 4) if gross_pnl &gt; 0 else gross_pnl -- a flat 7% of
  the WIN amount, not Kalshi's real per-contract curved fee. A prior
  2026-07-12 resolution (backlog ~L9843) declared this shape mismatch
  "moot in practice" because it only mattered where the fee was $0 anyway
  (maker fills) -- but record_live_exit_fill deliberately uses the TAKER
  fee rate (its own docstring: exits are always IOC), so the mismatch is
  live at exactly the one site that prior resolution's reasoning excluded.
  It's also unrounded to whole cents, while Kalshi rounds each fee up.
  Evidence (E1, executed against both formulas): qty=20 entry=0.40
  exit=0.90 -&gt; bot computes +9.30, real Kalshi fee gives +9.87 (delta
  -0.57); qty=50 entry=0.30 exit=0.35 -&gt; bot +2.325, real +1.70 (delta
  +0.625, +27%); qty=20 entry=0.45 exit=0.55 -&gt; bot +1.86, real +1.65
  (+11%). Near-50-cent exits OVERSTATE realized P&amp;L; near-0/1 exits
  UNDERSTATE it -- and since protective exits fire where the model has
  moved (not symmetrically around 50 cents), this doesn't average out.
  Every downstream ledger figure (the daily-loss breaker, dashboard, tax
  CSV) inherits the bias.
  Recommendation: Add a shared kalshi_taker_fee(contracts, price) helper
  implementing ceil(0.07*C*P*(1-P)) in whole cents (matching utils.py's
  own already-correct documentation), and use it in
  record_live_exit_fill, order_executor._poll_pending_orders, and
  backtest.py -- the same fix closes both this finding and the already-
  tracked win-only-fee omission at L22502, since both live in the same
  formula.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-25 -- batch-58 item 8] record_live_exit_fill never charges the ENTRY-side taker fee for a taker-entered position that closes via an early exit (stop-loss/breakeven/model-exit/manual sell) rather than natural settlement
Priority: MEDIUM-LOW -- same understating-realized-loss direction as the already-fixed win-only-fee bug, but requires a specific entry path (a taker-filled entry, i.e. main.cmd_order's live buy or the auto-path's taker-cross reprice fallback) AND an early exit (the common case for a protective exit, not the exception)
Files: execution_log.py (record_live_exit_fill, ~1245-1330), order_executor.py (_poll_pending_orders' settlement branch, ~1060-1140 -- the ONLY place an entry-side fee is ever computed, and it never runs for a row record_live_exit_fill has already marked settled_at)

Problem:
  Kalshi charges a taker fee on the ENTRY fill too, not just the exit fill,
  whenever the entry itself was a taker (IOC) order -- true for every
  cmd_order live buy (always IOC post-e5331a8d) and the auto-path's
  taker-cross reprice fallback. record_live_exit_fill only ever computes
  the EXIT leg's own fee (utils.kalshi_taker_fee(clamped_fill_count,
  exit_price), fixed as part of the win-only-fee batch-22 entry above) --
  it has no awareness of whether the ENTRY leg was maker or taker, and
  never charges that fee. The only place in the codebase that DOES compute
  an entry-side fee is order_executor._poll_pending_orders' natural-
  settlement branch (order_type-based maker/taker selection, also fixed as
  part of the same batch-22 work) -- but that branch only runs for rows
  still in get_filled_unsettled_live_orders(), and record_live_exit_fill's
  own settled_at write is exactly what removes a row from that set once it
  closes early. A position that's taker-entered and later exits early
  (the common case for any real protective exit -- stop-loss, breakeven,
  model-exit, or a manual cmd_order sell) has its entry fee permanently
  unrecorded.
  Financial risk: realized P&L on every taker-entered, early-exited live
  position is overstated by the unrecorded entry fee (e.g. 50 contracts
  entered at 0.30 -> kalshi_taker_fee(50, 0.30) = $0.74 never deducted),
  biasing add_live_loss() -> get_today_live_loss() -- the one live-aware
  daily-loss brake that exists -- toward under-halting.
  Recommendation: record_live_exit_fill (or its caller) needs the position's
  ORIGINAL entry quantity (not just the currently-remaining tracked
  quantity) to correctly prorate a one-time entry fee across potentially
  more than one partial exit -- recognizing the full entry fee on a
  position's FIRST exit event is fine when there's only ever one exit, but
  wrong the moment a position closes across two or more separate partial
  exits (the fee would need to be split proportionally, or recognized
  entirely on final close and tracked as pending in between). This needs a
  real design decision (which recognition-timing model to use) plus a
  position-dict/schema change to carry the original quantity and the entry
  row's own order_type through to record_live_exit_fill -- out of scope for
  a same-payload adjacency fix; needs its own implementation pass.


RESOLVED 2026-08-25 (batch-58 item 8):
  `record_live_exit_fill` now charges BOTH legs. The entry leg's maker/taker status IS recorded and
  readable -- the entry's "verify before assuming" caveat resolves positively: the position row's
  `order_type` column is exactly the discriminator AUD-0003 established for this purpose ("limit"
  = a resting GTC maker fill, anything else = taker), it is set correctly at every placement site,
  and an unreadable/missing value falls back to the TAKER rate, the same conservative direction
  AUD-0003 chose. No signature change and no schema change were needed; the row is read back via
  get_order_by_id inside the function rather than widening every caller's position dict.

  RECOGNITION MODEL -- this is what unblocked the deferral. The original note said a fix needs the
  ORIGINAL entry quantity to prorate a one-time fee across multiple partial exits. Charging per
  CLOSED CONTRACT sidesteps that entirely: each exit is charged
  fee(clamped_fill_count, entry_price) using the same curved per-contract formula the exchange
  itself uses. For a position closing in one exit the total equals the real entry fee exactly; for
  one closing across k exits it can exceed it by at most k-1 cents, because kalshi_taker_fee rounds
  UP to the whole cent independently per call -- an OVERstatement of cost, i.e. the same safe
  direction as the order_type fallback.

  Hand-computed and asserted (ceil(0.07*C*P*(1-P)) to the cent): entry 10 @ 0.40 = $0.17, exit
  10 @ 0.55 = $0.18, gross $1.50 -> pnl $1.15 (was $1.32 exit-leg-only). Maker entry -> $1.32
  unchanged. Partial 4-of-10 -> $0.46. Losing exit 10 @ 0.25 -> -$1.81, both legs charged, since
  the fee is charged on the FILL not the outcome.

  BACKFILL SCOPE (user decision, via AskUserQuestion): FORWARD-ONLY, and no backfill is needed --
  verified, not assumed. The production data/execution_log.db has ZERO live=1 rows and ZERO rows
  with settled_at set, and so does every retained backup (b70_cleanup, the 08-23/08-24 backups, and
  the pre-2026-08-01 stale copy). The bot has never settled a live position, so there is no
  historical corpus carrying the overstated P&L and this introduces no date boundary in the
  analytics. That fact is recorded in the function's own docstring so a future reader does not have
  to re-derive it.

  Opus review M5 found the same false claim this item killed in record_live_exit_fill's docstring
  still live at the caller (order_executor, above the full-exit call): "fee only discounts a
  genuine GAIN, never applied to a loss" and "the entry side already paid $0 (always a resting
  maker order)". Both false since batch-22 and this item respectively, in live-money fee code.
  Corrected. M3 found the multi-partial-exit test VACUOUS -- it computed both sides of its
  comparison from KALSHI_FEE_RATE inside the test and never read record_live_exit_fill's return
  value, so it passed unchanged with the entry fee deleted from production entirely. Rewritten to
  back the charged fee out of the returned pnl; re-ran that mutant to confirm it now fails.
  Files: execution_log.py, order_executor.py, tests/test_execution_log.py.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-22 -- see resolution below. Filed retroactively: batch-23.md
  (audit/handoff_prompts/batches/batch-23.md) cited a backlog.txt line number
  for this finding that never actually existed in the file -- no matching
  entry was found by line number or content search when this batch was
  implemented. This entry documents the fix per the user's own choice to add
  it after the fact rather than leave batch-23.md as the only record.]
  place_order()'s idempotency key is stable for a 12-hour forecast-cycle
  window and omits time_in_force, so genuinely DISTINCT order attempts can
  collide
Priority: HIGH -- flagged as the single most consequential item across
  batches 22-30 (audit/handoff_prompts/batches/INDEX.md)
Files: kalshi_client.py (place_order, amend_order), order_executor.py
  (_current_forecast_cycle, _replace_live_order, _amend_live_order,
  _exit_live_position)

Problem:
  idempotency_input = f"{ticker}:{side}:{action}:{count:.2f}:{price:.4f}:{cycle}"
  where cycle is constant for a 12-hour window and time_in_force wasn't part
  of the key at all. Three real collision shapes: (a) a GTC entry order and
  its later IOC taker-cross replacement hash identically whenever the
  midpoint price rounds to the same value as the taker price -- the resubmit
  dedups against the just-canceled original, the position closes with no
  re-entry, logged as success; (b) a repeated IOC exit at an unchanged book
  regenerates the identical key within the same 12h window, so a protective
  exit can never actually be re-placed; (c) amend_order's key can
  oscillate-collide on a price moving back to a prior value within one
  cycle, leaving the bot's own book price wrong relative to what's actually
  resting.
Full record: none in this backlog before this fix (see note above).

Resolution (2026-08-22):
  Design decision (AskUserQuestion): overload the existing `cycle` string
  parameter with a per-attempt discriminator at the 3 non-entry call sites,
  rather than adding a new parameter or making every place_order/amend_order
  call (including fresh entries) per-attempt-unique. Matches an existing
  precedent in this same codebase: main._quick_paper_buy already passes a
  minute-bucketed pseudo-cycle instead of the literal forecast cycle for the
  identical collision reason.
  kalshi_client.place_order() now folds time_in_force into the key
  (fixes collision (a) directly -- a GTC entry and an IOC taker-cross now
  always differ regardless of price). order_executor._replace_live_order
  passes cycle=f"{cycle}:replace:{replaces_order_id}" (deterministic across
  retries of the SAME replacement, since replaces_order_id repeats, but
  distinct from the original entry and from any other order's replacement).
  _amend_live_order and _exit_live_position pass
  cycle=f"{cycle}:amend:{log_id}" / f"{cycle}:exit:{log_id}" (log_id is the
  execution_log pre-log row id, monotonic per real attempt via AUTOINCREMENT
  with no DELETE anywhere in that table, so every retry of an unfilled exit
  or an oscillating reprice gets a genuinely fresh key). Fresh entries
  (_place_live_order) deliberately left unchanged -- they already have
  execution_log.was_ordered_this_cycle() as the real dedup mechanism, plus
  the bare-cycle key as a belt-and-suspenders cross-process race backstop
  (load-bearing per AUD-0013's note that cmd_watch's recovery pass runs
  outside the shared cron lock deliberately) that replace/amend/exit don't
  need since they have their own concurrency guards
  (_cancel_and_verify_safe_to_replace, a settled_at-race RuntimeError guard).
  Independent opus review (effort=high) traced every place_order/amend_order
  call site in the repo and confirmed none was missed, log_id's monotonicity
  guarantee, and that fresh entries' time_in_force is genuinely constant
  (always "good_till_canceled") so the new key component doesn't silently
  change entry dedup behavior. One accepted trade-off documented in-code
  (order_executor.py comments near the exit/amend cycle= calls): per-attempt
  keys mean a lost-response fill that BOTH place_order's own reconciliation
  AND the next cycle's _recover_pending_orders unknown-row re-check fail to
  resolve could see a second real order land on a cross-cycle retry, instead
  of Kalshi's own dedup catching it -- judged acceptable since
  _recover_pending_orders' atomic-claim-guarded unknown-row re-check is the
  real protection against this now, and the alternative (bare cycle) is the
  exact bug this fix closes.
  10 new/extended tests (tests/test_idempotency.py, tests/test_live_execution.py),
  each mutation-tested via Edit-revert-run-restore, including a direct repro
  of collision (b) (two unfilled IOC exit attempts against the same position
  now get provably distinct client_order_id keys).

[RESOLVED 2026-08-22 -- see resolution below. Same retroactive-filing note as
  the two entries above.] get_positions()/get_events()/get_series_list()
  don't paginate at all
Priority: LOW today, directly relevant to AUD-0025's still-open

  All three returned data.get(<key>, []) from a single unpaginated call,

Resolution (2026-08-22):
  Added a shared _paginate_get() helper (kalshi_client.py) with the same

  /portfolio/positions may return two parallel lists (event_positions +

[RESOLVED 2026-08-22 -- see resolution below. Same retroactive-filing note as
  the four entries above.] .env is never permission-hardened despite
  potentially carrying the full private key in plaintext
Priority: LOW
Files: kalshi_client.py (_check_key_permissions, .pem-only), cron.py
  (KALSHI_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM read), kalshi_ws.py (retains the raw PEM string
  for the process lifetime)

Problem:
  _check_key_permissions() hardens the .pem file via icacls on every
  KalshiClient construction. No equivalent existed for .env, which -- when
  the WebSocket feed is enabled -- can carry KALSHI_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM, the
  entire private key as a plaintext env value, on default (often broader)
  file permissions.
Full record: none in this backlog before this fix (see note above).

Resolution (2026-08-22):
  First implementation reused _check_key_permissions' Windows icacls path
  (/inheritance:r + /grant:r, strips ALL inherited ACEs including
  SYSTEM/Administrators) on .env. Independent opus review caught this as a
  real operational risk before it shipped: empirically demonstrated it would
  fire on every unpatched KalshiClient() construction (including 2 existing
  unguarded test-suite call sites) and could silently lock a future
  SYSTEM/service-account deployment (this project's own planned VM move) out
  of .env -- every authenticated call would then fail closed in
  _sign_headers with no obvious cause, a worse failure mode than the
  plaintext-exposure risk being guarded against. Redesigned to WARN-ONLY on
  both platforms: Windows runs a read-only `icacls <path>` call (no
  /inheritance:r, no /grant:r) and warns only if a broad principal
  (Everyone/BUILTIN\Users/Authenticated Users) shows up in the output; Unix
  keeps the existing chmod-based warning. Scoped to only ever check a .env
  that lives inside kalshi_client.py's own directory -- never
  find_dotenv()'s upward-walk fallback to an unrelated parent/home .env.
  9 new tests in tests/test_kalshi_client.py (TestEnvFilePermissions), each
  mutation-tested; the Unix test uses a monkeypatched kalshi_client.__file__
  pointing at a tmp_path so it never touches this repo's real .env (a first
  draft of this test wrote directly to the real repo .env before being
  caught and fixed).

[RESOLVED 2026-08-23 -- batch-25 item 1] cloud_backup.backup_data() silently produced empty/unreadable SQLite backups -- WAL never checkpointed
Priority: HIGH
Files: cloud_backup.py, safe_io.py

Problem:
  _BACKUP_EXTENSIONS = {".json", ".db"} copied .db files via plain shutil.copy2 -- no PRAGMA wal_checkpoint, no sqlite3.Connection.backup(). Every SQLite DB in this codebase runs PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL, so a committed transaction sitting only in the .db-wal sidecar (never touched by shutil.copy2) was silently omitted from the backup, up to and including the entire database's contents when a fresh WAL hadn't checkpointed yet. backup_data() still returned True/logged success regardless.
  Reproduced live this session (audit's own unwired repro script, audit/reproductions/verify_pass20_wal_backup.py): a row committed to execution_log.db's orders table, WAL never checkpointed, backed up via the real backup_data() -- backup copy came back with "no such table: orders".
  Full record: audit/handoff_prompts/batches/batch-25.md item 1 (original backlog.txt line citation is stale -- superseded by other sessions' concurrent edits since 2026-08-21; not recoverable, hence this fresh entry).

Resolution 2026-08-23 (batch-25 item 1, 3 rounds of opus review before push):
  New safe_io.backup_sqlite_db(src, dst) -> bool: WAL-safe copy via sqlite3.Connection.backup() (reads through a live connection, reflects everything committed whether checkpointed or not), writing to a sibling temp path first and only replacing dst (via the existing _replace_with_retry) once verified readable -- a pre-existing dst this function didn't just create is never touched on failure. Both cloud_backup.backup_data() and main.auto_backup() (item 2 below) now share this one implementation (user's explicit AskUserQuestion choice over duplicating the logic).
  Readability check evolved across review rounds: round 1 shipped requiring PRAGMA integrity_check == "ok", which round-1 opus review itself caught as WRONG before this ever reached round 2 -- verified live against this project's own data/execution_log.db, which has a real pre-existing `wrong # of entries in index idx_orders_ticker` integrity_check failure despite its orders table data being fully intact and queryable (243 rows). The integrity_check requirement made the fix refuse to keep ANY copy of the live-order ledger, strictly worse than the pre-fix shutil.copy2 behavior for the exact file this batch exists to protect. PRAGMA quick_check has the identical false-positive (confirmed against the same real file). Final check: table-existence, THEN (round-2-opus-review-caught, since table-existence alone accepts a copy whose sqlite_master page is intact but a table's own data pages are corrupted) a cheap `SELECT * FROM "{escaped_name}" LIMIT 1` probe per table -- catches the originally reported bug, any total-copy-failure shape, AND a corrupted-table-data shape integrity_check would have also caught, without rejecting an unrelated orthogonal issue like the real execution_log.db's index. Identifier escaping (`"` doubled) verified against 15 pathological table names.
  cloud_backup.backup_data() also gained: per-file exception isolation (round-2-opus-review-caught -- a single corrupt/unreadable source file used to abort the WHOLE run via backup_sqlite_db raising, silently skipping every OTHER file in data_dir including execution_log.db); and a _sqlite_source_is_empty() pre-check (round-2-opus-review-caught -- this project's real data/ has 4 vestigial zero-byte .db files that failed the new readability check on every single cron cycle forever, permanently flipping the return value to False and spamming 4 WARNINGs per run; a valid-but-empty source is now skipped silently as "nothing to back up", while a genuinely corrupt/non-SQLite file is still treated as a real failure).
  Tests: safe_io.backup_sqlite_db covered by 10 tests in tests/test_safe_io.py (WAL-survival, parent-dir creation, corrupt-copy rejection+cleanup, empty-source rejection, unrelated-index-corruption acceptance, corrupted-table-data rejection, pre-existing-good-backup preservation on both failure shapes, identifier-escaping). cloud_backup.backup_data() covered by 8 tests in tests/test_cloud_backup.py. Every fix mutation-tested (reverted via Edit, confirmed the specific test fails, restored).

[RESOLVED 2026-08-23 -- batch-25 item 3] main.auto_backup()'s local predictions.db backup has the identical WAL-copy issue, and verify_db_backup()'s result is discarded
Priority: MEDIUM
Files: main.py

Problem:
  Same underlying WAL-copy mechanism as item 1, applied to the local backup path. verify_db_backup() logs a row count and returns 0 on failure, but the caller never checked it -- a backup failing its own verification was still retained and still counted toward the backups[:-30] pruning window, potentially evicting the oldest genuinely-good backup.

And (opus-review-caught, defense in depth): verify_db_backup's table param is validated against the known set before SQL interpolation, since sqlite3 has no identifier parameter-binding.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-23 -- batch-25 item 4] /api/halt (the dashboard's emergency kill-switch button) writes .kill_switch with a bare, unretried Path.replace() that can fail under normal Windows concurrent-reader contention, and the repo's own bare-os.replace() regression guard doesn't catch it
Priority: HIGH
Files: web_app.py, main.py, safe_io.py, tests/test_bare_os_replace_guard.py

Problem:
  No try/except, no retry, on either /api/halt or /api/override. safe_io._replace_with_retry's own docstring documents this exact failure ("confirmed live and 100% reproducible") on Windows under concurrent readers -- and data/.kill_switch has guaranteed concurrent readers (cron, watch, the dashboard's own /health and /api/status polling). An operator clicking HALT during an actual incident could get an unhandled 500 while the kill switch was NOT installed. The repo's own regression guard test (tests/test_bare_os_replace_guard.py) only matched os.replace(/_os.replace( syntax, not the Path.replace() method form both web_app.py sites used, so this already slipped past the existing safety net. Also: the temp-file path (_KS_PATH.with_suffix(".tmp"), which resolves to the literal ".kill_switch.tmp" since ".kill_switch" is a dotfile with no suffix) collided with main.py's cmd_cron manual-override flow, which uses that exact same filename to park an active kill switch during a one-shot override window.
  Full record: audit/handoff_prompts/batches/batch-25.md item 4 (original backlog.txt line citation is stale -- see item 1's note above).

Resolution 2026-08-23 (batch-25 item 4):

Resolution (2026-08-25 -- batch-59 item 1):
  SHIPPED. weather_markets._metar_lock_in's above/below branch now carries a
  HIGH-market monotonic-safety veto, the exact mirror of the pre-existing
  `_is_low_mkt` one, as its own `elif not _is_low_mkt and _lockout.get(
  "locked"):` block (deliberately NOT merged into one shared comparison --
  afternoon-max and overnight-min have different diurnal timing, so a future
  direction-specific rule must be able to land on one without silently
  changing the other).

  Predicate: reject when `_comp_temp < threshold + margin`. Verified against
  check_metar_lockout's real branch logic for all four HIGH-market
  (direction x outcome) combinations -- `above`/YES and `below`/NO fire only
  at `comp >= T+3` (monotone-safe, allowed); `above`/NO and `below`/YES fire
  only at `comp <= T-3` (not safe, vetoed). Boundaries confirmed live:
  comp == T+3.0 locks, comp == T-3.0 is vetoed.

  NO hour-of-day escape, on either side. This was the batch file's one open
  design question ("verify the hour-of-day boundary you pick against real
  settled data, not intuition") and the answer turned out to be that no
  defensible boundary exists. Method, so it is reproducible rather than
  asserted -- the numbers below appear nowhere else in the repo, which an
  opus reviewer correctly flagged (L9):
    * Source: Iowa State Mesonet ASOS archive (hourly METAR, city-local tz)
      for all 21 traded stations, 2023-09-01..2026-08-25 -> 22,799
      station-days with >=20 observations.
    * Metric: P(the running daily extreme at local hour H still moves by
      >= 3.0F -- the lock's own margin -- before the day ends). That is
      exactly the error probability of a monotone-safety-violating lock at
      hour H.
    * Refinement: the running extreme is taken from HOURLY METAR (what
      metar._fetch_daily_temps_f actually returns) while the day's TRUE
      extreme is taken from 5-minute-sampled 1-minute ASOS (IEM asos1min),
      a far closer proxy for the official climate report Kalshi settles
      against. Measured on a 4-station high-risk subset (BOS/MSP/OKC/SAT,
      908 station-days, Sep 2025-Aug 2026); fine-vs-hourly max uplift is
      mean +0.77F, median +1.0F, p90 +2.0F.
    * HIGH (running max), hourly-truth over all 21 stations: 6.8% at 14:00,
      1.8% at 15:00, 0.8% at 16:00, 0.4% at 18:00, 0.1% at 20:00.
    * HIGH, fine-truth on the high-risk subset: 26.9% at 14:00, 8.9% at
      15:00, 4.4% at 16:00, 3.1% at 18:00, and a FLOOR of ~2.8% that never
      clears even at 21:00 -- because the hourly running max never quite
      catches the continuous max. Per-station at 14:00: SAT 39.0%, MSP
      31.2%, OKC 22.6%, BOS 15.4%. The two worst are the incident's own
      cities.
    * LOW (running min), fine-truth: 12.8% at 14:00 and still 9.7% at 20:00
      / 7.3% at 21:00 -- it never becomes safe before local midnight, which
      independently vindicates the existing LOW veto having no hour escape
      either.
  So the two directions genuinely differ in shape (HIGH has a knee at ~16:00
  then a floor; LOW has no knee at all), exactly as the batch file warned --
  but an hour cutoff would not remove the harm it appears to remove, because
  the residual never reaches zero and the lock's stated probability stays far
  from the true one at every hour. Consistent with the batch-40 decision
  ("what would give us the best chance of making money") not to add bespoke
  later cutoffs. A vetoed market is NOT a skipped market: it falls through to
  the normal, calibrated ensemble path.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-22 -- batch-30 item 1] cron.py's cron-lock staleness check relies solely on psutil.pid_exists(pid), with no create_time/cmdline verification -- Windows PID reuse after an unclean shutdown could leave the lock permanently unacquirable
Priority: HIGH (as a VM-move prerequisite; correction addendum in the original 2026-08-21 finding noted today's fully-manual cron invocation makes this a latent risk, not a live incident, until automation exists)
Files: cron.py (_acquire_cron_lock, _release_cron_lock, _is_cron_running, _cron_lock_pid_reused)
Note: this entry has no prior [OPEN] record in this branch's committed backlog.txt -- the original finding (audit/handoff_prompts/batches/batch-30.md item 1, from the 2026-08-21 live-trading readiness review) exists only as uncommitted work in the main clone, never committed to any branch (see project memory project_weather1_batch_backlog_shared_corpus.md). Added fresh per user's explicit choice, matching the batch-24/batch-25 sessions' precedent for the same gap.

Resolution 2026-08-22: data/cron.lock now additionally records psutil.Process(pid).create_time() at
  acquire time. A new _cron_lock_pid_reused(pid, lock_create_time) helper positively confirms
  Windows PID reuse (the live process's own create_time differs from the lock's recorded value by
  >= 2.0s) rather than trusting pid_exists() alone; _acquire_cron_lock and _is_cron_running both
  gate on it. An initial version of this fix also added a 1800s age-based override to
  _acquire_cron_lock's psutil-available branch (reasoning cron's own internal watchdog,
  _install_cron_watchdog, 720s default, bounds how old a genuine cron lock can get) -- independent
  opus review (effort:high) caught that this was unsound: cmd_watch (main.py, `watch --auto --live`)
  acquires the SAME lock across run_trade_cycle() with NO watchdog at all, so the override could have
  stolen the lock from a still-running, still-placing-real-orders watch session and let a second cron
  cycle start concurrently -- removed before ship, replaced with pure create_time verification (no age
  component) for the psutil-available branch. A second opus review round (fixes re-reviewed with fresh
  eyes, per this project's standing 2-round policy for live-order-adjacent changes) then found the
  create_time comparison itself lived OUTSIDE its own try/except (a malformed/non-numeric create_time
  value would raise an unhandled TypeError into this function's two unguarded web_app.py callers,
  api_run_cron/api_cron_status via _is_cron_running) -- fixed by moving it inside. That same round also
  found the removed age-backstop had thrown out a real, safe use case along with the unsafe one: a lock
  whose reuse can NEVER be positively confirmed (e.g. persistent AccessDenied querying a reassigned PID)
  would now block cron forever with no self-heal -- the exact permanent-lock-out failure mode this whole
  item exists to eliminate, just reachable via a different path. Added a new, much longer
  _STUCK_RUNNING_BACKSTOP_SECS (86400s/24h, shared by both _acquire_cron_lock and _is_cron_running) that
  IS safe at that age specifically, since neither cmd_cron (watchdog-bounded) nor a single cmd_watch
  auto-trade cycle can plausibly reach it.
  Adjacent fix (H2, opus-review-caught): _release_cron_lock() previously unlinked the lock file
  unconditionally regardless of which process currently held it -- a process whose own lock got
  overridden as stale by a later acquirer could, on its own delayed release, delete the NEW holder's
  fresh lock, letting a THIRD acquirer start concurrently. Now verifies the lock file's own recorded pid
  matches os.getpid() before unlinking (a corrupt/unreadable lock, with no pid to protect, is still
  deleted as before).
  Tests: 25 new/updated tests across tests/test_cron_lock.py and tests/test_p0_16_cron_endpoint.py,
  covering the create_time reuse check (matching/mismatched/vanished-process/AccessDenied/non-numeric
  cases), the acquire-side and is-running-side backstops, and the release-ownership check -- every
  production-code claim above mutation-tested individually (Edit-revert-restore against the real fix,
  confirmed each test actually fails on the reverted code). 378 tests pass in the final broader
  regression sweep (cron/trade-cycle/execution-stability suites). ruff/ruff-format/mypy clean.

  2026-08-22 -- see Note above).

[RESOLVED 2026-08-23 -- batch-31 item 1 (CR-1)] batch-22×batch-23 collision -- pre-logged idempotency key != wire key in _replace_live_order and _exit_live_position, so crash recovery marks REAL live orders 'failed'
Priority: CRITICAL -- gates live enablement; adversarially verified with an executed repro against both sites
Files: order_executor.py (_replace_live_order, _exit_live_position), tests/test_live_execution.py

Problem:
  Batch-23 scoped place_order's own idempotency key to f"{cycle}:replace:{replaces_order_id}" /
  f"{cycle}:exit:{log_id}" but left the PRE-LOG compute_client_order_id(...) calls at both sites on the
  bare cycle -- verified by executing the real function: the pre-logged client_order_id never matched
  the wire id place_order() actually derived. A crash in the pre-log-to-log_order_result window (the
  live-order watchdog's os._exit(1), cron.py, lands exactly there by design) then made crash recovery
  re-check the WRONG id, get a confirmed negative via _find_order_by_client_id, and write status='failed'
  onto a REAL live order. Replace: an untracked live position (no protective exits, no settlement
  accounting). Exit: settled_at stays NULL forever, so the exit scanner places a fresh real SELL every
  cycle against an already-sold position, permanently consuming a max_open_positions slot.
Resolution (2026-08-23):
  _replace_live_order: single-line fix -- the pre-log compute_client_order_id call now passes the same
  f"{cycle}:replace:{replaces_order_id}" string place_order() already receives.
  _exit_live_position: needed a two-step pre-log (confirmed via AskUserQuestion over an explicit
  client_order_id kalshi_client.place_order parameter and a position-id-keyed key -- the latter would
  have re-broken batch-23's per-attempt retry semantics for an illiquid no-fill IOC). The scoped cycle
  needs log_id, which doesn't exist until the row is created: log_order() now runs first (response left
  unset), then the client_order_id is computed from f"{cycle}:exit:{log_id}" and written via
  log_order_result() BEFORE place_order() is called, so the pre-logged and wire ids are byte-identical by
  construction. A crash between those two local writes leaves a response=NULL 'pending' row -- safe,
  since no wire call has happened yet; _recover_pending_orders reads ALL pending rows unconditionally
  (unlike _poll_pending_orders/_reprice_or_cancel_pending_orders, which skip rows with no response) and
  marks it 'sent' to block a duplicate retry.
  Tests: test_prelogged_client_order_id_matches_wire_cid added to both TestReplaceLiveOrder and
  TestExitLivePosition (test_live_execution.py) -- each independently re-derives the expected id from the
  cycle/time_in_force place_order() actually received and compares against the pre-log write captured via
  a spy (log_order for replace; log_order_result's first response-carrying call for exit, since a second
  call later overwrites it with the wire response). Both mutation-tested (reverted the fix via Edit,
  confirmed each test fails with a concrete id mismatch, restored).

[RESOLVED 2026-08-23 -- batch-31 item 2 (M-4)] no atomic position-row claim in _exit_live_position -- cron's and watch's exit scanners (deliberately unserialized, AUD-0013) can both derive the identical exit decision and both sell the same position
Priority: MEDIUM -- also closes CR-1's exit half and M-2's residual settlement race as a side effect of removing the double-attempt path
Files: execution_log.py (claim_position_for_exit, release_exit_claim, v18 migration), order_executor.py (_exit_live_position), tests/test_live_execution.py

Problem:
  Batch-23's per-attempt exit key removed the only (accidental, price-equality-dependent) server-side
  dedup against two scanners selling the same position. LivePositionStore.exit() had no row claim;
  record_live_exit_fill's settled_at guard only fires AFTER the second real SELL has already executed on
  the exchange. Pre-existing hazard (reported as defense-in-depth, not batch-23-introduced).
Resolution (2026-08-23):
  Confirmed via AskUserQuestion (TTL-bounded claim over a permanent claim or fully serializing the
  scanners): execution_log gained a v18 schema column (exit_claimed_at) plus
  claim_position_for_exit(position_id, ttl_minutes=10) -- an atomic CAS UPDATE mirroring
  claim_unknown_order's pattern, guarded on settled_at IS NULL, self-healing after the TTL so a crash
  between a successful claim and place_order() actually completing (the exact CR-1 watchdog window) never
  strands a position unprotected forever. _exit_live_position claims the position before doing anything
  else; the loser returns False without ever calling place_order(). release_exit_claim() clears the claim
  early for a legitimate immediate retry (no-fill/illiquid IOC, a genuine partial fill leaving the

  Adjacency: two existing race-loss tests (test_full_exit_race_loss_does_not_crash_the_caller,
  test_partial_exit_race_loss_does_not_crash_the_caller) pre-settled the position row BEFORE calling
  _exit_live_position -- with the new claim, that scenario is now caught earlier (correctly refusing to
  even attempt a duplicate live sell), which is a real improvement but no longer exercises the intended
  bookkeeping-race branch. Restructured both to inject the concurrent settlement via a
  record_live_exit_fill side effect that fires AFTER this attempt's own claim succeeds -- reproducing the
  race that genuinely still exists (a manual cmd_order sell, which does not go through
  claim_position_for_exit at all).
  Tests: 5 new tests (claim blocks a concurrent scanner; released after unfilled IOC allows immediate
  retry; retained after OrderStatusUnknownError; released after confirmed placement failure; the two
  restructured race-loss tests above), all mutation-tested (claim check removed, each release call
  removed individually, a wrong release added to the OrderStatusUnknownError branch).

  killed by a specific test" -- false. The reviewer executed the mutation removing release_exit_claim()

  finding:
  F1 (MEDIUM, claim_position_for_exit/release_exit_claim had zero direct tests -- the TTL self-heal, the
  ENTIRE reason the claim is time-bounded rather than permanent, was untested): added

  reworded the comment to state the real (small, bounded, cosmetic-audit-trail-only) gap honestly rather
  than re-engineering recovery for a two-local-write race window, per the reviewer's own "reword rather

  F7 (two claim tests asserted only the post-hoc claim state with no positive control proving the

RESOLVED 2026-08-25 (batch-58 item 7):
  Fixed the CLASS, not the instance, as the batch file preferred: `log_order_result` now COALESCEs
  `response` and `fill_quantity`, the same treatment filled_at/market_mid_at_fill already had.
  Both were unconditional column writes, so ANY caller that omitted them wiped whatever the row
  already held.

  Grepping every call site first (39 across main.py and order_executor.py, enumerated by a
  paren-balanced statement scan rather than a line-capped grep) found the bug was live in a SECOND
  place this entry did not name: _recover_pending_orders' pending-resolve branch passes
  fill_quantity but not response, wiping the order_id the row was recovered by. Two other sites had
  already worked around it by hand -- the resting branch re-passes response purely to avoid the
  wipe, and _finalize_cancel re-reads the row and passes its own prior values back. Those
  pass-throughs are now redundant but harmless and were left in place.

  No call site was found where preserving is wrong. Checked specifically: no reader consults
  `response` on a 'failed' row (the pending/sent/unknown recovery filters each select one status,
  and none of them selects 'failed'); no live path can put a nonzero fill_quantity on a row before
  it goes failed/canceled/amended except _finalize_cancel, which re-passes it explicitly. COALESCE
  only ever protects a None -- an explicitly passed value, fill_quantity=0 included, still
  overwrites, because 0 is not NULL in SQLite. One documented edge: `response` is bound as
  `json.dumps(response) if response else None`, so an explicitly passed EMPTY dict is falsy and
  preserves rather than clears; no production caller passes {}.

  One existing test changed behaviour and was updated with the reasoning rather than silently
  re-baselined: _finalize_cancel's malformed-stored-response test asserted the corrupt value got
  nulled. That was incidental (the fallback's json.loads failed, so it passed response=None), not
  intended -- the test exists to prove the defensive json.loads does not raise out of an
  already-handling except block, and it still does.

  Opus review M4 caught the documentation half: six comments across order_executor.py and
  execution_log.py asserted that log_order_result's UPDATE is "unconditional" / "does not
  COALESCE" -- now the opposite of the truth, and one of them was the stated RATIONALE for
  claim_sent_order's atomicity, so a future reader could have concluded that atomic claim was no
  longer needed. All six reworded.
  Files: execution_log.py, order_executor.py, tests/test_execution_log.py,
  tests/test_live_execution.py.

  touch the separate row filter that decides which hourly rows are even
  considered for that day's max/min: `day_rows = [r for r in rows if

  `.replace(tzinfo=UTC)`, confirming ftime is UTC in this API's payload
  shape generally, not just in that path.
  Financial risk: a city up to ~7h off UTC (matches the M-18c KLAX
  citation this entry is filed from) can have its GFS/NAM max/min computed
  over a row window that's misaligned with the actual city-local day in

  probability when NBS/METAR coverage is unavailable. Currently
  non-operative for live capital (LIVE_TRADING_ENABLED unset); affects
  paper-trading signal quality.
  Recommendation: convert `ftime` to the station's city tz before the

  `datetime.strptime(...).replace(tzinfo=UTC)` -> `.astimezone(tz)`

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-35 item 1 (M-15)] load_member_quarantine_state fails OPEN on a transient read error
Priority: MEDIUM
Files: weather_markets.py (load_member_quarantine_state), tests/test_weather_markets.py

Problem:
  `except Exception: return {}` discarded the last-known-good cached quarantine state on ANY read
  failure -- a mid-os.replace read or an AV scanner hold re-admits a quarantined ensemble member into the
  live blend for that call (ensemble_models_with_ecmwf), and the empty-cache tag misses the prewarmed
  entry, forcing a full per-market refetch; different markets in one scan could end up blended from
  different model sets. Every sibling loader in this file (_load_platt_models, _load_metar_calibration,
  _maybe_refresh_calibration_weights) already preserves its cache on transient failure with an explicit
  comment explaining why -- this loader was the one holdout still failing open.
Resolution (2026-08-24):
  Mirrors _load_platt_models's pattern: on any exception, coerce to {} only on a genuine first-ever load;
  otherwise log a WARNING naming the failure and return the existing cached dict object unchanged, without
  recording the (now-stale) cache key, so the next call retries instead of permanently discarding live
  state.
  Self-review correction (opus review was unavailable, 529 Overloaded, at push time -- see this batch's
  own summary note; self-review substituted at the user's explicit direction and caught this): the first
  cut used `_member_quarantine_state_cache_key is None` as the "first-ever load" test, mirroring
  _load_platt_models's `_PLATT_MODELS is None` check literally. But unlike _PLATT_MODELS (never reset after
  a successful load), _save_member_quarantine_state() deliberately resets the cache KEY to None on every
  successful save (to force the next read to re-parse) while leaving the cache's CONTENT untouched -- so
  the literal-mirror check misfired in exactly that post-save window, discarding still-good cached content
  on a transient read error right after a save, reproducing the M-15 bug this fix exists to close at a

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-36 item 2 (M-18b)] metar.py's two naive-datetime parsing gaps
Priority: MEDIUM -- live METAR lock-in pricing surface
Files: metar.py (fetch_metar, _extract_obs_time, check_metar_lockout), tests/test_metar.py

Problem:
  (a) fetch_metar's reportTime staleness fallback parsed the real aviationweather.gov payload shape
    ("2026-08-23 14:53:00" -- no "Z", no offset) via bare datetime.fromisoformat() into a NAIVE datetime.

    ~21s HTTP call on every scan instead of being absorbed by the 15-min TTL.
  (b) _extract_obs_time had the identical gap but failed silently WRONG instead of crashing: a naive
    result hits `.astimezone(tz)` at its only call site (_fetch_daily_temps_f), which Python interprets

    fetch_metar_daily_extreme -> _metar_lock_in's YES-lock and _compute_persistence_prob. Latent in
    production (the live obsTime field is an epoch int, not this string fallback) but on the wrong-trade
    path if ever hit.

    negative cache that every other failure path in the function already had, re-issuing the network
    call on every scan for a station stuck on either failure mode.
  (d) check_metar_lockout's ZoneInfo(city_tz) exception handler fell back to `local_time = obs_time`
    (UTC) -- passing the ">=2pm local" lock-in gate at whatever hour it happened to be in UTC, which for
    a west-of-UTC city could be well before that city's real local 2pm. Never reachable in production
    (all 20 traded cities use real, pinned IANA tz names) but fails open rather than closed on a bad tz.
Resolution (2026-08-24): New shared helper metar._parse_iso_utc() parses an ISO string via
  fromisoformat(), then attaches UTC (`.replace(tzinfo=UTC)`) if the result came back naive -- used at
  all three parse sites (fetch_metar's obsTime-string branch, fetch_metar's reportTime fallback,
  _extract_obs_time's string branch). (c): both failure paths now call `_METAR_CACHE.set(key, None)`
  before returning, matching every sibling failure path. (d): the ZoneInfo exception handler now returns
  NOT_LOCKED with a "fail closed" reason instead of falling through to the UTC-as-local hour check.
  Tests (tests/test_metar.py): test_reportTime_fallback_naive_no_z_does_not_crash (+ a stale-still-
  rejected positive control), test_missing_temp_fields_negative_caches,
  test_implausible_temp_negative_caches, test_extract_obs_time_naive_no_z_string_is_utc_aware (direct

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-36 item 8 (L-10/L-3)] encoding + docstring consistency across the batch-36 files
Priority: LOW
Files: forecast_cache.py, climatology.py, climate_indices.py, acis_precip.py, acis_snow.py,
  tests/test_forecast_cache.py

Problem:
  forecast_cache.py's PersistentForecastCache.load_from_disk() called path.read_text() without
  encoding="utf-8" -- safe_io.atomic_write_json (which dump_to_disk itself uses) always writes UTF-8, so
  a read relying on a different platform default codec could silently mis-decode a non-ASCII station
  identifier or future key. Same gap at climatology.py's two fetch_historical() open() calls plus
  _load_sigma_cache_file(), and acis_precip.py/acis_snow.py's four open(cache) calls, and climate_

  Also: ForecastCache's class docstring claimed "LRU eviction," but _evict_oldest() picks by each entry's
  INSERTION timestamp (set once in set()/set_with_ttl()/set_at()/set_at_with_ttl(), never touched by

Resolution (2026-08-24): encoding="utf-8" added to all `open()`/`read_text()` calls listed above
  (hurricane_climatology.py's two read_text() calls already had it, used as the reference pattern).

  get_with_ts() derive TTL expiry from that same insertion timestamp
  (`time.monotonic() - ts > ttl`) -- updating ts on every read would silently extend a negative-cached (or

  encoding="utf-8" keyword on this dev machine (mutation-tested and confirmed non-discriminating here,
  since this interpreter's platform default already resolves to UTF-8 per PEP 686) but is kept as real
  behavioral coverage for platforms where the default differs. The other encoding= additions are
  mechanical/ASCII-only in every existing test fixture and so aren't independently discriminated by any
  new test -- covered only by the full scoped suite continuing to pass.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-36 item 9 (L-1(nws))] _get_obs abandons timed-out futures
Priority: LOW -- fails closed, but obscures a real failure signal
Files: nws.py (_get_obs), tests/test_nws.py

Problem:
  _get_obs submits to a 4-worker ThreadPoolExecutor and calls .result(timeout=_OBS_WALL_SECS) for a
  reliable wall-clock deadline (Windows SSL can hang past socket-level timeouts). On timeout, the
  submitted future is abandoned -- it keeps running (and occupying a worker) until the underlying request
  itself eventually completes or errors on its own, since ThreadPoolExecutor has no cancellation for
  already-started work. Sustained hangs can permanently consume all 4 workers; every new submission after
  that queues behind them and times out too, but that failure looks identical in the logs to a normal
  single-request timeout -- no distinct signal that the pool itself is the bottleneck.
Resolution (2026-08-24): Added an in-flight counter (_obs_inflight, incremented on submit, decremented via
  future.add_done_callback() once the underlying task ACTUALLY finishes -- independent of whether the
  caller gave up on it at the wall-clock deadline). _get_obs logs a distinct "pool saturated" warning when
  a new submission arrives with the counter already at or above _OBS_POOL_WORKERS. Deliberately minimal
  (per this item's own LOW severity and "at minimum log pool saturation distinctly" framing) -- no per-
  call executor or cancellation added.
  Tests (tests/test_nws.py::TestGetObsPoolSaturation): test_not_saturated_does_not_log,
  test_saturated_logs_distinct_warning (counter manipulated directly for determinism, not real concurrent
  hangs), test_inflight_counter_decrements_after_completion (proves the counter returns to baseline once
  the task finishes, not stuck incremented forever). All 3 mutation-tested.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-37 item 2 (L-14)] _find_optimal_min_edge scored the YES-settlement rate, not a win rate -- inverted for NO-side trades
Priority: Low (fix while touching the file) -- currently harmless per the
  skeptic materiality check in the batch handoff (all 198 real settled
  trades have edge >=0.15, so every threshold in [0.04..0.10] ties and picks
  0.04 regardless of scoring method; also gated off entirely today since the
  real corpus produces 0 folds, see item 1 above) -- but a real bug once
  either condition changes.
Files: backtest.py, tests/test_walk_forward.py

Problem:
  _find_optimal_min_edge scored win rate as
  `sum(1 for t in subset if t.get("settled_yes")) / len(subset)` --
  settled_yes is `outcome == "yes"`, the YES-SETTLEMENT rate, not a win
  rate. paper.py's own convention (get_edge_realization_rate, paper.py:2491)
  is `win = outcome == side` -- 125/198 real settled trades are NO-side, and
  for a NO-side trade, settled_yes=True (outcome=="yes") means a LOSS, not a
  win. run_paper_walk_forward's trade-dict mapping dropped "side" entirely,
  so this metric was structurally inverted for the majority of real trades.

Resolution:
  Added a small _is_win(trade) helper: `outcome == side` when the trade
  carries a "side" key (reconstructing outcome as "yes" if settled_yes else
  "no", a faithful round-trip of how run_paper_walk_forward derived
  settled_yes in the first place), falling back to plain settled_yes when
  side is absent (older callers/test fixtures that predate side-tracking).
  _find_optimal_min_edge now sums _is_win(t) instead of t.get("settled_yes").
  run_paper_walk_forward's trade mapping now carries "side": t.get("side")
  through to the mapped dict.
  Tests: tests/test_walk_forward.py::TestIsWin (3 unit tests) and
  TestFindOptimalMinEdgeSideAware::test_scores_side_aware_win_rate_not_yes_
  settlement_rate -- a constructed scenario where 10 NO-side losses (edge
  0.04, outcome=yes) and 10 YES-side wins (edge 0.05, outcome=yes) make the
  old code pick threshold 0.04 (ties at 100% "win rate" including the
  losses) and the fixed code correctly pick 0.05 (50% vs 100%, excluding
  the lossy NO-side pool). Mutation-tested (reverted _is_win(t) back to
  t.get("settled_yes") via Edit, confirmed the test fails with result=0.04
  instead of 0.05, restored).

  Also investigated param_sweep.py's L-17 (run_sweep sweeps PAPER_MIN_EDGE
  candidates [0.15..0.40] but load_swept_min_edge clamps to [0.03, 0.15] --
  only 0.15 can ever load) per the same batch item, but the fix turned out
  deeper than the handoff scoped -- see the new entry immediately below
  ("PAPER_MIN_EDGE'S ENTIRE SOFT-OVERRIDE SCALE...") rather than a
  same-file one-line patch here. Confirmed with the user (AskUserQuestion)
  to defer rather than ship either narrow direction.

[OPEN -- filed 2026-08-24 by batch-37 item 2 investigation (L-17 turned out deeper than scoped); OWNER ASSIGNED 2026-08-25 to batch-66 item 2 -- see the note at the end of this entry, do NOT pick this up standalone] PAPER_MIN_EDGE's entire soft-override scale (config.py + param_sweep.py + backtest.py's walk-forward thresholds) may be set below net_edge's real operating floor, making the edge gate a near no-op
Priority: Medium -- live paper-trading gate, but currently a no-op in the
  SAFE direction (nothing is being wrongly filtered) rather than the unsafe
  one, so not urgent.
Files (would need to change together, none owned by batch-37): config.py
  (_compute_paper_min_edge_from_files's [0.03, 0.15] walk-forward clamp),
  param_sweep.py (run_sweep's [0.15..0.40] candidates vs
  load_swept_min_edge's [0.03, 0.15] clamp), backtest.py
  (_find_optimal_min_edge's [0.04..0.10] threshold list), order_executor.py
  (read-only reference: the actual live gate).

Problem:
  Measured real data/paper_trades.json: net_edge is ALWAYS >= 0.15 (n=244,
  min=0.1504, max=0.8721, mean=0.4164). order_executor.py:3221-3260
  (_validate_trade_opportunity) sets `edge = opp.get("net_edge")` and gates
  `if edge < min_edge: return False, ...` where min_edge =
  get_paper_min_edge() -- the SAME net_edge field param_sweep.py's own
  docstring already documents as "0.15-0.87 scale." But PAPER_MIN_EDGE's
  entire soft-override chain is capped at 0.15 or below: config.py's
  walk-forward path only accepts optimal_min_edge in [0.03, 0.15];
  backtest.py's own _find_optimal_min_edge only ever searches thresholds in
  [0.04, 0.10]; param_sweep.py's load_swept_min_edge clamps to [0.03, 0.15].
  Since every real net_edge is >= 0.15 and PAPER_MIN_EDGE can never exceed
  0.15, `edge < min_edge` is essentially never true for any real trade --
  this whole edge-check gate is currently a near no-op regardless of which
  narrow, single-file fix gets applied to param_sweep.py's L-17 range
  mismatch (item 2 above investigated this and deliberately did NOT ship
  either direction -- widening load_swept_min_edge's clamp to match
  run_sweep's real [0.15, 0.40] candidates would be internally consistent
  with param_sweep.py alone, but leaves config.py's walk-forward clamp and
  backtest.py's threshold list still on the old, mismatched small scale;
  narrowing run_sweep's candidates to match the small scale instead would
  make param_sweep.py's OWN sweep never discriminate between thresholds
  either, since every real net_edge would then clear every candidate).

What it would look like:
  A holistic pass across all three files (plus verifying order_executor.py's
  other "edge" concept -- get_min_edge_for_confidence's confidence-tiered
  threshold, which fires INSTEAD of PAPER_MIN_EDGE whenever
  opp["ensemble_spread"] is present -- to understand how much of the live
  gate's real filtering already happens through that path instead) rather
  than a piecemeal one-file patch. Needs a real decision on what
  PAPER_MIN_EDGE is semantically supposed to represent (a net_edge-scale
  threshold, matching the field it's actually compared against; or a
  different, currently-unused "raw edge" concept the walk-forward/param-
  sweep search machinery was actually designed around) before touching any
  of the three files' ranges.

Why not now:
  Genuinely spans 3 files, none of which batch-37 owns, and touches a live
  paper-trading gate's real filtering behavior -- widening the range
  unilaterally (in either direction) is a real behavior change, not a
  no-op cleanup, and deserves its own scoped investigation/AskUserQuestion
  rather than being folded into an L-17 "one-line fix" that turned out not
  to be one.

MEASURED 2026-08-25 -- batch-66 item 2 (premise CONFIRMED, not disproven; the
numeric-range fix is still open and is deliberately NOT shipped):
  The entry asked for the real net_edge distribution to be measured before
  assuming the floor binds. Measured, on data/paper_trades.json as of
  2026-08-25 (n=247 all / n=200 settled): min 0.1504, p05 0.1730, p25 0.3161,
  median 0.3873, p95 0.7094, max 0.8721. This reproduces the entry's own
  earlier n=244 measurement exactly and CONFIRMS the premise: 100% of real
  candidates clear 0.15, so no threshold anywhere in the declared range
  rejects anything.
  Checked against every floor the gate can actually apply, not just
  PAPER_MIN_EDGE: utils._EDGE_TIERS is {HIGH: paper 0.05 / live 0.08,
  MODERATE: 0.07 / 0.10, LOW: 0.10 / 0.15} and the untiered fallbacks are
  get_paper_min_edge() (hard-capped at 0.05) and MIN_EDGE (0.15 via .env).
  The highest of those is 0.15, still below the observed minimum of 0.1504 --
  so the net_edge comparison `if edge < min_edge` rejects ZERO of 247 real
  candidates on every path, not merely "near" no-op.

  ROOT CAUSE (this is the part the entry was missing, and it changes what the
  fix should be): the mismatch is not a mis-tuned number, it is a UNIT error.
  net_edge is EV per dollar of COST -- order_executor divides net EV by
  entry_price -- so it is the raw probability edge amplified by 1/entry_price,
  empirically 2-4x larger at this bot's typical 25-50c entries. The whole
  PAPER_MIN_EDGE soft-override family (config.py's [0.03, 0.15] clamp,
  load_swept_min_edge's [0.03, 0.15], backtest.py's [0.04..0.10]) is stated on
  the RAW probability-edge scale and then compared against a net_edge-scale
  field. Rescaling the ranges without naming which scale they are on would
  just move the same confusion.

  CONFIRMED LIVE, not just by reading the code: the soft-override chain is
  active and returns exactly 0.15 -- an untouched process start logs
  "PAPER_MIN_EDGE loaded from param_sweep_results.json: 0.1500". That is the
  arithmetic consequence of finding (1): run_sweep's candidates are
  [0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40] and load_swept_min_edge clamps to
  [0.03, 0.15], so 0.15 is the ONLY candidate that can ever survive the clamp;
  any other winner makes load_swept_min_edge return None and the override
  silently no-ops. utils.get_paper_min_edge() then applies min(0.15, 0.05) and
  the value that actually reaches the gate is 0.05.
  Finding (1) re-verified against current master: config.py:224 [0.03, 0.15],
  param_sweep.py:123 [0.03, 0.15] vs run_sweep's [0.15..0.40] at
  param_sweep.py:167, backtest.py:931 THRESHOLDS [0.04..0.10]. All three still
  disagree. Note backtest._find_optimal_min_edge reads t["edge"] (RAW edge),
  not net_edge, so it is the one of the three already on the scale its own
  range implies -- its thresholds are merely too low to discriminate.

  WHAT DOES BIND: the gate's separate raw-edge check, `abs(raw_edge) <
  MIN_EDGE` (order_executor.py:3742 in current master, not the :3317 the batch
  file cites -- line drift). MIN_EDGE is 0.15 from .env, and raw edge on
  settled predictions has p10 = 0.1554, so that check is where the real
  filtering happens. Any future rescale must account for it or it will
  double-count.

  NOT SHIPPED, deliberately: changing any of the three ranges alters which
  trades are permitted, and the entry's own "Why not now" reasoning still
  holds -- it needs a decision on what PAPER_MIN_EDGE semantically represents
  (net_edge-scale or raw-edge-scale) before any file changes. Batch-66 item 2
  shipped only the measurement above plus display-only machinery:
  utils.required_gross_edge()/kalshi_fee_rate_at() (which express the floor as
  a function of contract price and show that the price-dependence comes from
  net_edge dividing by cost, NOT from the fee) and a correctness fix to
  order_executor._clears_taker_fee. Entry stays OPEN for the rescale decision.

  data/temperature_scale.json (main-clone commit 1faf7b58, same commit as
  item 3's METAR git-tracking, pushed to origin). apply_temperature_scaling
  now falls through to the real GLOBAL T (4.601267428939456 as of this
  writing) for below-condition predictions instead of the T=1.0 no-op --
  imperfect (not condition-specific) but a real, non-trivial calibration
  correction instead of none, and takes effect immediately (no code change
  needed, config._blend_weights-style fallback chain already exists in
  apply_temperature_scaling for exactly this case).

  Root cause (below-condition raw probabilities showing directional bias
  strong enough to repeatedly hit _fit_T's T-upper-bound) is NOT fixed here
  -- filed as its own follow-up below, since a correct fix needs
  understanding WHY below is directionally biased (a model issue, not a
  data-volume one), not just re-triggering the fit.

[OPEN -- filed 2026-08-24 by batch-37 item 4's investigation] "below" condition-type predictions show directional bias strong enough to repeatedly hit ml_bias._fit_T's T-upper-bound, blocking any T-scaling refit
Priority: Low-Medium -- below-condition predictions currently get the
  GLOBAL T as an imperfect substitute (see the resolved entry immediately
  above), not zero calibration, so this is a quality gap, not a total gap.
Files: ml_bias.py (train_all_temperature_scaling, _fit_T) -- investigation
  only, no code change proposed yet.

Problem:
  ml_bias._fit_T's NLL-minimization (minimize_scalar, bounds=(0.5, 8.0))
  has hit the 8.0 upper bound on the "below" condition-type pool on every
  weekly retrain since at least 2026-06-27 (see the resolved entry above for
  the full trace), despite the pool growing from presumably near-zero to 33
  real settled rows over that period. Per _fit_T's own docstring, hitting
  the upper bound means the mean predicted probability and mean actual
  outcome disagree in DIRECTION, not just confidence -- T-scaling (a single
  monotonic squash toward 0.5) structurally cannot fix directional bias, so
  no amount of additional "below" data will make this refit succeed as-is.

What it would look like:
  Needs someone to actually pull the below-condition prediction/outcome
  pairs and look at the mean_pred vs mean_actual _fit_T's own warning log
  already computes (train_all_temperature_scaling: %s T=%.4f hit upper
  bound... mean_pred=%.4f mean_actual=%.4f) to characterize the bias's
  direction and magnitude, then decide whether it's a real model issue in
  the below-condition ensemble/blend path (worth fixing upstream) or a
  data-quality issue (e.g. a systematic mislabeling of below outcomes) --
  out of scope for a data-file fix.

Why not now: Needs its own investigation session; the immediate live gap
  (zero calibration on "below") is already mitigated by the resolved entry
  above's global-T fallback.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-33 item 1 (M-1)] batch-24's two fixes defeat each other -- halt-transition edge consumed on delivery failure
Priority: MEDIUM (skeptic-corrected scope -- see below)
Files: alerts.py, notify.py, cron.py, order_executor.py, tests/test_batch33_reliability.py, tests/test_cron_integration.py

Problem:
  check_halt_transition() persists state[halt_type]=active and returns the false->true edge BEFORE any
  delivery is attempted; send_system_alert()'s own rollback (_system_cooldown_rollback) restores only its
  OWN cooldown state in a different file/module, never check_halt_transition's flag. A total delivery
  failure at the instant a halt engages permanently eats that engagement's alert -- the next cycle's
  observation sees was_active=True and never reports a fresh edge again, silently defeating batch-24's own
  stated rollback intent. Skeptic scope corrections (kept from the handoff): drawdown/daily_loss have a
  redundant second observer (cron tracks "{type}_paper", order_executor tracks the unsuffixed name --
  same cooldown_key means a same-cycle second attempt), only "anomaly" is single-observer, and this
  deployment currently has zero push channels configured (only the plyer toast can succeed) -- so today's
  real impact is "drops the one toast retry," not a full alert loss. Still worth fixing before a webhook
  is ever configured.
Resolution (2026-08-24):
  Chose the "give send_system_alert a success return" option over "defer the persist until after
  delivery" -- the deferred-commit shape would have required reworking check_halt_transition's existing,
  already-tested write contract; a plain bool return + a new rollback function is a smaller, additive
  change that mirrors notify.py's own established _system_cooldown_reserve/_system_cooldown_rollback
  pattern (project convention favors reusing an existing pattern over inventing a new one). Not put through
  AskUserQuestion -- the existing-convention argument was strong enough to not be a genuine toss-up.
  send_system_alert() now returns bool: True when delivered on >=1 channel OR when the cooldown suppressed
  the attempt entirely (nothing left undelivered by THIS call); False only when delivery was actually
  attempted and every channel failed. New alerts.rollback_halt_transition(halt_type) sets
  state[halt_type]=False (best-effort, skips the write on an unreadable state file -- same "don't clobber
  other keys" reasoning check_halt_transition's own read-failure branch already uses) so the NEXT
  observation reports a fresh edge again. Wired into all 6 halt-alert call sites: cron.py's anomaly halt
  (both the normal and run_anomaly_check-failed paths) and its daily-loss/drawdown pre-cycle observer
  (rolling back the "{type}_paper" flag specifically, not the unsuffixed one order_executor.py owns), plus
  order_executor.py's own cycle-level drawdown/daily-loss checks and its mid-cycle drawdown-breach check.
  Tests: alerts.py unit tests (rollback resets the flag and the next check reports a fresh edge; rollback
  doesn't clobber a different halt_type's own flag; rollback is a silent no-op on an unreadable state
  file), notify.py unit tests for send_system_alert's 3 return-value cases (success / total failure /
  cooldown-suppressed), and 2 new cron_integration tests (2 cycles of total delivery failure retry the
  alert both times; a positive control confirms a successfully-delivered alert does NOT re-fire on the
  next cycle). All mutation-tested (Edit-revert-confirm-restore), including the cron.py wiring itself.

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-33 item 2 (M-3)] _release_cron_lock fails open to unlink() in exactly the case batch-30's check protects against
Priority: MEDIUM
Files: cron.py, tests/test_cron_lock.py, tests/test_execution_stability.py

Problem:
  The release-side ownership check read `owner_pid = json.loads(lp.read_text()).get("pid")`, defaulting
  owner_pid=None on ANY exception (torn/empty/PermissionError read, or an old plain-integer-PID-format
  lock, which parses as a bare JSON int with no .get method). The guard `owner_pid is not None and
  owner_pid != os.getpid()` then treated None as "nothing to protect" and fell through to
  lp.unlink(missing_ok=True) -- deleting a possibly-FRESH lock a different process just wrote, the exact
  H2 scenario this whole ownership check exists to prevent. cmd_watch --auto --live also acquires/releases
  this same lock each cycle, not just cmd_cron.
Resolution (2026-08-24):
  Split the read failure into FileNotFoundError (already gone -- nothing to release, safe early return)
  and any other exception (torn read, PermissionError, legacy int-format lock -- fail closed, skip the
  unlink, log a warning, return). Simplified the ownership comparison to a plain `owner_pid !=
  os.getpid()` now that every read-failure path returns before reaching it, so a missing "pid" key on
  otherwise-valid JSON and an unreadable file both correctly skip the unlink via the same comparison. An
  unreadable/unverifiable lock left behind by release isn't stuck forever -- _acquire_cron_lock's own
  existing self-heal (`except: lp.unlink(); return False`) cleans it up on the very next acquire attempt.
  Two pre-existing tests asserted the OLD (unsafe) behavior as correct -- test_cron_lock.py's
  test_deletes_a_corrupt_unreadable_lock and test_execution_stability.py's test_release_lock_removes_file
  (the latter used the legacy bare-int format as its fixture) -- both rewritten to assert the new fail-
  closed behavior, with the old test's own docstring reasoning ("has no readable pid to protect -- must
  still be deleted") called out as exactly the wrong reasoning this fix corrects. Added
  test_skips_unlink_when_pid_field_is_missing (valid JSON, no pid key -- same skip, different code path)
  and test_release_skips_unowned_legacy_format_lock (positive-control pairing for the legacy-format case)
  as siblings. All 4 tests mutation-tested against the real fix (reverted to the old owner_pid-is-not-None
  guard, confirmed both rewritten tests fail, restored).

Problem:
  The cmd_cron finally block's last_full_scan write keyed off the `sameday_only` ARGUMENT only, ignoring

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-33 item 5 (M-21)] cloud_backup.backup_data's all_readable return discarded at its only caller, plus two same-file LOWs
Priority: MEDIUM (main finding) + 2 LOW

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-33 item 6 (M-28)] Discord webhook URLs (bearer credentials) logged at WARNING
Priority: MEDIUM
Files: notify.py, tests/test_batch33_reliability.py

Problem:
  _send_discord's exception handler logged `"request to %s failed: %s", url, exc` -- a Discord webhook
  URL's path IS its bearer token (/api/webhooks/{id}/{token}), and batch-24 rerouted every safety alert
  through this function while making failures retry every cycle, so an outage accumulates the full secret
  URL repeatedly in bot.log. No redaction helper existed in the repo. The exception object itself is a
  second leak vector the handoff's own citation didn't call out: `requests`' own exception text (e.g.
  ConnectionError) commonly embeds the full request url, including the token, in its str() representation
  -- redacting only the explicit `url` argument would have left the token reachable via `exc`.
Resolution (2026-08-24):
  New notify._redact_webhook_url(url) keeps only scheme + host + a short id-segment prefix
  ("https://discord.com/.../12345678***"). Applied to both the explicit url AND to the exception's own
  string representation (via a literal substring replace of the raw url with its redacted form) before
  either reaches the log call, closing both leak vectors in one fix. Latent today (no webhook configured
  in this deployment) -- fixed ahead of one ever being set.
  Tests: unit test on _redact_webhook_url's output shape, plus an integration-style test simulating a
  requests.ConnectionError whose message embeds the full url (a realistic mock of the real leak vector)
  and asserting the raw bearer token never appears in the captured log output. Mutation-tested (reverting
  to the raw `url, exc` log call made the token-in-log assertion fail as expected).

[RESOLVED 2026-08-24 -- batch-33 item 8 (L-5/L-6)] cron-lock bookkeeping honesty: dead heartbeat field, epoch-default started_at, non-atomic write, naive local dates
Priority: LOW
Files: cron.py, tests/test_cron_lock.py, tests/test_execution_stability.py, tests/test_batch33_reliability.py

Problem:
  (a) The lock's "heartbeat" field was written once at acquire time and never refreshed again, so the
  no-psutil fallback's age check ("lock age") was really reading a second, redundant copy of started_at
  while calling it heartbeat age -- misleading, not a real liveness signal. (b) started_at (and the old
  heartbeat) defaulted to 0 on a missing key, so a valid-JSON lock missing that field computed an age of

  process wrote moments ago; backwards from this function's fail-closed intent. (c) `lp.write_text(json.
  dumps(lock_data))` was the one non-atomic write left on the cron-lock path. (d) _check_prod_reminder's 3
  date.today() calls were the file's only remaining naive-local-time sites.
Resolution (2026-08-24):

  cmd_cron_body() invocation (i.e. once per lock hold), which wouldn't distinguish "still working" from
  "hung" WITHIN a single hold -- the actual gap a real heartbeat would need to close -- so genuine refresh
  would need a background thread with no natural checkpoint to hook into, disproportionate for a LOW item.
  Both the acquire-side no-psutil fallback and _is_cron_running's mirrored branch now read started_at
  directly; confirmed via the existing test suite that no test ever set heartbeat and started_at to
  DIFFERENT values (the two were always redundant copies in every existing fixture), so this is a pure
  simplification, not a behavior change for the age-check logic itself. (b) started_at now defaults to
  _time.time() (fresh) instead of 0 (the epoch) at both call sites. (c) routed through safe_io.
  atomic_write_json(..., emergency_copy=False) -- same emergency_copy=False reasoning as alerts.
  check_halt_transition's own small, trivially-reconstructible state file. (d) all 3 date.today() calls
  replaced with a single utc_today() call, matching this file's own established convention elsewhere
  (e.g. the Monday-sweep check).
  Tests: (a) test_lock_file_contains_pid_and_timestamps updated to assert "heartbeat" NOT in the written
  lock (was asserting it WAS present); the sibling test_execution_stability.py assertion updated the same
  way. (b) 2 new unit tests (_acquire_cron_lock and _is_cron_running each treat a missing started_at as
  fresh, not ancient) mutation-tested by reverting the default back to 0 -- both failed as expected. (c)/(d)
  covered by the existing broader cron-lock/prod-reminder test coverage continuing to pass unchanged (no
  behavior change to assert on beyond "still works"). Full existing test_cron_lock.py/test_execution_
